area: Long-term memory for LLM agents (2015–2026): write/read/forget architectures, from OS-style virtual context and memory streams to agentic note graphs, temporal knowledge graphs, hippocampus-inspired PPR retrieval, surprise-segmented episodic KV memory, and parametric episodic memory control — surveyed with an eye to what can be rebuilt as a fully local memory store on a macOS laptop.

papers.title: MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
papers.venue_or_id: arXiv:2310.08560 (preprint; basis of the Letta open-source framework)
papers.core_idea: Virtual context management borrowed from OS hierarchical memory. Two tiers: main context (system instructions + editable 'working/core' context + FIFO message queue) and external context (recall storage = full searchable conversation history; archival storage = arbitrary agent-written documents). The LLM itself issues function calls (core_memory_append/replace, conversation_search, archival_memory_insert/search) to page data in and out; 'memory pressure' warnings at ~70% context utilization trigger recursive summarization and eviction of the FIFO queue. Interrupts/yields manage control flow between agent and user.
papers.relevance: The canonical self-editing-memory agent pattern. WRITE = LLM tool calls; READ = LLM tool calls; FORGET = FIFO eviction + recursive summarization. Reported 93.4% DMR accuracy with gpt-4-turbo vs 35.3% for a recursive-summarization baseline on the MSC-derived Deep Memory Retrieval task, and it can analyze documents far beyond the base context window. Directly reimplementable locally.

papers.title: Sleep-time Compute: Beyond Inference Scaling at Test-time
papers.venue_or_id: arXiv:2504.13171 (Letta / UC Berkeley Sky Computing Lab)
papers.core_idea: Move memory work off the critical path: while idle, the agent 'thinks' offline over accumulated context, anticipating likely queries and precomputing derived facts, then rewrites its memory state. Test-time then reads a pre-digested state instead of re-deriving it.
papers.relevance: The consolidation half of a memory system, formalized. Reported ~5x reduction in test-time compute for equal accuracy on Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME, and up to 13% higher accuracy. This is the mechanism to use for background consolidation in a local store (cron job during laptop idle).

papers.title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
papers.core_idea: An append-only natural-language 'memory stream' of timestamped observations. Retrieval scores each record as a sum of three min-max-normalized components — recency (exponential decay, factor 0.995 per sandbox hour since last access), importance (LLM 'poignancy' rating, ~1–10 scale), relevance (embedding cosine similarity to the query) — with equal weights in the released implementation. Reflections are higher-level LLM-synthesized assertions written back into the stream (forming a reflection tree) when accumulated importance of recent observations crosses a threshold; plans are also written into the stream and recursively decomposed.
papers.relevance: The most-copied read-path scoring function in the field, and the origin of write-back reflection as consolidation. Ablation shows observation, planning, and reflection each contribute critically to believability. Note: there is no true forgetting — the stream only grows, which is precisely the failure mode later systems attack.

papers.title: A-Mem / A-MEM: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents
papers.core_idea: Zettelkasten-style atomic notes. On write, the LLM generates a structured note (verbatim content + contextual description + keywords + tags + embedding), then analyzes the k nearest historical notes and autonomously decides which links to create. 'Memory evolution': integrating a new note can trigger LLM rewrites of the contextual descriptions/tags of the linked older notes, so the network continuously re-interprets its own past.
papers.relevance: The clearest example of an agent-controlled (not rule-controlled) write path with retroactive consolidation — closest computational analogue to reconsolidation. Abstract claims superior results over SOTA baselines across six foundation models. Secondary write-ups report LOCOMO multi-hop ROUGE-L 44.27 vs 18.09 for the LOCOMO baseline with GPT-4o-mini and 85–93% fewer tokens per memory operation — UNVERIFIED against the paper itself; note Mem0's own paper reports A-Mem far lower (multi-hop 18.85), so cross-paper numbers conflict.

papers.title: Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory
papers.core_idea: Two-phase pipeline. (1) Extraction: prompt built from a rolling conversation summary + last m=10 messages + the new exchange; an LLM emits candidate salient facts. (2) Update: for each candidate, fetch top s=10 similar existing memories by vector similarity and have the LLM choose via tool call among ADD / UPDATE / DELETE / NOOP. Summary regeneration runs asynchronously. Mem0^g variant stores a directed labeled graph (entities as nodes, typed relations as edges, Neo4j), with an entity extractor + relationship generator, similarity-threshold node reuse, and conflict detection that marks contradicted edges obsolete rather than deleting them; retrieval combines entity-centric traversal with semantic triplet matching.
papers.relevance: The best-specified explicit reconciliation write path in the literature — DELETE/obsolescence is a first-class LLM decision, not a decay heuristic. Reported 26% relative improvement in LLM-as-a-Judge over OpenAI's memory on LOCOMO, 91% lower p95 latency and >90% token savings versus full-context. Graph variant ~2% higher overall, notably on temporal and open-domain questions, at ~2x latency.

papers.title: Zep: A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory
papers.core_idea: Three hierarchical subgraphs — episode subgraph (raw messages/JSON/text, non-lossy), semantic entity subgraph (extracted entities and fact edges, with entity resolution/deduplication against existing nodes), community subgraph (label-propagation clusters with LLM-generated community summaries, incrementally maintained). Bi-temporal model: every edge carries both a transaction timeline (when the system learned it) and a validity timeline (t_valid / t_invalid). On ingestion an LLM checks new facts against semantically related existing edges and invalidates contradicted ones by setting t_invalid rather than deleting them.
papers.relevance: The reference design for temporal reasoning and knowledge updates — the two categories where flat vector memory collapses. Reported 94.8% vs MemGPT's 93.4% on Deep Memory Retrieval, and up to 18.5% accuracy improvement with ~90% latency reduction on LongMemEval. Retrieval is a hybrid: cosine similarity + Okapi BM25 full-text + breadth-first depth-2 graph traversal, fused/reranked (RRF, MMR, node distance, episode mentions, cross-encoder).

papers.title: Human-inspired Episodic Memory for Infinite Context LLMs (EM-LLM)
papers.core_idea: Segment the KV cache itself into episodes online. Boundary detection uses Bayesian surprise (negative log-likelihood of the next token under the model — a spike means the model did not predict it), then a graph-theoretic refinement step adjusts boundaries to maximize modularity / minimize conductance of the token-similarity adjacency matrix, producing internally coherent, externally distinct events. Retrieval is two-stage: k-NN similarity search over event representative keys fills a similarity buffer, plus a contiguity buffer holding temporally adjacent events — mirroring the human temporal-contiguity effect in free recall. No fine-tuning required.
papers.relevance: The only system here that operates below the text layer, on attention KV states, so it needs open-weights local inference — which is exactly what a laptop-hosted agent has. Reported 4.3% overall relative improvement over InfLLM on LongBench with a 33% gain on PassageRetrieval; beats RAG at similar resource cost; surpasses full-context models on most tasks; demonstrated retrieval over 10M tokens. Segmentation correlates with human-annotated event boundaries.

papers.title: HippoRAG: Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for Large Language Models
papers.core_idea: Hippocampal indexing theory made concrete. Offline (write): an LLM runs OpenIE over each passage to produce triples, which are merged into a schemaless open knowledge graph ('hippocampal index'); a retrieval encoder adds synonymy edges between near-duplicate phrase nodes. Online (read): extract named entities from the query, link them to graph nodes as seeds, run Personalized PageRank over the KG to spread activation, weight seeds by node specificity (an IDF-like measure), then score passages by the PPR mass of the phrases they contain.
papers.relevance: Single-step multi-hop retrieval — the pattern-completion step happens in the graph, not in iterative LLM calls. Reported up to 20% improvement over SOTA retrieval on multi-hop QA, matching or beating iterative retrieval (IRCoT) while being 10–30x cheaper and 6–13x faster; combining the two gives further gains. Fully local-capable: NetworkX PPR over a few hundred thousand nodes is trivial on a laptop.

papers.title: From RAG to Memory: Non-Parametric Continual Learning for Large Language Models (HippoRAG 2)
papers.core_idea: Fixes HippoRAG 1's brittleness. Passages become first-class nodes in the KG connected to their triples by 'context edges' (deeper passage integration); retrieval switches from query→NER→node seeding to direct query→triple embedding retrieval; an LLM 'recognition memory' filter discards triples that are not genuinely relevant before seeding; PPR is seeded from the surviving triples and passage scores are combined with dense-retriever scores.
papers.relevance: The current strongest neurobiologically-motivated memory retriever and the right starting point over HippoRAG 1. Reported 7% improvement in associative-memory (multi-hop) tasks over the SOTA embedding model, while also being better than standard RAG on factual memory and sense-making — i.e., it stops the graph from hurting on the easy single-hop cases, which was HippoRAG 1's weakness.

papers.title: Larimar: Large Language Models with Episodic Memory Control
papers.core_idea: A distributed episodic memory matrix M (K rows x C columns; e.g. K=512, C=768) sitting between a BERT-style encoder and a GPT-2/GPT-J decoder, built on Generative Pseudo-inverse Memory / Kanerva Machine ideas. WRITE: encode the episode, solve a least-squares/pseudo-inverse problem for addressing weights and update M in one shot (Bayesian posterior update reduced to a matrix computation); a running covariance term supports 1000+ sequential edits. READ: encode the query, compute reading weights, and broadcast the memory readout as a KV-cache-like conditioning signal across decoder layers. FORGET: re-run the same update with alpha = -1 to subtract a previously written encoding. A scope detector (external MiniLM-1NN, ~2.9% EER, or an internal classifier) decides whether memory should be consulted at all.
papers.relevance: The only entry that makes forgetting an exact algebraic inverse of writing rather than a heuristic decay — and the only parametric-adjacent memory here. Reported 4–10x speed-ups over gradient-based editors (e.g. GPT-2 editing 4.8s -> 1.1s), edit-retention 0.97–0.98 over 1000 sequential ZsRE edits vs 0.93 for GRACE at ~10x the speed, 99.6–100% CounterFact edit success, and information-leakage attack success cut from 49.3% (MEMIT) to 17.6% by writing censored responses.

papers.title: Needle in the Haystack for Memory Based Large Language Models
papers.core_idea: Stress-tests Larimar's external associative memory on passkey and needle-in-a-haystack recall, showing the memory can be written and read at test time to handle contexts far longer than those seen in training, including a recursive memory-search procedure.
papers.relevance: Confirms that Larimar's memory generalizes past its training context length — the practical question for anyone considering a parametric episodic memory in a long-lived local agent.

papers.title: MemoryBank: Enhancing Large Language Models with Long-Term Memory
papers.core_idea: Three stores: raw dialogue records, LLM-generated daily/event summaries, and a continuously updated user personality portrait. Retrieval is dense (FAISS-style) over the summarized events. Forgetting is an explicit Ebbinghaus forgetting-curve model: memory strength S increases each time an item is recalled and retention decays as exp(-t/S), so unreinforced memories probabilistically drop out while frequently retrieved ones consolidate.
papers.relevance: The first agent memory system to make principled forgetting a design goal rather than an afterthought, and the origin of the recall-reinforces-retention rule now reused everywhere. Instantiated as the SiliconFriend companion chatbot; evaluated qualitatively on real user dialogs and quantitatively on ChatGPT-simulated multi-persona long-term dialogs. Works with both closed (ChatGPT) and open (ChatGLM) models.

papers.title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
papers.core_idea: Verbal RL. After a failed trial, an evaluator produces a feedback signal (scalar or free-form, external or self-simulated), a self-reflection LLM converts it into natural-language 'what went wrong and what to do differently', and that text is appended to an episodic memory buffer (a sliding window, typically the last 1–3 reflections) that is prepended to the next attempt. No weight updates.
papers.relevance: Establishes episodic memory as a policy-improvement channel — memory as gradient substitute. Reported 91% pass@1 on HumanEval versus 80% for the previous GPT-4 SOTA, with gains also on sequential decision-making (AlfWorld) and language reasoning (HotPotQA). The bounded buffer is a deliberate forgetting policy, and its narrowness is the main limitation later work (cross-task skill libraries) attacks.

papers.title: Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
papers.core_idea: Procedural memory as an ever-growing library of executable JavaScript skills. WRITE: a skill is only committed after self-verification confirms the program achieved the task; the code is stored keyed by the embedding of an LLM-generated description of what it does. READ: embed the current sub-goal (plus environment feedback) and retrieve the top-k nearest skill programs to compose into the next program. Skills are temporally extended, interpretable, and compositional, so complex skills call simpler ones.
papers.relevance: The canonical procedural/skill memory design, and the cleanest quality gate on the write path in the literature — nothing enters memory unless it verifiably worked. Reported 3.3x more unique items, 2.3x longer traversal, and up to 15.3x faster tech-tree milestone unlocking versus prior SOTA, plus zero-shot transfer of the skill library to a fresh world. Code-as-memory 'alleviates catastrophic forgetting' because skills are immutable, append-only artifacts.

papers.title: Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)
papers.core_idea: A framework mapping language agents onto the classical cognitive-architecture vocabulary: modular memory (working, episodic, semantic, procedural), a structured action space split into internal actions (retrieval, reasoning, learning/writing to memory) and external actions (grounding), and a generalized decision-making loop that proposes, evaluates, and selects actions.
papers.relevance: The organizing schema for this whole survey — it is what lets you say Reflexion is episodic, Voyager is procedural, HippoRAG is semantic, MemGPT is working-memory management. Use its four-way memory split as the top-level schema of any local store; it makes the write/read/forget policy per memory type explicit rather than accidental.

papers.title: Synergistic Integration of Large Language Models and Cognitive Architectures for Robust AI: An Exploratory Analysis
papers.core_idea: Three integration patterns between LLMs and classical cognitive architectures (Soar, ACT-R, Sigma / the Common Model of Cognition): a modular approach (LLM as a component called by the architecture, with chain-of-thought as simulated cognition), an agency approach (LLM and CA as separate agents), and a neuro-symbolic approach.
papers.relevance: The clearest statement of the design space when combining an LLM with a Soar/ACT-R-style memory system — specifically whether the symbolic declarative/procedural memory drives the LLM or vice versa.

papers.title: Bootstrapping Cognitive Agents with a Large Language Model
papers.core_idea: Use the LLM's noisy world knowledge to instantiate a cognitive architecture's knowledge base (which is normally hand-authored at enormous cost), then let the interpretable cognitive model refine and correct it through embodied kitchen-task experience.
papers.relevance: Answers the standing objection to Soar/ACT-R for LLM agents — the knowledge-engineering bottleneck. Reports better efficiency than a purely LLM-based agent.

papers.title: Cognitive LLMs: Towards Integrating Cognitive Architectures and Large Language Models for Manufacturing Decision-making
papers.core_idea: Injects ACT-R-derived decision-making structure into LLMs for production settings, transferring the architecture's constrained, human-like reasoning process into the model's inference.
papers.relevance: Evidence that cognitive-architecture priors improve reliability in a deployed decision domain, not just in simulation — the practical case for the ACT-R side of the literature.

papers.title: NL2GenSym: Natural Language to Generative Symbolic Rules for SOAR Cognitive Architecture via Large Language Models
papers.core_idea: LLMs generate Soar production rules from natural language, with an execution-grounded refinement loop validating them against the Soar engine; explicitly targets the gap that prior LLM+Soar work was conceptual and lacked experimental validation.
papers.relevance: The procedural-memory analogue of Voyager but in a symbolic architecture: LLM writes the rule, the engine verifies it before it enters long-term procedural memory.

papers.title: CogRec: A Cognitive Recommender Agent Fusing Large Language Models and Soar for Explainable Recommendation
papers.core_idea: Pairs an LLM's preference understanding with Soar's structured, interpretable reasoning and online chunking-style learning to address black-box behavior, hallucination, and limited online learning in recommender agents.
papers.relevance: A recent, concrete Soar+LLM system showing the argument has moved from position papers to implementations.

papers.title: Evaluating Very Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents (LOCOMO)
papers.core_idea: A benchmark of very long conversations (avg ~600 turns / ~16K tokens over up to 32 sessions, persona- and temporal-event-graph-grounded), with QA, event summarization, and multimodal dialogue tasks; question categories include single-hop, multi-hop, temporal, open-domain and an adversarial category.
papers.relevance: The de-facto evaluation for conversational agent memory (Mem0, A-Mem, Zep, LangMem all report on it) — and, as of 2026, the epicenter of a reproducibility dispute. Its own finding still stands: long-context LLMs and RAG both remain substantially below human performance on long-range temporal and causal dynamics.

papers.title: LongMemEval: Benchmarking Chat Assistants on Long-Term Interactive Memory
papers.core_idea: 500 curated questions over freely scalable user-assistant histories, targeting five distinct abilities: information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention.
papers.relevance: Better-factored than LOCOMO because it separates knowledge updating and abstention (knowing you don't know) from plain retrieval — the two axes where naive vector memory fails silently. Zep's headline gains are reported here.

papers.title: A Survey on the Memory Mechanism of Large Language Model based Agents
papers.core_idea: First systematic review of agent memory: why memory is needed, how it is designed (sources, forms, operations), how it is evaluated, and application-level uses.
papers.relevance: Baseline survey for the 2023–2024 slice of this literature.

papers.title: Rethinking Memory in LLM based Agents: Representations, Operations, and Emerging Topics
papers.core_idea: Splits memory into parametric (in weights) vs contextual (external, structured/unstructured) and defines six atomic operations: Consolidation, Updating, Indexing, Forgetting, Retrieval, Condensation — then maps existing systems onto that grid, surfacing four research themes (long-term, long-context, parametric modification, multi-source memory).
papers.relevance: The most useful taxonomy for engineering: it gives you exactly the six knobs a local memory store must implement, and shows most published systems implement only three or four of them.

papers.title: Memory OS of AI Agent (MemoryOS)
papers.core_idea: An OS-inspired hierarchical memory manager with four modules — Memory Storage, Updating, Retrieval, Generation — over short-term / mid-term / long-persona tiers, with page-replacement-style promotion and eviction between them.
papers.relevance: The current maturation of the MemGPT idea: explicit OS paging semantics (segmented pages, heat-based promotion) instead of ad-hoc summarization.

papers.title: On the Structural Memory of LLM Agents
papers.core_idea: Controlled comparison of four memory structures — chunks, knowledge triples, atomic facts, summaries — plus mixed structures, and of retrieval methods, across QA and dialogue tasks.
papers.relevance: Rare ablation-level evidence on the representation choice itself. Read this before deciding whether your local store keeps chunks, triples, or atomic facts; the answer is task-dependent and mixed structures often win.

papers.title: Echo: A Large Language Model with Temporal Episodic Memory
papers.core_idea: Trains episodic-memory competence into the model itself via a multi-agent data-generation framework producing multi-session dialogues with temporal structure, rather than bolting on an external store.
papers.relevance: The parametric counterpoint to every external-store system here: some episodic ability can be trained in, which changes the cost calculus for a local deployment where you control the weights.

papers.title: Memory in Large Language Models: Mechanisms, Evaluation and Evolution
papers.core_idea: Operational definition of LLM memory as persistent state written during pretraining/finetuning/inference that is later addressable; four-part taxonomy (parametric, contextual, external, procedural/episodic) plus a memory quadruple (location, persistence, write/access path, controllability) and a three-setting evaluation protocol to prevent apples-to-oranges comparisons.
papers.relevance: The write -> read -> inhibit/update chain it proposes is the right skeleton for specifying a memory system, and its protocol critique explains why published numbers disagree so much.

papers.title: Graph-based Agent Memory: Taxonomy, Techniques, and Applications
papers.core_idea: Survey of graph-structured agent memory specifically — relational dependency modeling, hierarchical organization, and efficient retrieval — consolidating the HippoRAG / Zep / Mem0^g / A-Mem line.
papers.relevance: Current map of the graph-memory design space if you decide the local store should be a graph rather than a flat vector index.

papers.title: Memory for Autonomous LLM Agents: Mechanisms, Evaluation, and Emerging Frontiers
papers.core_idea: Formalizes agent memory as a write–manage–read loop and reviews designs, implementations, and evaluations from 2022 through early 2026.
papers.relevance: The most current end-to-end survey covering the full window requested, and it uses exactly the write/manage/read decomposition this survey is organized around.

papers.title: Exploring Cross-Scenario Generality of Agentic Memory Systems: Diagnostics and a Strong Baseline
papers.core_idea: Re-evaluates eight published memory systems across five scenarios (single-turn QA, multi-session chat, agentic-trajectory QA, memory stress tests, long-horizon agentic tasks) and finds most are tuned to one scenario; introduces an agentic harness that self-manages flat text files as a strong baseline.
papers.relevance: The most important negative result in this survey: a plain self-managed flat-file memory driven by a competent agent is competitive with elaborate graph/vector architectures across heterogeneous trajectories. Build the simple thing first and make the sophisticated system beat it on your own workload.

papers.title: D-MEM: Dopamine-Gated Agentic Memory via Reward Prediction Error Routing
papers.core_idea: Notes that append-and-evolve systems like A-MEM incur O(N^2) write latency and heavy token cost, and routes writes by a Critic Router scoring Surprise and Utility (reward prediction error): low-RPE inputs bypass or land in an O(1) fast buffer, high-RPE inputs (contradictions, novelty) trigger slow cognitive restructuring.
papers.relevance: Direct evidence of the main scaling flaw in agentic-note memory, plus a concrete fix — gate the expensive write path on a cheap surprise/utility signal. Highly relevant if you plan to run A-MEM-style memory locally where every LLM write call is expensive.

papers.title: Oblivion: Self-Adaptive Agentic Memory Control through Decay-Driven Activation
papers.core_idea: Casts forgetting as decay-driven reduction in accessibility rather than deletion, and decouples read from write: the read path decides whether to consult memory at all, based on agent uncertainty and buffer state.
papers.relevance: Modernizes MemoryBank's Ebbinghaus idea with an ACT-R-style activation view and adds the frequently-missing 'should I retrieve at all?' gate (compare Larimar's scope detector). Both gates matter more locally, where every retrieval costs latency.

papers.title: TERAG: Token-Efficient Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.core_idea: Builds a HippoRAG-style graph with Personalized PageRank retrieval but at drastically lower LLM token cost during graph construction, reporting at least 80% of the accuracy of stronger baselines at a fraction of the indexing spend.
papers.relevance: The indexing cost of LLM-based OpenIE is the single biggest practical barrier to running HippoRAG-style memory locally over a large personal corpus; this is the mitigation.

methods.name: OS-style tiered virtual context (MemGPT / Letta / MemoryOS)
methods.mechanism: WRITE: the LLM issues explicit tool calls to edit a small in-context core/working block and to insert into out-of-context archival storage; all raw turns are also appended verbatim to recall storage. READ: tool calls (conversation_search over recall, archival_memory_search over a vector index) pull pages back into the context window. FORGET/CONSOLIDATE: a memory-pressure trigger at high context utilization evicts the FIFO queue and replaces it with a recursive summary; MemoryOS adds heat-based promotion/eviction between short/mid/long-persona tiers. GAINS: 93.4% DMR (gpt-4-turbo) vs 35.3% recursive-summarization baseline; unbounded document analysis.
methods.strengths: Model-agnostic; no training; the agent's own reasoning decides what is worth remembering, so it degrades gracefully on unanticipated data; excellent interpretability (memory is human-readable text you can inspect and hand-edit); Letta ships a production implementation.
methods.weaknesses: Every write and every read is an extra LLM call, so latency and token cost scale with memory activity; weak models make bad paging decisions and the whole system inherits them; recursive summarization is lossy and irreversible; no principled forgetting beyond eviction; nothing prevents a slowly growing archive of near-duplicate facts.
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local. Letta runs self-hosted against Ollama/llama.cpp/LM Studio endpoints; storage is Postgres or SQLite. The only real constraint is that a 7–14B local model is noticeably worse than GPT-4-class at deciding when to page. Recommended as the top-level control loop for a macOS agent.

methods.name: Memory stream with recency/importance/relevance scoring (Generative Agents)
methods.mechanism: WRITE: append every observation as timestamped natural language, with an LLM-assigned importance (poignancy) score at write time; periodically synthesize reflections from high-importance recent records and append those too. READ: score = w_recency*0.995^(hours since last access) + w_importance*normalized_poignancy + w_relevance*cosine(query, record), each min-max normalized, weights equal in the reference implementation; take top-k under a token budget. FORGET: none — the recency term only de-prioritizes. GAINS: ablating observation, planning, or reflection each measurably reduces behavioral believability.
methods.strengths: Trivial to implement and debug; the three-term score is cheap (one embedding + two scalars) and empirically strong; importance-at-write-time is a one-time cost amortized over all future reads; reflection gives free hierarchical abstraction; 'last access' recency naturally reinforces frequently used memories.
methods.weaknesses: Unbounded growth — retrieval quality and cost degrade as the stream lengthens; weights are hand-tuned and task-dependent; no deduplication, no contradiction handling, so stale facts and current facts compete on equal footing; poor at multi-hop questions because retrieval is flat top-k.
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local and cheap. SQLite (or sqlite-vec / LanceDB) for the stream, a local sentence-transformer via MLX or llama.cpp for embeddings, importance scoring batched to a small local model. This should be the v0 of any local memory store.

methods.name: Agentic Zettelkasten note network (A-MEM)
methods.mechanism: WRITE: LLM converts each interaction into an atomic note with contextual description, keywords, tags, and embedding; it then inspects the k nearest existing notes and autonomously creates links; integration can trigger LLM rewrites of the linked older notes' descriptions and tags (memory evolution). READ: embedding retrieval over notes, expanded along the agent-created links. FORGET: no deletion — consolidation happens by rewriting, so obsolete content is superseded in place rather than removed. GAINS: reported superior to SOTA baselines across six foundation models; secondary reports of ~2x LOCOMO multi-hop ROUGE-L and 85–93% fewer tokens per memory op (UNVERIFIED, and contradicted by Mem0's reproduction).
methods.strengths: The only widely-cited design with retroactive reinterpretation of old memories; links are semantic and agent-justified rather than mere embedding neighbors; structure emerges without a predefined schema, so it adapts across task types.
methods.weaknesses: Write cost is the problem — link analysis plus evolution rewrites make it approach O(N^2) LLM calls as the store grows (this is exactly D-MEM's critique); results are contested across papers; rewriting history destroys the audit trail; no forgetting at all.
methods.local_feasibility: Feasible but the write path is the bottleneck on a laptop. Mitigations: gate expensive writes on a surprise/utility signal (D-MEM), cap the link-analysis candidate set, and run evolution as a batched idle-time job (sleep-time compute) rather than inline.

methods.name: LLM-reconciled fact store with ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP (Mem0)
methods.mechanism: WRITE: two phases — extract candidate salient facts from (rolling summary + last m=10 messages + new exchange), then for each candidate fetch top s=10 similar existing memories and have the LLM emit a tool call choosing ADD, UPDATE, DELETE, or NOOP. READ: dense vector search over the compact fact store. FORGET: explicit, semantic, and immediate — DELETE fires when new information contradicts an old memory; the graph variant marks contradicted edges obsolete instead. GAINS: +26% relative LLM-as-a-Judge over OpenAI memory on LOCOMO; 91% lower p95 latency and >90% token savings vs full-context; graph variant ~2% better overall, mainly on temporal/open-domain.
methods.strengths: Keeps the store small and non-redundant, which is what actually makes retrieval fast and precise at scale; contradiction resolution is a first-class operation, not a decay heuristic; the cheapest read path of any system here (p95 search ~0.2s); mature open-source implementation.
methods.weaknesses: Extraction is lossy and irreversible — anything the extractor misses is gone, so it is weak on questions requiring verbatim detail; DELETE decisions by a small model are risky; the flat fact store underperforms on multi-hop; and its own benchmark numbers are contested by Zep.
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local. Mem0 OSS supports Ollama for both LLM and embeddings, with Qdrant/Chroma/FAISS as vector store; the graph variant wants Neo4j (Docker on macOS) — substitute Kuzu (embedded, no server) if you want a single-process deployment.

methods.name: Bi-temporal knowledge graph memory (Zep / Graphiti)
methods.mechanism: WRITE: raw episodes stored non-lossily; an LLM extracts entities and fact edges, resolves/dedupes them against existing nodes, and stamps each edge with both a transaction time and a validity interval (t_valid, t_invalid); an LLM contradiction check invalidates superseded edges by setting t_invalid. Communities are formed by label propagation and incrementally maintained with LLM-written summaries. READ: hybrid cosine + Okapi BM25 + breadth-first depth-2 traversal, fused/reranked via RRF, MMR, node distance, episode mentions, or a cross-encoder. FORGET: invalidation, not deletion — history stays queryable, which is what enables 'what did I believe last March?'. GAINS: 94.8% vs MemGPT's 93.4% on DMR; up to +18.5% accuracy and ~90% latency reduction on LongMemEval.
methods.strengths: Best-in-class on temporal reasoning and knowledge updates — the two categories where flat memory silently returns stale facts; nothing is ever lost, so it supports auditing and point-in-time reconstruction; hybrid retrieval is robust to embedding failures on names, IDs, and rare tokens.
methods.weaknesses: Heaviest write path (multiple LLM calls per episode for extraction, resolution, invalidation) and heaviest storage; entity resolution errors compound and are hard to repair; conversational data produces mega-hub nodes that dilute graph relevance; its published LOCOMO numbers are the subject of an open dispute with Mem0.
methods.local_feasibility: The Graphiti library is open-source and runs locally against Neo4j, FalkorDB, or Kuzu (Kuzu is embedded — best macOS choice) with Ollama for LLM and embeddings. The bi-temporal model and hybrid retrieval are the parts worth stealing even if you don't adopt the whole system.

methods.name: Surprise-segmented episodic KV memory (EM-LLM)
methods.mechanism: WRITE: during the forward pass, compute Bayesian surprise (token NLL) over the incoming stream; spikes above a running threshold propose event boundaries, which are then refined by maximizing modularity / minimizing conductance over the token-similarity graph so each event is internally coherent; the KV blocks for each event are stored as an episode with a representative key. READ: two-stage — k-NN similarity over representative keys fills a similarity buffer, plus a contiguity buffer of temporally adjacent events, both fed back into attention. FORGET: bounded local context plus buffer eviction; older events remain on disk and are recalled only if selected. GAINS: +4.3% overall over InfLLM on LongBench with +33% on PassageRetrieval; beats RAG at similar cost; exceeds full-context models on most tasks; retrieval demonstrated over 10M tokens; segmentation correlates with human-perceived event boundaries.
methods.strengths: Operates on the model's own representations, so there is no text-extraction information loss and no extra LLM calls on the write path — segmentation is nearly free given you are already running the forward pass; the temporal-contiguity buffer recovers narrative context that pure similarity retrieval destroys; no fine-tuning needed.
methods.weaknesses: Requires white-box access to attention/KV internals, so it is unusable with any API model; KV storage is large (GBs for long histories) and tied to one specific model+tokenizer — change models and the memory is worthless; it addresses long-context recall, not cross-session semantic knowledge, so it does not replace a fact store.
methods.local_feasibility: Feasible only locally, and that is the point — this is the one architecture whose requirements (open weights, control of the inference loop) a laptop deployment satisfies and a cloud API does not. Needs a Transformers/vLLM-style local runtime plus enough unified memory for offloaded KV blocks; Apple Silicon with 32–64GB is workable for 7–8B models. UNVERIFIED whether the official implementation supports MPS out of the box.

methods.name: Personalized PageRank over an open knowledge graph (HippoRAG / HippoRAG 2)
methods.mechanism: WRITE (offline indexing): LLM OpenIE turns passages into triples, merged into a schemaless KG; a retrieval encoder adds synonymy edges; HippoRAG 2 additionally inserts passages as nodes joined to their triples by context edges. READ: HippoRAG 1 extracts query named entities as PPR seeds; HippoRAG 2 retrieves triples directly by embedding, filters them with an LLM 'recognition memory' step, seeds PPR from the survivors, and blends the resulting passage scores with dense-retriever scores. Seeds weighted by node specificity (IDF-like). FORGET: none intrinsically — the graph is append-only; new documents integrate without catastrophic forgetting, which is the design goal. GAINS: HippoRAG up to +20% on multi-hop QA, 10–30x cheaper and 6–13x faster than IRCoT; HippoRAG 2 +7% on associative memory over the SOTA embedding model while also improving factual and sense-making retrieval.
methods.strengths: Multi-hop pattern completion in a single retrieval step — the graph does the hop-chaining that would otherwise cost several LLM round trips; PPR is deterministic, fast, and fully inspectable; continually integrates new documents; HippoRAG 2 fixes v1's regression on simple single-hop queries.
methods.weaknesses: LLM-based OpenIE indexing is the dominant cost and it scales with corpus size (TERAG exists precisely to fix this); extraction quality caps end-to-end quality; graph gets hub-heavy on conversational data; retrieves passages, so you still need a separate mechanism for episodic/temporal state.
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local and one of the best fits here. Indexing with a local 7–8B model is slow but is a one-off batch job (run it overnight); retrieval is NetworkX or igraph PPR over a modest graph, which is milliseconds on CPU. Use HippoRAG 2, and consider TERAG-style cheap indexing for large personal corpora.

methods.name: Parametric episodic memory matrix with algebraic write/forget (Larimar)
methods.mechanism: WRITE: encode an episode, solve a least-squares/pseudo-inverse problem for addressing weights, and update the K x C memory matrix M in one shot (Kanerva-Machine / Generative Pseudo-inverse Memory formulation of Bayesian posterior update); a running covariance term supports 1000+ sequential edits. READ: encode the query, compute reading weights, broadcast the readout as KV-cache-like conditioning across decoder layers; an optional scope detector (MiniLM 1-NN, ~2.9% EER) decides whether memory applies at all. FORGET: exact — re-apply the same update with alpha = -1 to subtract a previously written encoding. GAINS: 4–10x speed-ups over gradient-based editors; 99.6–100% CounterFact edit success; edit retention 0.97–0.98 across 1000 sequential ZsRE edits vs 0.93 for GRACE at ~10x speed; extraction-attack success cut from 49.3% (MEMIT) to 17.6%.
methods.strengths: Forgetting is mathematically exact rather than heuristic — genuinely important for privacy, right-to-erasure, and removing poisoned memories; writes are one-shot with no gradient steps; the scope detector prevents memory from corrupting out-of-scope answers; fastest edit latency of any knowledge-editing method surveyed.
methods.weaknesses: Not model-agnostic in practice — it needs a paired encoder/decoder architecture, so you cannot drop it onto an arbitrary off-the-shelf chat model; demonstrated on GPT-2/GPT-J scale, not on modern instruct models; fixed-capacity memory matrix (e.g. K=512) means capacity planning and eventual interference; memory contents are latent vectors, so they are not human-inspectable.
methods.local_feasibility: Partially feasible. The IBM/larimar code is public and GPT-2-scale runs comfortably on Apple Silicon; GPT-J-6B is tight but possible on 32GB+. The blocker is integration: you would be running a bespoke small model for memory alongside your main agent model, not augmenting the agent model itself. Treat as a research option, or borrow just two ideas — the scope detector and exact subtractive forgetting.

methods.name: Ebbinghaus / activation-decay forgetting (MemoryBank, Oblivion, ACT-R base-level learning)
methods.mechanism: WRITE: store dialogue records plus LLM-generated event summaries and a running user-personality portrait; attach a memory-strength parameter S. READ: dense retrieval over summaries, with retention weighting R = exp(-t/S). FORGET: every successful recall increments S, so unreinforced items decay out of contention and repeatedly used items consolidate — the classic Ebbinghaus curve, formally the same shape as ACT-R base-level activation decay. Oblivion (2026) generalizes this to accessibility reduction rather than deletion and adds a gate on whether to consult memory at all. GAINS: MemoryBank's SiliconFriend showed strong long-term companionship behavior in both real-user qualitative and simulated-dialog quantitative evaluation (no single headline accuracy number).
methods.strengths: The only cheap, principled answer to unbounded growth — decay costs one scalar update per access and no LLM calls; recall-reinforcement naturally surfaces what the user actually cares about; well-grounded in decades of human memory research; composes with any of the other read paths as a re-ranking multiplier.
methods.weaknesses: Time-based decay is wrong for facts that are rarely mentioned but permanently true (your birthday, your allergy) — you need a type-conditioned or importance-conditioned decay rate, not a global one; tuning S dynamics is empirical; deletion-by-decay is unrecoverable if you actually delete rather than de-prioritize.
methods.local_feasibility: Trivially local — it is arithmetic over a SQLite column. Strong recommendation: implement decay as an accessibility multiplier over a Generative-Agents-style score, never as hard deletion, and exempt a 'permanent facts' class.

methods.name: Verbal self-reflection buffer (Reflexion)
methods.mechanism: WRITE: after a trial, an evaluator produces feedback (scalar or free-form, external or self-generated); a reflection LLM turns it into natural-language corrective guidance which is appended to an episodic buffer. READ: the buffer (typically a sliding window of the last 1–3 reflections) is prepended to the next attempt's prompt. FORGET: the sliding window is the forgetting policy — old reflections fall off. GAINS: 91% pass@1 on HumanEval vs 80% for the prior GPT-4 SOTA, plus gains on AlfWorld and HotPotQA.
methods.strengths: Memory as a substitute for gradient updates — measurable capability improvement with zero training; extremely simple; the reflection text is fully auditable; works with any model that can follow instructions.
methods.weaknesses: Within-task only in the original formulation: lessons do not persist across tasks or sessions, so the same mistake recurs on the next problem; the tiny sliding window is a severe capacity limit; self-evaluation without a ground-truth signal can reinforce wrong conclusions; no consolidation into reusable abstractions.
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local and nearly free. The upgrade path is to make the buffer persistent and cross-task, which turns it into a semantic-memory 'lessons learned' store; note that a 2026 diagnostic found flat self-managed text files at this level of sophistication competitive with far more elaborate systems.

methods.name: Procedural skill library of verified executable code (Voyager)
methods.mechanism: WRITE: a candidate program is generated iteratively from environment feedback and execution errors, and is committed to the library only after self-verification confirms it achieved the goal; it is indexed by the embedding of an LLM-written description of what it does. READ: embed the current sub-goal plus environment state, retrieve top-k skill programs, compose them into the next program (skills call other skills). FORGET: effectively none — skills are immutable append-only artifacts, which is why the paper argues it alleviates catastrophic forgetting. GAINS: 3.3x more unique items, 2.3x longer traversal, up to 15.3x faster tech-tree milestones vs prior SOTA; the library transfers zero-shot to a fresh world.
methods.strengths: The strongest write-path quality gate in the entire literature — verified-before-commit means memory cannot be poisoned by plausible-but-wrong content, which is the dominant failure mode of every text-based system here; compositional skills compound; code is executable, so 'retrieval' produces action, not just context.
methods.weaknesses: Requires an environment with a programmatic interface and an automatic success signal — most conversational or knowledge-work domains have neither; the library grows monotonically and eventually needs pruning/refactoring (the 2025–2026 skill-library papers exist to address this); description-embedding retrieval misfires when skills are semantically close.
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local for anything with a CLI, filesystem, or scriptable API surface — arguably the single most valuable pattern for a local macOS coding/ops agent, where 'did the test pass?' is a free verification signal. Store skills as versioned files in a git repo plus an embedding index; git gives you history, diffing, and rollback for free.

methods.name: CoALA-style four-way memory partition (working / episodic / semantic / procedural)
methods.mechanism: Not a system but the schema that should govern one. Working memory = the live context window. Episodic = what happened, timestamped, verbatim-ish. Semantic = distilled facts and beliefs about the world and the user. Procedural = how to do things (skills, rules, prompts). Each gets its own WRITE policy (append vs reconcile vs verify-then-commit), READ policy (recency-weighted vs similarity vs graph vs exact-match), and FORGET policy (decay vs invalidate vs never). Internal actions (retrieve, reason, learn) are made explicit alongside external grounding actions in a single decision loop.
methods.strengths: Prevents the most common architectural mistake — one undifferentiated vector store serving four incompatible purposes with one retrieval policy; makes forgetting policy an explicit per-type decision; forty years of Soar/ACT-R results transfer, including base-level activation decay, spreading activation, and chunking as procedural consolidation.
methods.weaknesses: It is a framework, not an implementation — no code, no benchmark numbers; over-partitioning adds routing complexity and a new failure mode (writing to the wrong store); the boundaries genuinely blur (is a user preference semantic or episodic?).
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local; it is a design decision, not a dependency. Concretely on macOS: SQLite FTS5 + sqlite-vec for episodic, a Mem0-style reconciled fact table or Kuzu graph for semantic, a git-backed skill directory for procedural, and the context window for working memory.

methods.name: Sleep-time / idle consolidation compute (Letta)
methods.mechanism: WRITE (deferred): while the agent is idle, replay recent episodic memory, anticipate likely future queries, precompute derived facts and summaries, resolve contradictions, and rewrite the semantic store. READ: unchanged and cheaper, because it now hits a pre-digested state. FORGET: consolidation is where decay, deduplication, and invalidation are actually applied in batch. GAINS: ~5x less test-time compute for equal accuracy on Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME; up to +13% accuracy.
methods.strengths: Moves every expensive memory operation off the user-facing critical path — which is exactly the fix for the write-cost weakness of A-MEM, Zep, and Mem0; batching makes local-model inference dramatically more efficient; a laptop is idle most of the day, so the compute is genuinely free.
methods.weaknesses: Consolidation can be wrong, and errors introduced offline are silent and hard to trace back; requires idempotent, resumable jobs or interruption corrupts state; adds an operational component (scheduler, job queue) to what was a library.
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local and unusually well suited to it — a launchd job or cron on macOS running a batched local model during idle/charging hours. This is the highest-leverage architectural choice for making an expensive memory design affordable on a laptop.

methods.name: Agent-managed flat text files (2026 strong baseline)
methods.mechanism: WRITE: the agent reads, edits, and appends to plain markdown/text files with ordinary file tools, organizing them however it sees fit. READ: grep/full-text search plus reading whole files into context. FORGET: the agent rewrites or deletes files. No embeddings, no graph, no database required. GAINS: reported competitive with eight published memory systems across five heterogeneous scenarios in a 2026 cross-scenario diagnostic (arXiv:2606.04315).
methods.strengths: Zero infrastructure; perfectly inspectable and hand-editable by the user; versionable with git; no embedding-model lock-in and no re-indexing when you change models; the agent's general competence substitutes for bespoke retrieval machinery, and that competence keeps improving for free as models improve.
methods.weaknesses: Scales poorly past the point where grep results exceed the context window; no semantic recall for paraphrased queries; no temporal reasoning; retrieval quality depends entirely on how well the agent chose to organize files earlier; no principled forgetting.
methods.local_feasibility: Maximally local — this is just the filesystem. Use it as the control baseline: any sophisticated architecture you build must beat agent-managed markdown plus ripgrep on your actual workload, measured, or it is not earning its complexity.

takeaways: The field converged on a three-part contract — WRITE / READ / FORGET — but almost nobody implements all three well. Surveys formalize it as write-manage-read (arXiv:2603.07670) or as six atomic operations: consolidation, updating, indexing, forgetting, retrieval, condensation (arXiv:2505.00675). Mapped onto that grid, most published systems are strong on two operations and absent on the rest: Generative Agents and A-MEM have no forgetting at all; Reflexion has no cross-task consolidation; HippoRAG has no temporal invalidation; EM-LLM has no semantic layer. When designing a local store, pick the operations you need first and compose mechanisms from different papers, rather than adopting any one system whole.

Forgetting is the least-solved and most-differentiating problem, and there are exactly four distinct mechanisms in the literature. (1) Eviction plus lossy summarization (MemGPT) — simple, irreversible, information-destroying. (2) Time/frequency decay of accessibility (MemoryBank's Ebbinghaus curve, Oblivion, ACT-R base-level learning) — cheap and principled, but wrong for rarely-mentioned permanent facts unless the decay rate is type-conditioned. (3) Semantic invalidation (Zep's t_invalid, Mem0's DELETE, Mem0^g's obsolescence flags) — the only approach that handles contradiction correctly, and Zep's variant preserves history so you can still ask what was believed at a past date. (4) Exact algebraic subtraction (Larimar, alpha = -1) — the only mechanism that actually erases, which matters for privacy and for removing poisoned memories. A serious system needs (2) or (3) for routine hygiene and (4)-like semantics for deletion requests; these are complementary, not alternatives.

Write-path cost, not retrieval quality, is what breaks agentic memory at scale — and it is the binding constraint on a laptop. A-MEM's link analysis plus memory evolution approaches O(N^2) LLM calls; Zep spends several LLM calls per episode on extraction, resolution, and invalidation; HippoRAG's OpenIE indexing dominates its total cost. Three published mitigations exist and should be combined: gate expensive writes on a cheap surprise/utility signal (D-MEM, arXiv:2603.14597; EM-LLM's Bayesian surprise is the same idea at the token level), cut indexing token cost directly (TERAG, arXiv:2509.18667), and move all of it off the critical path into idle-time batch consolidation (sleep-time compute, arXiv:2504.13171, ~5x test-time compute reduction and up to +13% accuracy). A macOS laptop is idle most of the day; that is free consolidation compute nobody is using.

Treat every published benchmark number in this area as contested. Mem0 reports Zep at 58.44% on LOCOMO after reproduction; Zep rebuts that it was misconfigured and reports 75.14%; the disagreement turns on whether the adversarial question category is included, which API version was tested, and whether timestamp support was available — none of which the benchmark prescribes. Mem0's own paper reports A-Mem's LOCOMO multi-hop at 18.85 while A-Mem's authors report 44.27. Cross-paper comparisons here are close to meaningless. LongMemEval (arXiv:2410.10813) is the better-factored benchmark because it separates knowledge updating and abstention from plain retrieval, and arXiv:2509.18868 proposes a three-setting protocol specifically to stop these distorted comparisons. Benchmark on your own workload.

Build the trivial thing first and force the sophisticated thing to beat it. A 2026 cross-scenario diagnostic (arXiv:2606.04315) re-ran eight memory systems across five scenario types and found each was tuned to one scenario, with an agentic harness self-managing flat text files serving as a competitive baseline throughout. Combined with the ablation evidence on representation choice (arXiv:2412.15266, comparing chunks vs triples vs atomic facts vs summaries, where mixed structures often win), the honest engineering conclusion is: start with agent-managed markdown plus ripgrep plus a Generative-Agents-style recency/importance/relevance score over SQLite, measure, and only add a graph or a KV-episode layer where you can show it wins.

For a fully local macOS deployment, the specific stack the literature supports is: CoALA's four-way partition as the schema (working / episodic / semantic / procedural); Letta or MemoryOS-style tiered paging as the control loop; SQLite with FTS5 plus sqlite-vec or LanceDB for episodic, scored Generative-Agents-style with an Ebbinghaus accessibility multiplier; Mem0-style ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP reconciliation into a compact semantic fact table, upgraded to Kuzu (embedded, no server, unlike Neo4j) with Zep's bi-temporal t_valid/t_invalid edges if temporal reasoning matters; HippoRAG 2 with NetworkX Personalized PageRank for multi-hop retrieval over any document corpus, indexed once overnight; a git-backed Voyager-style skill directory with verify-before-commit for procedural memory; and Zep's hybrid BM25 + dense + graph fusion at the read path, because pure embeddings fail on names, IDs, and rare tokens. Everything except EM-LLM and Larimar runs against Ollama or llama.cpp with no external service.

EM-LLM (ICLR 2025, arXiv:2407.09450) is the one architecture whose requirements a local deployment satisfies and a cloud API cannot: it segments the KV cache itself using Bayesian surprise refined by graph modularity/conductance, and retrieves with a similarity buffer plus a temporal-contiguity buffer that reproduces the human contiguity effect in free recall. It needs white-box access to attention internals — impossible through any API. Reported +4.3% over InfLLM on LongBench with +33% on PassageRetrieval, beating full-context models on most tasks and retrieving across 10M tokens. Caveats for a laptop: KV storage is large and is bound to one specific model and tokenizer, so switching models invalidates the memory, and MPS support in the official implementation is UNVERIFIED. It solves long-context recall, not cross-session semantic knowledge, so it complements rather than replaces a fact store.

The strongest quality control in the entire literature is Voyager's verify-before-commit rule, and it is underused outside embodied settings. Text-based memory systems are all vulnerable to the same failure: a plausible-but-wrong extraction enters the store and is thereafter retrieved as ground truth, with A-MEM's evolution mechanism actively propagating the error into linked notes. Voyager admits nothing to its skill library until self-verification confirms it worked, which is why its skills transfer zero-shot to a new world (3.3x items, 2.3x distance, 15.3x faster milestones vs prior SOTA). For a local coding or ops agent, 'did the test pass / did the command exit 0' is a free verification signal — apply the same gate to procedural memory, and where possible to semantic memory too.

The cognitive-architecture thread (Soar, ACT-R) has moved from analogy to implementation and is worth mining for specific mechanisms rather than adopted wholesale. CoALA (TMLR 2024) supplies the memory taxonomy everyone now uses implicitly; arXiv:2308.09830 lays out the modular / agency / neuro-symbolic integration options; arXiv:2403.00810 uses the LLM to bootstrap the knowledge base and thereby dissolves the hand-authoring bottleneck that historically killed these architectures; NL2GenSym (arXiv:2510.09355) has an LLM generate Soar production rules with execution-grounded validation; CogRec (arXiv:2512.24113) ships a working Soar+LLM recommender. The transferable mechanisms are concrete: ACT-R base-level activation decay is already the mathematics behind MemoryBank and Oblivion, spreading activation is what HippoRAG's Personalized PageRank implements, and Soar chunking is what Voyager's skill library approximates. The field keeps rediscovering these; read the originals.

There is a real parametric-versus-external fork that most surveys understate. Larimar (ICML 2024) writes episodes into a memory matrix via a one-shot pseudo-inverse solve, reads by broadcasting the readout as KV-cache-like conditioning, and forgets by exact subtraction (alpha = -1) — yielding 4-10x faster edits than gradient-based editors, 0.97-0.98 edit retention across 1000 sequential edits, and extraction-attack success dropped from 49.3% to 17.6%. Echo (arXiv:2502.16090) instead trains temporal episodic competence directly into the weights. Both require model control you only have locally. The practical recommendation is to keep the main memory external and text-based for inspectability and model-portability, but borrow Larimar's two best ideas independently: the scope detector that decides whether to consult memory at all (~2.9% EER, and note Oblivion independently rediscovers this gate), and exact subtractive deletion for anything that must be provably erased.

area: Retrieval and indexing (2015-2026) for a local, single-laptop agent memory store: graph/quantization ANN indexes (HNSW, DiskANN/Vamana, IVF-PQ, ScaNN, RaBitQ), lexical and learned-sparse retrieval (BM25/FTS5, SPLADE), late interaction (ColBERT/PLAID), hybrid fusion (RRF), cross-encoder reranking, Matryoshka/binary/scalar embedding compression, SQLite-embedded stacks (sqlite-vec + FTS5, FAISS), and the recall-vs-latency arithmetic that decides when an ANN index is worth building at all.

papers.title: Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs
papers.core_idea: Multi-layer proximity graph; element's max layer drawn from an exponentially decaying distribution; greedy beam search descends layers, with a heuristic neighbor-selection rule that keeps the graph navigable and diverse. Fully graph-based, no separate coarse quantizer.
papers.relevance: The default in-memory ANN index in essentially every vector DB. Its cost knobs (M, efConstruction, efSearch) are the canonical recall-vs-latency dial you would tune -- and the thing you can skip entirely below ~10^5 vectors.

papers.title: DiskANN: Fast Accurate Billion-point Nearest Neighbor Search on a Single Node
papers.core_idea: Vamana graph with alpha-pruned long-range edges, built so that a beam search touches few nodes; full-precision vectors live on SSD, PQ-compressed vectors in RAM guide traversal, with a final exact re-rank from disk reads.
papers.relevance: The reference design for 'index bigger than RAM on one machine.' Reported billion-point SIFT1B at >5000 QPS, <3 ms mean latency, 95%+ 1-recall@1 on 64 GB RAM + SSD. Overkill for 10^3-10^5 chunks, but it is the correct migration target if a local store ever outgrows memory.

papers.title: FreshDiskANN: A Fast and Accurate Graph-Based ANN Index for Streaming Similarity Search
papers.core_idea: Adds real-time insert/delete to Vamana via an in-memory delta index plus periodic StreamingMerge consolidation, keeping recall stable under continuous mutation.
papers.relevance: Directly names the failure mode that matters for agent memory: static graph indexes degrade under deletes/updates. This is a strong argument for a flat/SQL store where delete is a row delete.

papers.title: OOD-DiskANN: Efficient and Scalable Graph ANNS for Out-of-Distribution Queries
papers.core_idea: Data-dependent graph indexes overfit to the index distribution; when queries come from a different distribution (text query vs. image index, or instruction-style queries), latency at fixed recall degrades by an order of magnitude or more.
papers.relevance: Agent memory queries are systematically out-of-distribution relative to stored notes/logs. A quantified warning that measured ANN recall on a synthetic query set will overstate real recall.

papers.title: SPANN: Highly-efficient Billion-scale Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
papers.core_idea: Memory-disk hybrid inverted index: posting-list centroids in RAM, long posting lists on SSD, with list-length balancing and query-aware dynamic pruning.
papers.relevance: The IVF-family counterpart to DiskANN. Useful contrast when reasoning about partition-based vs. graph-based disk indexes; not needed at laptop scale.

papers.title: AiSAQ: All-in-Storage ANNS with Product Quantization for DRAM-free Information Retrieval
papers.core_idea: Offloads DiskANN's PQ-compressed vectors to SSD too, reaching ~10 MB query-time DRAM at billion scale without critical latency loss.
papers.relevance: Shows the extreme end of the memory/latency trade space, which frames just how much headroom a 10^5-chunk laptop store actually has.

papers.title: Product quantization for nearest neighbor search
papers.core_idea: Split the vector into m subspaces, k-means each subspace into 256 centroids, store an m-byte code; asymmetric distance computation (ADC) compares an uncompressed query against codes via cache-resident lookup tables. Combined with a coarse IVF quantizer this is IVFADC / IVF-PQ.
papers.relevance: Foundational for every compressed index (IVF-PQ, DiskANN's in-RAM guide, ScaNN). Pre-2015 but you cannot reason about IVF-PQ without it.

papers.title: Billion-scale similarity search with GPUs
papers.core_idea: GPU-efficient k-selection running at up to 55% of theoretical peak, plus GPU IVF-PQ, enabling billion-scale ANN on a handful of GPUs.
papers.relevance: Origin of FAISS. Its k-selection and blocked-scan lessons carry over to CPU: a well-blocked exact scan is far faster than naive per-vector loops.

papers.title: The Faiss library
papers.core_idea: Systematizes the vector-search trade-off space (accuracy / memory / speed) and documents FAISS's index-factory composition of transforms, coarse quantizers, encodings, and refinement stages.
papers.relevance: The best single reference for how to compose 'quantize then exact-rescore' pipelines, which is precisely the pattern a small local store should use instead of an ANN graph.

papers.title: Accelerating Large-Scale Inference with Anisotropic Vector Quantization
papers.core_idea: For MIPS, quantization error parallel to the datapoint hurts high-inner-product (i.e. top-ranked) pairs far more than orthogonal error. Defines a score-aware anisotropic loss that penalizes the parallel component more, changing the learned codebooks.
papers.relevance: The key theoretical correction to 'minimize reconstruction error.' Matters whenever you use inner-product/cosine (i.e. always, for text embeddings) and are compressing vectors.

papers.title: Norm-Explicit Quantization: Improving Vector Quantization for Maximum Inner Product Search
papers.core_idea: Decomposes quantization error into norm error and direction error, shows norm error dominates inner-product distortion, and quantizes norms explicitly.
papers.relevance: Explains why normalizing embeddings before quantization (or handling norms separately) is a cheap, large win.

papers.title: RaBitQ: Quantizing High-Dimensional Vectors with a Theoretical Error Bound for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
papers.core_idea: Randomized 1-bit-per-dimension quantization with an unbiased distance estimator and a provable error bound; SIMD/popcount-friendly, unlike PQ which has strong empirical results but no bound and can fail badly on some datasets.
papers.relevance: The current best answer for binary quantization. Makes 32x compression respectable enough that a binary flat scan plus fp32 rescoring often beats building any graph index at small/medium N.

papers.title: Practical and Asymptotically Optimal Quantization of High-Dimensional Vectors in Euclidean Space for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
papers.core_idea: Generalizes RaBitQ beyond 1 bit/dim to arbitrary bit budgets (2-8 bits) with asymptotic optimality, filling the gap between binary and fp32.
papers.relevance: Gives a principled scalar-quantization ladder (1/2/4/8-bit) rather than the ad-hoc int8 min-max scaling most libraries ship.

papers.title: Quicker ADC: Unlocking the hidden potential of Product Quantization with SIMD
papers.core_idea: Uses SIMD shuffle instructions to hold PQ lookup tables in registers (4-bit sub-quantizers), removing the memory-access bottleneck of classic ADC.
papers.relevance: The mechanism behind FAISS's 'fast-scan' PQ4 variants. Explains why PQ speed is about memory layout, not arithmetic -- the same insight that makes flat scans fast.

papers.title: Polysemous codes
papers.core_idea: Trains PQ codebooks so codes are simultaneously good ADC estimators and good Hamming codes, letting a cheap Hamming filter discard most candidates before asymmetric distance computation.
papers.relevance: Early, clean instance of the cascade pattern (cheap filter -> expensive exact score) that a small local store should copy.

papers.title: PDX: A Data Layout for Vector Similarity Search
papers.core_idea: Partition Dimensions Across: store many vectors per block with a vertical (dimension-major) layout so distance kernels operate on multiple-vectors-at-a-time in auto-vectorizable scalar loops. Reported ~40% faster on average than SIMD-optimized kernels over conventional horizontal storage, and composes with dimension-pruning.
papers.relevance: Direct evidence that exact/flat search is a data-layout problem, not a hopeless one. Most 'flat search is too slow' claims come from row-major per-vector loops rather than blocked/BLAS-style scans.

papers.title: To Index or Not to Index: Optimizing Exact Maximum Inner Product Search
papers.core_idea: A hardware-efficient brute-force blocked matrix multiply (BMM) outperforms state-of-the-art exact MIPS indexes by over an order of magnitude on many inputs; proposes MAXIMUS and an input-dependent choice between indexing and scanning.
papers.relevance: The paper to cite when arguing that an index can be a pessimization. Its framing -- decide per workload whether to index at all -- is exactly the decision facing a 10^3-10^5 chunk local store.

papers.title: ANN-Benchmarks: A Benchmarking Tool for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Algorithms
papers.core_idea: Standardized harness sweeping each algorithm's parameters and plotting the recall-vs-QPS Pareto frontier on common datasets.
papers.relevance: Establishes the evaluation convention (QPS at fixed recall) and the empirical shape of the recall-latency curve -- steeply concave, with the last few points of recall costing multiples of the compute.

papers.title: VIBE: Vector Index Benchmark for Embeddings
papers.core_idea: Rebuilds ANN benchmarking on datasets generated by modern embedding models (rather than SIFT/GloVe/MNIST), including out-of-distribution query sets.
papers.relevance: Modern replacement for ANN-Benchmarks numbers. Important because HNSW/IVF behaviour on 768-1536d transformer embeddings differs materially from SIFT-era results.

papers.title: Results of the NeurIPS'21 Challenge on Billion-Scale Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
papers.core_idea: Billion-scale competition comparing algorithms by hardware cost, accuracy, and performance across in-memory, SSD, and limited-compute tracks.
papers.relevance: Baseline for what ANN buys you at scale, and by contrast how little it buys at 10^5.

papers.title: Results of the Big ANN: NeurIPS'23 competition
papers.core_idea: Tracks for filtered, out-of-distribution, sparse, and streaming ANN; advances in graph indexing, quantization, hybrid vector+metadata structures, and memory-access strategies.
papers.relevance: Shows that filtered, streaming, and sparse retrieval are the open hard problems -- and those are exactly the four properties an agent memory store needs, which is another reason a flat+SQL design is defensible.

papers.title: Down with the Hierarchy: The 'H' in HNSW Stands for "Hubs"
papers.core_idea: Large benchmarking study finding a flat navigable small-world graph matches HNSW's latency and recall on high-dimensional data with less memory; proposes the Hub Highway Hypothesis (a well-connected set of frequently traversed hub nodes performs the hierarchy's role).
papers.relevance: Deflates the 'logarithmic hierarchy' story. If you do build a graph, the layers are dispensable; the real cost driver is the beam-search work per query.

papers.title: Worst-case Performance of Popular Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Implementations: Guarantees and Limitations
papers.core_idea: Proves DiskANN's slow-preprocessing variant supports constant-approximation ANN in polylog query time under bounded intrinsic dimension, and gives negative results (worst-case failures) for other popular variants including HNSW and NSG.
papers.relevance: The honest statement of what graph ANN does and does not guarantee. For a memory store where a silently missed memory is a user-visible bug, absence of guarantees is a real cost.

papers.title: The Impacts of Data, Ordering, and Intrinsic Dimensionality on Recall in Hierarchical Navigable Small Worlds
papers.core_idea: Empirical study of HNSW on deep-learning embeddings and synthetic sets with controlled intrinsic dimensionality, showing recall depends strongly on intrinsic dimension and even on insertion order.
papers.relevance: Quantifies that HNSW recall is data- and build-order-dependent, so a recall figure measured once does not transfer to an incrementally written agent memory.

papers.title: Navigable Graphs for High-Dimensional Nearest Neighbor Search: Constructions and Limits
papers.core_idea: Theory of how sparse a navigable graph can be for a given point set; sparsest navigable graphs need O(n*sqrt(n)) edges in the worst case.
papers.relevance: Explains the memory floor of graph indexes and why the practical heuristics (M, alpha-pruning) are heuristics.

papers.title: Which BM25 Do You Mean? A Large-Scale Reproducibility Study of Scoring Variants
papers.venue_or_id: ECIR 2020 -- Kamphuis, de Vries, Boytsov, Lin
papers.core_idea: Compares eight BM25 variants (including Lucene's approximated document-length encoding) on three newswire collections and finds no significant effectiveness differences between them.
papers.relevance: Settles a common time-sink: SQLite FTS5's hard-coded k1=1.2, b=0.75 BM25 is fine. Effort belongs in tokenization and field weighting, not the scoring formula.

papers.title: Reciprocal rank fusion outperforms Condorcet and individual rank learning methods
papers.core_idea: score(d) = sum over systems i of 1/(k + rank_i(d)), conventionally k=60. Rank-based fusion beats Condorcet Fuse, CombMNZ, and individual learning-to-rank methods on LETOR 3.
papers.relevance: The one-line algorithm behind every hybrid BM25+dense stack. Rank-based means no score normalization, which is essential when combining FTS5's unbounded negated BM25 with cosine in [-1,1].

papers.title: SPLADE: Sparse Lexical and Expansion Model for First Stage Ranking
papers.core_idea: Uses the MLM head to project text into a |V|-dimensional non-negative sparse vector over the wordpiece vocabulary, with explicit L1/FLOPS sparsity regularization so it can be served from an inverted index.
papers.relevance: The learned-sparse option: keeps exact-match and inverted-index efficiency while adding term expansion. Attractive in principle for agent memory; heavy in practice (needs a transformer at index time and a tuned inverted index).

papers.title: SPLADE v2: Sparse Lexical and Expansion Model for Information Retrieval
papers.core_idea: Max-pooling over the MLM logits, document-only expansion, and distillation; substantially better than v1 while remaining index-servable.
papers.relevance: The version people actually deploy; document-only expansion keeps query-time cost near BM25.

papers.title: From Distillation to Hard Negative Sampling: Making Sparse Neural IR Models More Effective
papers.core_idea: Shows most of SPLADE's remaining gap closes through training recipe (hard negatives + cross-encoder distillation) rather than architecture, and studies the effectiveness/efficiency trade-off explicitly.
papers.relevance: The canonical SPLADE++ reference and a reminder that training recipe, not index structure, drove the gains.

papers.title: Efficient Inverted Indexes for Approximate Retrieval over Learned Sparse Representations
papers.core_idea: Statically prunes inverted lists, groups each list into geometrically cohesive blocks, and attaches a summary vector per block so query processing can skip whole blocks by an inner-product bound.
papers.relevance: Explains why classic BM25-era dynamic pruning (WAND/MaxScore) underperforms on SPLADE: learned weight distributions differ from term-frequency ones. If you serve learned sparse locally, you need Seismic-class machinery, not just FTS5.

papers.title: Faster Learned Sparse Retrieval with Block-Max Pruning
papers.core_idea: Block-max pruning tailored to learned-sparse index statistics (longer queries, sub-word tokenization, different score distributions).
papers.relevance: Second data point on the same cost: learned sparse imports a whole query-processing research program that BM25 does not.

papers.title: Bridging Dense and Sparse Maximum Inner Product Search
papers.core_idea: Shows clustering/IVF machinery designed for dense vectors can be applied effectively to sparse vectors, unifying the two literatures under one MIPS framing.
papers.relevance: Useful if you want a single index type serving both a dense and a learned-sparse representation in one local store.

papers.title: ColBERT: Efficient and Effective Passage Search via Contextualized Late Interaction over BERT
papers.core_idea: Encode query and document independently into per-token vectors; score by MaxSim (for each query token, max cosine over document tokens, summed). Document token vectors are precomputable, so cross-encoder-like quality comes at bi-encoder-like query cost.
papers.relevance: The quality ceiling for cheap-at-query-time retrieval. But storage is one vector per token, which is the killer objection for a laptop memory store.

papers.title: ColBERTv2: Effective and Efficient Retrieval via Lightweight Late Interaction
papers.core_idea: Denoised supervision plus residual compression: cluster token embeddings into centroids and store only a quantized residual per token, cutting the index footprint by an order of magnitude.
papers.relevance: Makes late interaction storage-tolerable, and the centroid+residual trick is a reusable compression pattern.

papers.title: PLAID: An Efficient Engine for Late Interaction Retrieval
papers.core_idea: Centroid interaction: treat each passage as a bag of centroid ids, score cheaply against centroids to prune aggressively, then progressively refine with residuals and finally exact MaxSim.
papers.relevance: Shows the multi-stage-pruning pattern in its purest form; also the system most local ColBERT deployments would need to reimplement.

papers.title: A Reproducibility Study of PLAID
papers.core_idea: Reproduces PLAID and adds the missing baseline: ColBERTv2 re-ranking a BM25 candidate pool. Re-ranking gives better efficiency-effectiveness trade-offs in low-latency settings; it plateaus at high latency only because of lexical recall limits, which neighbor-expansion of top-scoring docs fixes. Also finds PLAID's clusters are mostly single-token aligned.
papers.relevance: Arguably the single most important paper for this question. It is a rigorous demonstration that at low latency budgets, cheap-first-stage + rerank beats a purpose-built ANN engine, and that first-stage recall is the binding constraint.

papers.title: SPLATE: Sparse Late Interaction Retrieval
papers.core_idea: Adds an MLM adapter to frozen ColBERTv2 token embeddings, mapping them into a sparse vocabulary space so candidate generation can run on a plain inverted index before exact MaxSim re-ranking.
papers.relevance: A route to late-interaction quality using only inverted-index infrastructure -- i.e. plausibly implementable over FTS5-style machinery.

papers.title: Passage Re-ranking with BERT
papers.core_idea: Feed [CLS] query [SEP] passage [SEP] into BERT and train a binary relevance classifier; rerank the top-k of a BM25 run. 27% relative improvement over prior SOTA on MS MARCO passage.
papers.relevance: The origin of the retrieve-then-rerank cascade that dominates practical IR and is the right shape for a small local corpus.

papers.title: Document Ranking with a Pretrained Sequence-to-Sequence Model
papers.core_idea: Frames ranking as generating a 'true'/'false' target token and uses the logits as relevance probabilities; notably data-efficient in low-resource settings.
papers.relevance: The other standard cross-encoder family; its low-data robustness matters when you have no labeled data for your own memory corpus.

papers.title: Shallow Cross-Encoders for Low-Latency Retrieval
papers.core_idea: Under a fixed small latency budget, few-layer transformers outperform full-size BERT/T5 cross-encoders, because they can score many more candidates in the same wall-clock time.
papers.relevance: Directly answers 'which reranker on a laptop CPU': a shallow one over a bigger pool, not a big one over 10 documents.

papers.title: Set-Encoder: Permutation-Invariant Inter-Passage Attention for Listwise Passage Re-Ranking with Cross-Encoders
