papers.core_idea: Cross-encoder with inter-passage attention that is invariant to input passage order, getting listwise effectiveness without listwise instability or cost.
papers.relevance: Fixes the order-sensitivity that makes LLM listwise rerankers unreliable; relevant if you want an LLM-free listwise stage.

papers.title: Matryoshka Representation Learning
papers.core_idea: Train one embedding so that nested prefixes (e.g. first 64/128/256/512/768 dims) are each independently usable, by applying the loss at multiple truncation points. Gives adaptive compute/accuracy at inference with no retraining.
papers.relevance: The cleanest local lever: scan a truncated prefix, then rescore the shortlist at full dimension. Caveat: it only works with an MRL-trained model; truncating a non-MRL embedding degrades sharply.

papers.title: Optimization of embeddings storage for RAG systems using quantization and dimensionality reduction techniques
papers.core_idea: Systematic MTEB study of float16 / int8 / binary / float8 quantization against PCA, kernel PCA, UMAP, and random projection for embedding storage.
papers.relevance: Empirical grounding for the compression ladder: which rungs are near-free and which cost measurable quality.

papers.title: Dimension vs. Precision: A Comparative Analysis of Autoencoders and Quantization for Efficient Vector Retrieval on BEIR SciFact
papers.core_idea: Head-to-head on BEIR SciFact of autoencoder dimensionality reduction (384 -> 12) versus precision reduction (float16, int8, binary) on 384-dim vectors.
papers.relevance: Same trade-off measured on a small corpus, which is the regime in question. Useful for choosing between 'fewer dims' and 'fewer bits'.

papers.title: Projection and Quantisation: A Unifying View of Learning to Hash, from Random Projections to the RAG Era
papers.core_idea: Projection-quantisation-organisation lens over LSH, binary hashing, PQ, and modern quantizers, with an open BitBudget benchmark; finds the quantisation axis delivers the largest memory savings.
papers.relevance: The best modern framing of the whole compression design space, and a data-backed argument that bits-per-dimension is the lever that pays, not exotic index organisation.

papers.title: BEIR: A Heterogenous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models
papers.core_idea: 18 datasets across tasks and domains for zero-shot IR evaluation; repeatedly shows BM25 is a very strong out-of-domain baseline that many dense retrievers fail to beat.
papers.relevance: The evidence base for keeping BM25 in a hybrid: an agent memory corpus is by definition out-of-domain for any off-the-shelf embedding model.

papers.title: On the Theoretical Limitations of Embedding-Based Retrieval
papers.core_idea: Connects retrievable top-k document sets to sign-rank/communication-complexity bounds, showing a d-dimensional single-vector embedding cannot represent all relevance sets even for simple, natural queries; demonstrates the failure empirically on LIMIT.
papers.relevance: The rigorous reason not to make dense retrieval your only channel. Motivates hybrid (lexical + dense) and multi-vector approaches on principle, not just empirics.

papers.title: Multi-Vector Embeddings are Provably More Expressive than Single Vector Embeddings
papers.core_idea: Formal separation showing single-vector inner-product similarity cannot approximate multi-vector Chamfer similarity at comparable representation size.
papers.relevance: Theoretical complement to the LIMIT result; justifies late interaction (or a reranker) as a second stage rather than a luxury.

papers.title: vstash: Local-First Hybrid Retrieval with Adaptive Fusion for LLM Agents
papers.core_idea: Entire document memory in one SQLite file: sqlite-vec for vector search, FTS5 for keyword, combined by RRF with adaptive per-query IDF weighting. Adaptive RRF beats fixed weights on all 5 BEIR datasets tested (up to +21.4% NDCG@10 on ArguAna); hybrid disagreement between vector-heavy and FTS-heavy rankings gives a free fine-tuning signal (74.5% of 753 queries disagree in top-10). Reports 20.9 ms median search latency at 50K chunks. Reports a negative result: cross-encoder reranking, frequency+decay, and history-augmented recall all failed to improve NDCG on top of adaptive RRF.
papers.relevance: The closest published system to the exact question asked -- same substrate (SQLite + sqlite-vec + FTS5 + RRF), same scale (50K chunks), same use case (LLM agent memory), with measured latency and BEIR numbers. Its negative reranking result is a useful caution against assuming a reranker always helps.

papers.title: Diagnosing Retrieval vs. Utilization Bottlenecks in LLM Agent Memory
papers.core_idea: 3x3 study crossing write strategies (raw chunks, Mem0-style fact extraction, MemGPT-style summarization) with retrieval methods (cosine, BM25, hybrid reranking) on LoCoMo. Retrieval method dominates: 57.1% to 77.2% average accuracy across retrieval methods versus only 3-8 points across write strategies. Raw chunked storage (zero LLM calls) matches or beats lossy extraction/summarization.
papers.relevance: Quantifies the engineering priority order for an agent memory store: fix retrieval (hybrid + rerank) before investing in clever write-time memory construction. A 20-point spread attributable to retrieval is a strong argument for not sacrificing recall to an ANN index.

papers.title: Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory
papers.core_idea: Memory-centric agent architecture that dynamically extracts, consolidates, and retrieves salient facts across sessions, with a graph-based variant for relational structure.
papers.relevance: The reference point for write-side memory design; read alongside arXiv:2603.02473, which finds this style of lossy extraction underperforms raw chunks under good retrieval.

papers.title: Late Chunking: Contextual Chunk Embeddings Using Long-Context Embedding Models
papers.core_idea: Embed the whole long document first with a long-context encoder, then pool token embeddings into chunk vectors, so each chunk vector carries surrounding context instead of being encoded in isolation.
papers.relevance: Cheap, index-agnostic quality win that costs nothing at query time -- exactly the kind of improvement worth making before touching the index structure.

papers.title: Rethinking Chunk Size For Long-Document Retrieval: A Multi-Dataset Analysis
papers.core_idea: Systematic evaluation of fixed-size chunking across embedding models: 64-128 token chunks are best for concise fact-based answers, 512-1024 token chunks for long-form.
papers.relevance: Chunk size sets N, which sets whether you need an index at all. Concrete numbers for sizing a memory store.

papers.title: Distance Adaptive Beam Search for Provably Accurate Graph-Based Nearest Neighbor Search
papers.core_idea: Replaces the fixed beam-width termination condition in graph ANN with a distance-based criterion, yielding provable accuracy alongside adaptive per-query cost.
papers.relevance: If you do run HNSW/DiskANN locally, this is the direction for making efSearch adaptive rather than a static global guess that is wrong for most queries.

methods.name: Exact flat (brute-force) scan, fp32, blocked/BLAS
methods.mechanism: Store all N vectors contiguously (or in PDX-style dimension-major blocks) and compute all N dot products per query with a single sgemv/sgemm or auto-vectorized blocked loop, then top-k select.
methods.strengths: Recall = 1.0 by construction, so retrieval quality is bounded only by the embedding model. Zero build time, trivially incremental (append a row), delete is a row delete, and metadata pre-filters make it strictly faster. Deterministic and reproducible; no tuning knobs to get wrong. Memory-bandwidth-bound, which modern laptops are good at.
methods.weaknesses: Cost is Theta(N*d) per query, so it scales linearly. Becomes uncomfortable past roughly 10^6 chunks at 768d fp32 (~3 GB scanned per query). Naive row-major per-vector loops are 2-5x slower than a blocked/BLAS scan, which is why people wrongly conclude flat is slow.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes, ideal. At 10^5 x 768 fp32 the scan block is ~307 MB, ~1.5-6 ms per query at realistic laptop bandwidth; at 10^4 it is ~30 MB and sub-millisecond; at 10^3 it fits in L2/L3. NumPy + BLAS, or sqlite-vec, or faiss.IndexFlatIP all do this out of the box.

methods.name: Binary quantization (1 bit/dim, RaBitQ) flat scan + fp32 rescoring
methods.mechanism: Random rotation then sign quantization to one bit per dimension; scan with popcount/Hamming (or RaBitQ's unbiased estimator) to build a shortlist of R candidates, then rescore those R with full fp32 vectors and return the top-k.
methods.strengths: 32x less memory traffic, so 10^5 x 768 becomes ~9.6 MB and largely cache-resident: sub-millisecond scans. RaBitQ gives a provable error bound, unlike PQ. Final ranking is exact over the shortlist, so quality loss is confined to shortlist recall, which oversampling controls directly and interpretably.
methods.weaknesses: Needs an oversampling factor (typically R = 10k to 40k) that must be validated per corpus. Binary quality is sensitive to embedding geometry (coordinate heterogeneity, anisotropy) -- some embedding families binarize far better than others. Requires keeping fp32 vectors around for rescoring, so it saves bandwidth, not disk.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes. sqlite-vec supports bit vectors with Hamming distance natively; FAISS supports binary indexes and RaBitQ. This is the first thing to reach for if a fp32 flat scan ever gets slow.

methods.name: Int8 / scalar quantization flat scan
methods.mechanism: Per-dimension (or per-vector) affine min-max or calibrated scaling to 8-bit integers; SIMD integer dot products; optionally rescore top-R in fp32.
methods.strengths: 4x bandwidth and memory reduction, typically near-lossless for retrieval on normalized text embeddings. Simplest possible compression, no codebook to train, no corpus-dependent state (so it never goes stale as the store grows).
methods.weaknesses: Only 4x, so it delays the flat-search wall rather than moving it far. Naive min-max scaling is suboptimal versus principled schemes (Extended RaBitQ, TurboQuant-style). Outlier dimensions can dominate the scale.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes. sqlite-vec has int8 columns with L2 and cosine; FAISS has ScalarQuantizer. Safe default for a laptop store above ~10^4 chunks.

methods.name: Matryoshka (MRL) prefix truncation + full-dimension rescoring
methods.mechanism: Use an MRL-trained embedding model; scan on a truncated prefix (e.g. 256 of 768 dims), take top-R, rescore at full dimension.
methods.strengths: Linear reduction in scan cost with a quality knob you can move at runtime with no re-embedding. Composes multiplicatively with int8/binary (e.g. 256 dims at int8 = 12x less traffic than 768 fp32). Storage of the truncated copy is tiny.
methods.weaknesses: Requires an MRL-trained model -- truncating a non-MRL embedding degrades badly. Adds a second copy of the vectors unless you store only the prefix and accept approximate final ranking. Not all strong open embedding models are MRL-trained.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes, and free if your embedding model already supports it (many recent open models and OpenAI's text-embedding-3 family do). Pure win when available.

methods.name: HNSW (in-memory proximity graph)
methods.mechanism: Layered navigable small-world graph with heuristic diverse neighbor selection; greedy descent through layers then beam search of width efSearch at layer 0.
methods.strengths: Best-in-class recall-vs-latency for in-memory ANN at 10^6-10^8 scale; sublinear query cost; mature implementations (hnswlib, FAISS, usearch) and one intuitive runtime knob (efSearch).
methods.weaknesses: Build cost and memory overhead (M*2 neighbor ids per node, ~128 B/node at M=16, plus the vectors). Recall is data- and insertion-order-dependent and degrades on out-of-distribution queries. Deletes are tombstones that decay quality until rebuild. Random memory access pattern is exactly what a small cache-resident flat scan avoids. The hierarchy itself is not the source of the benefit (flat NSW matches it in high dimensions).
methods.local_feasibility: Yes technically, but usually unnecessary and often counterproductive below ~10^6 vectors. The ~2-5 ms it saves is invisible next to an LLM call, and the recall it costs is not.

methods.name: Flat NSW (HNSW without the hierarchy)
methods.mechanism: Single-layer navigable small-world graph with the same neighbor-selection heuristic; beam search from a fixed or random entry point.
methods.strengths: Matches HNSW latency and recall on high-dimensional embeddings with lower memory overhead; simpler to implement and reason about.
methods.weaknesses: Same mutation, determinism, and OOD-recall weaknesses as HNSW. Less library support than HNSW.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes, but the same 'why bother at this scale' objection applies. Relevant mainly as evidence that HNSW's complexity is not buying what its name implies.

methods.name: IVF-Flat (inverted file with coarse k-means partitions)
methods.mechanism: k-means the corpus into nlist cells; at query time probe the nprobe nearest centroids and exhaustively scan those cells.
methods.strengths: Cheap to build, easy to reason about, memory overhead is just the centroids, and nprobe is a clean recall dial. Supports rebuild-free appends reasonably well.
methods.weaknesses: Breaks down at small N. FAISS's own rule is nlist ~ 4*sqrt(N) to 16*sqrt(N), which at N=10^5 means 1264-5056 cells, i.e. 20-80 vectors per cell -- cell-boundary effects then force a large nprobe, so you scan a large fraction of the index anyway and have gained nothing over a flat scan. Needs periodic re-clustering as the corpus grows.
methods.local_feasibility: Technically yes, practically pointless at 10^3-10^5. IVF earns its keep from 10^6 upward.

methods.name: IVF-PQ / OPQ+PQ (compressed inverted file)
methods.mechanism: IVF coarse partitioning plus product quantization of residuals into m-byte codes; asymmetric distance computation via cache-resident (or SIMD-register, fast-scan) lookup tables; optional exact re-rank of top candidates.
methods.strengths: Extreme memory reduction (e.g. 768 fp32 = 3072 B down to 32-64 B), which is what makes billion-scale in-RAM search possible. Mature and heavily optimized in FAISS.
methods.weaknesses: No theoretical error bound and documented catastrophic failures on some datasets (the motivation for RaBitQ). Codebooks are fit on an initial sample and go stale as the corpus grows, silently losing recall in streaming settings. Two layers of approximation (partition + quantization) compound. Training cost and complexity.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes but wrong tool. A laptop store of 10^5 x 768 fp32 is 307 MB -- it already fits in RAM, so the entire premise of PQ (memory pressure) does not apply. Prefer RaBitQ/int8 with exact rescoring if you want compression.

methods.name: ScaNN (anisotropic vector quantization + SOAR)
methods.mechanism: Score-aware quantization loss that penalizes the component of quantization error parallel to the datapoint more heavily, since parallel error is what distorts high inner products; combined with partitioning and SIMD-friendly reordering plus an exact rescoring stage.
methods.strengths: Best-in-class MIPS accuracy at a given code size; the anisotropic-loss insight is correct and generalizes. Strong published QPS/recall results.
methods.weaknesses: Heavier dependency (TensorFlow-adjacent historically), less portable than FAISS or a hand-rolled scan, and tuning surface is large. Benefits concentrate at large N.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes on macOS but rarely worth the dependency for <10^5 vectors. The transferable lesson -- normalize, and weight quantization error by its effect on inner products -- is worth taking even if you never install ScaNN.

methods.name: DiskANN / Vamana (SSD-resident graph)
methods.mechanism: Vamana graph built with alpha-pruning to keep search paths short; PQ-compressed vectors in RAM guide beam search while full-precision vectors and adjacency lists are read from SSD, with a final exact rescore.
methods.strengths: The right answer when the index exceeds RAM; reported billion-point search at <3 ms mean latency with 95%+ 1-recall@1 on 64 GB + SSD. FreshDiskANN adds streaming inserts/deletes. Has the strongest worst-case theoretical support of the graph family (slow-preprocessing variant, bounded intrinsic dimension).
methods.weaknesses: Long build times, complex to operate, I/O now accounts for 70-90% of query latency in disk-based graph indexes. Massive overkill below 10^7 vectors.
methods.local_feasibility: Runs on a laptop (that is literally its design point: one commodity machine), but there is no scenario at 10^3-10^5 chunks where it is the right choice.

methods.name: BM25 over an inverted index (SQLite FTS5)
methods.mechanism: Classic probabilistic term weighting: sum over query terms of IDF(q) * tf-saturation with document-length normalization. FTS5 hard-codes k1=1.2, b=0.75 and returns the negated score (numerically smaller = better), exposed as bm25() or the cached rank column, with optional per-column weights.
methods.strengths: Exact lexical match on identifiers, file paths, error codes, names, dates, API symbols -- precisely the tokens an embedding model was never trained on and provably cannot always represent. Zero embedding cost at index or query time. Sublinear via posting lists. Strong out-of-domain baseline (BEIR). Choice among BM25 variants is empirically immaterial.
methods.weaknesses: No semantic generalization; vocabulary mismatch is fatal. FTS5's tokenizers are limited (unicode61, ascii, porter, trigram) with no lemmatization or synonym expansion built in. Scores are unbounded and not comparable across queries, so they need rank-based fusion.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes, and it is already in the SQLite you have. FTS5 is a first-class virtual table with prefix indexes, column weights, and an ORDER BY rank fast path. Non-negotiable component of a local agent memory store.

methods.name: Learned sparse retrieval (SPLADE / SPLADE++) over an inverted index
methods.mechanism: MLM head projects text to a non-negative |V|-dim sparse vector with explicit sparsity regularization; document-side expansion adds terms the document does not literally contain; served from an inverted index.
methods.strengths: Combines exact-match semantics with learned term expansion, closing much of the vocabulary-mismatch gap while keeping interpretability. Competitive with dense retrieval and often more robust out-of-domain.
methods.weaknesses: Requires a transformer forward pass per document at index time and (for query expansion variants) per query. Its weight distribution breaks BM25-era dynamic pruning, so you need Seismic-class or Block-Max-Pruning query processing rather than a stock inverted index. Longer effective queries and sub-word tokenization inflate posting traversal. 'Wacky weights' hurt the interpretability claim.
methods.local_feasibility: Possible but a poor cost/benefit fit at this scale: you inherit both an encoder dependency and a specialized index, when a small cross-encoder reranker over a BM25+dense pool gets you comparable quality with far less machinery.

methods.name: Late interaction (ColBERTv2 / PLAID)
methods.mechanism: One vector per token; MaxSim scoring (per query token, max similarity over document tokens, summed). ColBERTv2 compresses with centroid + quantized residual; PLAID prunes via centroid interaction before residual refinement and exact MaxSim.
methods.strengths: Near cross-encoder quality with precomputable document representations; strong on BEIR and provably more expressive than any single vector at comparable size.
methods.weaknesses: Storage is ~1 vector per token, roughly 100x the vector count of a chunk-level dense index. Needs PLAID-class pruning machinery to be fast. The reproducibility study found PLAID's centroid clusters are mostly single-token-aligned, and that BM25 -> ColBERTv2 reranking gives better efficiency-effectiveness trade-offs in low-latency settings.
methods.local_feasibility: Feasible as a reranker over a top-50 pool on a laptop; not advisable as a first-stage index for a local memory store because of the storage blowup and the engine complexity.

methods.name: Hybrid retrieval with Reciprocal Rank Fusion
methods.mechanism: Run lexical (BM25/FTS5) and dense (flat vector scan) retrieval independently, take top-n from each, and fuse by score(d) = sum_i w_i / (k + rank_i(d)) with k=60 conventionally. Weighted or per-query-IDF-adaptive w_i improves on fixed weights.
methods.strengths: Rank-based, so no score normalization is needed across incomparable scales (unbounded negated BM25 vs cosine in [-1,1]). Raises the first-stage recall ceiling, which is what binds end-to-end quality. Roughly ten lines of code. Robust: it degrades gracefully when one channel fails on a query, and the two channels disagree on the majority of queries (74.5% top-10 disagreement across 753 BEIR queries), so the complementarity is real and measurable.
methods.weaknesses: Discards score magnitude, so a confident top-1 ties with a weak top-1. k=60 is a convention, not a derived optimum. Fixed weights are suboptimal; adaptive weighting is measurably better but adds tuning surface.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes -- trivially. This is the single highest value-per-line component of a local agent memory store.

methods.name: Cross-encoder reranking (monoBERT / monoT5 / shallow cross-encoders)
methods.mechanism: Jointly encode (query, candidate) with full attention and emit a relevance score; apply only to the top-20 to top-100 of a fused first-stage pool.
methods.strengths: Highest-quality scoring available; full query-document interaction. Under a fixed low-latency budget, shallow (few-layer) cross-encoders beat full-size ones because they score more candidates per millisecond. monoT5-style models are notably data-efficient with little training data.
methods.weaknesses: Cost is linear in pool size and cannot be precomputed. Cannot recover documents the first stage missed, so it multiplies first-stage recall rather than replacing it. Not always a win: the vstash study reports cross-encoder reranking failing to improve NDCG on top of a well-tuned adaptive-RRF hybrid. Adds a model dependency and 50-500 ms of CPU on a laptop.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes for pools of 20-50 with a shallow model (MiniLM-class) on CPU, or any size with GPU/ANE. Measure the delta on your own corpus before shipping it -- it is the most commonly assumed and least commonly verified stage.

methods.name: sqlite-vec (vec0 virtual table)
methods.mechanism: Pure-C, dependency-free SQLite extension. vec0 virtual tables store vectors in shadow tables alongside your relational data; KNN queries are expressed in plain SQL. Element types float32, int8, and bit; distances L2 and cosine (float32/int8) and Hamming (bit); metadata columns, auxiliary columns, and partition keys for filtering. Search is brute-force by default -- there is no IVF or HNSW index.
methods.strengths: One file, no server, no separate process, runs everywhere SQLite runs. Vectors sit in the same transaction as your metadata, so filters, joins, and deletes are ordinary SQL and are ACID. Brute-force means recall = 1.0 and no index staleness. Binary and int8 columns give the compression ladder in-engine.
methods.weaknesses: Brute-force only, so it inherits the Theta(N*d) wall. Documentation is explicitly work-in-progress. Fewer distance metrics and no built-in reranking pipeline. Community forks exist for features like distance constraints and space reclamation.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes -- this is the reference substrate for the stated use case. Paired with FTS5 in the same database file it gives hybrid retrieval with zero infrastructure.

methods.name: FAISS as an in-process library
methods.mechanism: Index factory composing a preprocessing transform (PCA/OPQ), a coarse quantizer (Flat/IVF/HNSW), an encoding (Flat/SQ/PQ/RaBitQ), and an optional refinement/rescoring stage.
methods.strengths: The most complete and best-optimized toolkit; IndexFlatIP is a fast blocked exact scan and IndexHNSWFlat, IVF variants, scalar/product/RaBitQ quantizers, and refine wrappers are all one factory string away. Excellent for measuring your own recall-vs-latency curve before committing.
methods.weaknesses: Indexes are separate from your metadata store, so you own the id mapping, persistence, and crash consistency yourself -- exactly what sqlite-vec avoids. Deletion support varies by index type. Native dependency to ship.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes on macOS (pip install faiss-cpu). Best used at this scale as a measurement instrument and as IndexFlatIP, not as an ANN engine.

methods.name: SQLite FTS5 as the lexical half
methods.mechanism: Virtual table with an inverted index; MATCH for querying; bm25() / rank for scoring with optional per-column weights; unicode61 (default), ascii, porter, and trigram tokenizers; configurable prefix indexes.
methods.strengths: Already present, transactional with the rest of your data, no server, ORDER BY rank uses a cached score and is faster than ORDER BY bm25(). Trigram tokenizer gives substring search, prefix indexes give fast wildcards -- both useful for identifier-heavy agent memory.
methods.weaknesses: k1 and b are hard-coded (though variant choice is empirically immaterial). No stemming beyond Porter, no synonyms, no field-level BM25F. Score sign convention (negated, smaller is better) trips people up. External-content tables need manual trigger maintenance.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes -- built in. Combine with sqlite-vec in the same file and fuse with RRF.

methods.name: Metadata pre-filtering with exact scan (SQL WHERE + flat)
methods.mechanism: Apply recency windows, session/thread ids, source, tags, or user scoping as SQL predicates, then scan only the surviving vectors exactly.
methods.strengths: Filters make a flat scan strictly faster (fewer vectors) with no recall loss. This is the inverse of the ANN situation and is a genuine structural advantage of the flat/SQL design. Agent memory is filter-heavy by nature.
methods.weaknesses: Requires the filter to be selective enough to matter; a non-selective filter buys nothing. Needs ordinary B-tree indexes on the metadata columns.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes. Note the contrast: selective filters break HNSW graph connectivity, forcing either post-filtering (recall loss) or heavy over-fetching -- an open problem serious enough to have its own Big-ANN'23 competition track and a filtered-ANN benchmark literature.

methods.name: LSH / random-projection hashing
methods.mechanism: Data-independent random hyperplane or p-stable projections into buckets; probe colliding buckets.
methods.strengths: Data-independent (no training, no staleness), sublinear with theoretical guarantees, and simple.
methods.weaknesses: Empirically dominated by graph and quantization methods on modern embeddings across every benchmark generation since 2016; needs many hash tables for good recall, which costs memory. Its enduring contribution is the projection-then-quantize framing that modern quantizers formalize.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes but no reason to. Listed for completeness; superseded.

takeaways: Do the arithmetic before choosing an index. A flat scan is Theta(N*d) and memory-bandwidth-bound, not FLOP-bound. At N=10^5, d=768, fp32 the scan block is 10^5*768*4 = 307 MB, so at realistic laptop bandwidth (~50-200 GB/s) a query costs roughly 1.5-6 ms, and lower with a BLAS sgemm across cores. At N=10^4 it is ~30 MB and sub-millisecond. At N=10^3 it is 3 MB, fits in L2/L3, and costs tens of microseconds. Exact search is free at 10^3-10^4 and cheap at 10^5.

Compare that number to the rest of the agent loop, not to zero. Embedding the query on CPU is typically 5-50 ms; the LLM call is 300 ms to 10 s. Shaving 2-5 ms off retrieval with an ANN index is invisible end-to-end, while the recall it costs is not. Build an ANN index only when measured retrieval latency exceeds roughly 10-20% of turn latency.

The honest headline: for 10^3-10^5 chunks on a single laptop, an ANN index is unnecessary and usually harmful. Use exact flat search. You get recall = 1.0, zero build time, O(1) inserts and deletes, deterministic results, no parameters to mis-tune, and metadata filters that make search faster instead of breaking it. FAISS's own guidance says Flat is the only index guaranteeing exact results and is the right choice when you will run only ~1000-10000 searches; sqlite-vec ships brute-force-only for exactly this regime; and arXiv:1706.01449 showed a blocked brute-force matmul beating purpose-built exact MIPS indexes by over an order of magnitude on many inputs.

IVF specifically breaks at this scale, and it is worth naming why. FAISS's rule of thumb is nlist ~ 4*sqrt(N) to 16*sqrt(N). At N=10^5 that is 1264-5056 cells, i.e. 20-80 vectors per cell. At that granularity cell-boundary effects dominate, so you need a large nprobe to reach acceptable recall, which means scanning a large fraction of the index anyway -- you have paid for clustering, added staleness, and gained nothing. IVF-PQ is a memory-pressure tool for 10^8-10^9 vectors; a 307 MB corpus has no memory pressure.

If flat ever gets slow, compress before you approximate. The ladder, in order, each rung keeping an exact final stage: fp32 flat -> int8 scalar (4x less traffic, near-lossless) -> MRL prefix truncation (768 -> 256, another 3x, requires an MRL-trained model) -> binary / RaBitQ (32x, popcount scan) with fp32 rescoring of an oversampled shortlist. Composed, 256-dim binary is ~96x less memory traffic than 768-dim fp32: a 10^5-chunk store becomes ~3 MB and searches in microseconds, still with an exact final ranking. Every rung of this ladder is deterministic; an ANN graph is not.

The two-stage quantize-then-rescore recall model is simple and worth internalizing: end-to-end recall@k = P(true top-k is contained in the size-R shortlist). Only the shortlist stage is approximate; the rescore is exact. So you tune exactly one interpretable number, the oversampling factor R (commonly 10k to 40k), and you can measure the shortlist recall directly by running the flat scan as ground truth -- which is cheap at this scale. Rescore cost is R*d, negligible for R <= 1000.

Graph ANN recall is a concave, brutally diminishing function of work. HNSW's cost is roughly efSearch * out-degree distance evaluations; QPS falls about linearly in efSearch while recall saturates. The empirical shape across ANN-Benchmarks and VIBE: 0.90 -> 0.99 recall typically costs 3-10x more distance computations, and 0.99 -> 0.999 costs another 3-10x. Since exact search already costs only a few milliseconds at 10^5, paying multiples of compute to buy back recall you already had for free is the wrong side of the trade.

Graph ANN recall is also not a fixed property of the algorithm. It depends on intrinsic dimensionality and even on insertion order (arXiv:2405.17813), degrades by an order of magnitude in latency-at-fixed-recall on out-of-distribution queries (OOD-DiskANN), and has worst-case guarantees only for the slow-preprocessing DiskANN variant under bounded intrinsic dimension (arXiv:2310.19126). For an incrementally written agent memory store, a recall number measured once at build time does not transfer.

Mutation is the second structural argument against a graph index for agent memory. Memories are superseded, corrected, and forgotten. Static graph indexes handle deletes by tombstoning and decay until rebuild -- FreshDiskANN exists precisely to solve this. In a flat/SQL store, a delete is a DELETE.

If you ever do build a graph, note that the hierarchy is not where the benefit comes from: a flat navigable small-world graph matches HNSW's latency and recall on high-dimensional data with less memory overhead, with a hub-highway effect substituting for the layers (arXiv:2412.01940). Budget the complexity accordingly.

Lexical retrieval is not optional, and this is a theorem, not a preference. Agent memory queries are dense with exact tokens the embedding model never saw: identifiers, file paths, error codes, ticket numbers, person names, dates, API symbols, internal project names. Single-vector embeddings provably cannot represent arbitrary relevance sets at fixed dimension (arXiv:2508.21038), and BEIR has shown for years that BM25 is a strong out-of-domain baseline. Your own memory corpus is out-of-domain for every off-the-shelf embedding model by construction.

SQLite FTS5 gives you competent BM25 in-process for free. Specifics that matter: k1=1.2 and b=0.75 are hard-coded; the score is negated so numerically smaller is better (use ORDER BY rank, which is cached and faster than ORDER BY bm25(ft)); trailing real arguments to bm25() set per-column weights; tokenizers are unicode61 (default), ascii, porter, and trigram; prefix indexes are configurable via prefix='2 3'. Do not spend time on BM25 variants -- eight variants show no significant effectiveness differences (Kamphuis et al., ECIR 2020). Spend it on tokenization and field weighting.

Hybrid + RRF is the highest value-per-line change available. score(d) = sum_i w_i / (k + rank_i(d)) with k=60. Because it is rank-based, it needs no score normalization -- essential when fusing FTS5's unbounded negated BM25 with cosine in [-1,1]. The complementarity is measurable, not folkloric: 74.5% of 753 BEIR queries produce top-10 disagreement between vector-heavy and FTS-heavy rankings (arXiv:2604.15484). Adaptive per-query IDF weighting beat fixed weights on all 5 BEIR datasets tested there, up to +21.4% NDCG@10.

Fusion matters because first-stage recall is the binding constraint, and no downstream stage can undo a miss. End-to-end recall = P(relevant doc in first-stage pool) * P(reranker keeps it in top-k). The cleanest demonstration is the PLAID reproducibility study (arXiv:2404.14989): BM25 -> ColBERTv2 reranking gives better efficiency-effectiveness trade-offs than the purpose-built PLAID engine at low latency, and plateaus at high latency only because of lexical recall limits -- which neighbor-expansion of top-scoring documents then fixes. Widen the pool before you deepen the scorer.

Rerank, but verify. A shallow cross-encoder over a top-30 to top-50 fused pool is affordable on a laptop CPU and is usually the largest remaining quality jump; under a fixed low-latency budget, few-layer models beat full-size ones because they score more candidates per millisecond (arXiv:2403.20222). But this is not automatic: vstash reports cross-encoder reranking failing to improve NDCG on top of a well-tuned adaptive-RRF hybrid. Measure the delta on your own corpus before shipping the dependency.

Learned sparse (SPLADE) and late interaction (ColBERT/PLAID) are the wrong first stage at this scale -- for infrastructure reasons, not quality reasons. SPLADE needs an inverted index tuned to its weight distribution (Seismic, Block-Max Pruning) because BM25-era dynamic pruning underperforms on it; ColBERT stores one vector per token, roughly 100x the vector count. Both are reasonable as a reranking stage over a small pool. SPLATE (arXiv:2404.13950) is the interesting middle path if you want late-interaction quality on inverted-index infrastructure.

Metadata pre-filtering is a structural advantage of the flat/SQL design and a genuine weakness of ANN indexes. Recency windows, session ids, source, tags, and user scoping are pervasive in agent memory. With a flat scan, a selective WHERE clause makes retrieval strictly faster with zero recall loss. With HNSW, a selective filter fragments graph connectivity and forces post-filtering (recall loss) or heavy over-fetching -- hard enough to warrant its own Big-ANN'23 competition track and an entire filtered-ANN benchmark literature.

Concrete recommended architecture for 10^3-10^5 chunks on a macOS laptop: one SQLite file containing (a) an FTS5 virtual table over chunk text, (b) a sqlite-vec vec0 table (or a BLOB column plus a NumPy/BLAS scan) holding fp32 or int8 embeddings, (c) ordinary columns and B-tree indexes for source, timestamp, session, and tags. Per query: retrieve top-100 from FTS5 by rank and top-100 by exact vector scan (applying metadata predicates in SQL), fuse with weighted RRF at k=60, optionally rerank the top-30 with a shallow cross-encoder, return top-5 to top-10. This is essentially the vstash configuration, which measured 20.9 ms median search latency at 50K chunks with stable NDCG.

Spend your quality budget on retrieval, not on clever write-time memory construction. On LoCoMo, retrieval method spans 20 points of average accuracy (57.1% to 77.2%) while write strategy spans only 3-8 points, and raw chunked storage -- zero LLM calls -- matches or beats Mem0-style fact extraction and MemGPT-style summarization (arXiv:2603.02473). Failures concentrate at the retrieval stage, not at utilization. Cheap write-side wins that do help: late chunking (arXiv:2409.04701) for context-aware chunk vectors at no query-time cost, and chunk sizing (64-128 tokens for fact lookup, 512-1024 for long-form; arXiv:2505.21700).

Measure these four things, and nothing else at first: (1) recall@k against exact ground truth -- trivial here, just run the flat scan; (2) nDCG@10 on 50-200 hand-labeled queries drawn from real agent traffic; (3) p50/p95 retrieval latency as a fraction of turn latency; (4) the fraction of queries where lexical and dense disagree in the top-10, which tells you how much your hybrid is actually buying. If (3) is under ~10%, an ANN index is a solution to a problem you do not have.

Migration triggers, in order. Revisit the design when per-query scan volume exceeds roughly 1-2 GB, i.e. about 10^6 chunks at 768d fp32 or about 10^7 at binary. Then: (1) int8, then MRL truncation, then binary/RaBitQ flat with fp32 rescoring; (2) only if that is still too slow, an in-memory graph -- HNSW or flat NSW -- accepting the recall, determinism, and delete costs; (3) only if the index no longer fits in RAM, DiskANN/Vamana on SSD. Skip IVF-PQ on a laptop entirely; its premise is memory pressure you do not have.

UNVERIFIED items flagged for honesty: the specific memory-bandwidth figures (50-200 GB/s) and the derived millisecond latencies in these takeaways are my own arithmetic from standard laptop hardware characteristics, not measurements from any cited paper -- benchmark them on your target machine. The binary-quantization oversampling range of 10k-40k is practitioner folklore consistent with the cited RaBitQ work but is not a number I verified in a specific paper. sqlite-vec's metadata columns, auxiliary columns, and partition keys are listed as features in its API reference, but the reference is explicitly marked work-in-progress and the implementation details were not documented at the page I fetched. The venue attributions for ColBERT (SIGIR 2020), ColBERTv2 (NAACL 2022), PLAID (CIKM 2022), SPLADE (SIGIR 2021), ScaNN (ICML 2020), MRL (NeurIPS 2022), RaBitQ (SIGMOD 2024), and Seismic (SIGIR 2024) come from my background knowledge; the arXiv identifiers and titles are what I verified in search results.

area: Graph-structured and temporal memory for LLM agents (2015–2026): GraphRAG-style hierarchical community summarization, bi-temporal knowledge graphs, temporal KG embeddings, RDF/property-graph/hypergraph modeling, PROV provenance, personalized-PageRank retrieval, entity resolution, and Zettelkasten-style linked-note memory — with an eye to what runs fully locally on a macOS laptop.

papers.title: From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization
papers.venue_or_id: arXiv:2404.16130 (Edge, Trinh, Cheng, Bradley, Chao, Mody, Truitt, Metropolitansky, Ness, Larson — Microsoft Research)
papers.core_idea: Two-stage LLM-built graph index: (1) extract an entity/relation knowledge graph from source chunks; (2) partition it with hierarchical community detection and pre-generate a community summary for every community at every level. A global query fans out over community summaries into map-reduce partial answers, then a final reduce.
papers.relevance: The canonical 'graph memory answers global/sensemaking questions that top-k vector RAG structurally cannot' result. Pre-generated summaries are the expensive part and the thing that must be invalidated when memory changes — the central tension for an agent memory store.

papers.title: From Louvain to Leiden: guaranteeing well-connected communities
papers.venue_or_id: Scientific Reports 9:5233, doi:10.1038/s41598-019-41695-z; arXiv:1810.08473 (Traag, Waltman, van Eck)
papers.core_idea: Louvain can return badly connected or even disconnected communities (up to 25% badly connected, 16% disconnected in their experiments); Leiden adds a refinement phase that guarantees connected communities, runs faster, and finds better partitions.
papers.relevance: This is the clustering algorithm GraphRAG and its descendants use to build the community hierarchy. Its guarantees (and its sensitivity to resolution parameter and graph sparsity) directly determine the quality of the summary hierarchy in a graph memory.

papers.title: Core-based Hierarchies for Efficient GraphRAG
papers.core_idea: Proves that on sparse knowledge graphs (constant average degree, most nodes low-degree) modularity optimization admits exponentially many near-optimal partitions, making Leiden output unstable; proposes k-core-based hierarchies instead.
papers.relevance: Direct theoretical attack on the Leiden step in GraphRAG. LLM-extracted personal/agent memory graphs are exactly the sparse regime described, so community summaries built this way can be non-reproducible run to run.

papers.title: LightRAG: Simple and Fast Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.core_idea: Graph-augmented text index with a dual-level retrieval paradigm: low-level retrieval over specific entities/relations and high-level retrieval over broader themes, plus incremental index updates so new documents do not force a full rebuild.
papers.relevance: The cheaper, incrementally-updatable alternative to full GraphRAG; the dual-level (entity keyword + theme keyword) split is the standard design pattern for agent memory that must serve both 'what did I say about X' and 'what have I been working on'.

papers.title: Zep: A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory
papers.core_idea: Memory-layer service built on Graphiti, a temporally-aware knowledge graph engine that fuses unstructured conversation and structured business data into a graph with bi-temporally scoped edges; outperforms MemGPT on Deep Memory Retrieval and on longer enterprise-style evaluations.
papers.relevance: The reference architecture for bi-temporal agent memory. Its core move — never delete, invalidate an edge by closing its valid-time interval — is what lets an agent answer 'what did I believe then' as well as 'what is true now'.

papers.title: Graphiti (getzep/graphiti): temporally-aware knowledge graph engine for agent memory
papers.venue_or_id: Open-source library + Zep and Neo4j engineering documentation (help.getzep.com/graphiti, blog.getzep.com, neo4j.com developer blog)
papers.core_idea: Builds dynamic time-aware KGs where every edge carries temporal metadata for the relationship lifecycle; supports point-in-time queries and automatic edge invalidation when new episodes contradict prior facts. Documentation describes four timestamps per edge as part of a bi-temporal model.
papers.relevance: The concrete implementation most agent-memory projects reach for. Note the exact bi-temporal semantics live in docs, not a peer-reviewed spec — the '(t_valid_from, t_valid_to, t_ingested, t_invalidated)' quadruple is the de facto standard. UNVERIFIED: precise release year and whether the four timestamps map exactly onto SQL:2011 valid/transaction time.

papers.title: A Graph-Native Bitemporal Memory Store for Conversational AI Agents
papers.core_idea: Agent-local Neo4j property graph plus HNSW vector indexes and a full bitemporal model: immutable identity node linked to versioned content nodes, each carrying two closed-open intervals (valid time = when true in the world; transaction time = when the DB recorded it). Point-in-time semantic retrieval without overwriting history. On 60 sampled LongMemEval questions: 46.7% R@10 overall for current-state search, 80% on knowledge-update questions; the time-travel path also hits 80% on knowledge-update but drops temporal-reasoning recall from 50% to 37.5% due to post-filter dilution.
papers.relevance: The single most on-point paper for 'local agent memory store': explicitly motivated by not sending personal data to a third-party memory service, and it reports the honest failure mode — naive time-travel filtering hurts temporal reasoning recall because filtering after ANN search shrinks the candidate pool.

papers.title: TGMS: An Agent-Native Bi-Temporal Graph Management System
papers.core_idea: Bi-temporal property graph exposing thirteen verified temporal operators as agent tools — each typed, deterministic, bounded, cost-guarded and bi-temporal by default. The LLM plans operator calls; the system does all graph computation.
papers.relevance: Answers the 'LLMs are bad at date arithmetic and identity' problem by moving temporal computation out of the model and into typed database operators. Important design pattern: separate correction (transaction time) from world-change (valid time) so the agent can answer 'we were wrong' vs 'it changed'.

papers.title: Less Context, More Accuracy: A Bi-Temporal Memory Engine for LLM Agents (Engram)
papers.core_idea: Open-source dual-process memory engine on a bi-temporal data model: fast write path appends lossless episodic records, slower path consolidates. Argues most memory systems beat full-context on cost/latency but lose on accuracy, and that reported benchmark numbers are non-reproducible across harnesses.
papers.relevance: Useful cost/accuracy framing and an explicit warning that memory-system leaderboards are harness-dependent — relevant when choosing between architectures on published numbers.

papers.title: Temporal Validity in Retrieval Memory: Eliminating Stale-Fact Errors for AI Agents over Evolving Knowledge
papers.core_idea: Shows the stale-fact problem is structural, not a tuning issue: on a calibrated dataset, cosine similarity distinguishes a contradicted fact from a duplicated one with AUROC 0.59 — near chance — because contradictions are often *more* embedding-similar to the original than rephrased duplicates.
papers.relevance: The cleanest quantitative argument for why flat vector memory cannot self-correct and why explicit valid-time intervals (not recency heuristics) are required. Cite this when justifying bi-temporal modeling cost.

papers.title: Time is Not a Label: Continuous Phase Rotation for Temporal Knowledge Graphs and Agentic Memory (RoMem)
papers.core_idea: Drop-in temporal KG module that encodes time as continuous phase rotation rather than discrete metadata, with a pretrained 'semantic speed' notion to distinguish persistent facts from fast-evolving ones — avoiding an LLM call per ingestion.
papers.relevance: Bridges the temporal-KG-embedding literature (TeRo/ChronoR rotations) to agent memory, and addresses the ingestion-cost problem: no LLM call per write.

papers.title: A-TMA: Decoupling State-Aware Memory Failures in Long-Term Agent Memory
papers.core_idea: Names and studies 'ghost memory': old, current, and transition facts coexisting in the bank, staying mixed through retrieval, and misleading the answer model. Proposes a state-aware overlay operating at three levels — bank maintenance, retrieval, answer-time resolution.
papers.relevance: Good taxonomy of where temporal errors are actually introduced. Useful for deciding whether to fix staleness at write time (invalidation), read time (filtering), or generation time (conflict resolution in the prompt).

papers.title: RAG Meets Temporal Graphs: Time-Sensitive Modeling and Retrieval for Evolving Knowledge
papers.core_idea: Argues current RAG lacks time-aware representations (same fact at different times is indistinguishable to embeddings and to conventional KGs) and that evaluations assume static corpora, hiding update cost and retrieval instability.
papers.relevance: Frames the two evaluation gaps an agent-memory designer must not skip: index update cost and retrieval stability as memory grows.

papers.title: HippoRAG: Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for Large Language Models
papers.core_idea: Hippocampal-indexing analogy: an LLM builds a schemaless open KG ('neocortex'), a retrieval encoder links query entities to graph nodes, and Personalized PageRank over the KG ('hippocampal index') performs single-step multi-hop retrieval by diffusing probability mass from seed entities.
papers.relevance: The key retrieval primitive for graph memory: PPR replaces iterative multi-round retrieval with one graph diffusion, so hop-2 evidence with near-zero query similarity still gets scored. This is precisely what flat vector top-k cannot do.

papers.title: From RAG to Memory: Non-Parametric Continual Learning for Large Language Models (HippoRAG 2)
papers.core_idea: Extends HippoRAG by applying PPR over a graph that includes passage nodes alongside entity nodes and using deeper LLM-in-the-loop context integration, improving associative memory and sense-making without sacrificing simple factual recall.
papers.relevance: Shows the practical fix for entity-only graphs: keep passages as first-class nodes so context is not collapsed into triples. Relevant to the 'context collapse' cost of extraction.

papers.title: Equivalence of Personalized PageRank and Successor Representations
papers.core_idea: Short note showing that personalized PageRank (proposed for hippocampal memory retrieval) and successor representations (proposed for planning/navigation) are isomorphic — both are the stationary distribution of the same underlying random walk.
papers.relevance: Theoretical grounding for why PPR is the natural retrieval operator over an associative memory graph, not just an engineering convenience.

papers.title: Breaking the Static Graph: Context-Aware Traversal for Robust Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.core_idea: Identifies the 'Static Graph Fallacy' in HippoRAG-style PPR: transition probabilities are fixed at index time, ignoring query-dependent edge relevance, so random walks get captured by high-degree hub nodes before reaching the critical downstream evidence (semantic drift).
papers.relevance: The main known failure mode of PPR retrieval on real memory graphs, where a few hub entities (the user, 'work', 'project') dominate degree. Motivates degree normalization or query-conditioned edge reweighting.

papers.title: TERAG: Token-Efficient Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.core_idea: HippoRAG-inspired framework that keeps PPR retrieval but builds the graph far more cheaply, reporting at least 80% of baseline accuracy at a small fraction of construction token cost.
papers.relevance: Quantifies the accuracy-you-give-up-for-cheap-indexing trade, which is the decisive number for a laptop-local store where every extraction token is a local-model second.

papers.title: PathRAG: Pruning Graph-based Retrieval Augmented Generation with Relational Paths
papers.core_idea: Argues the limitation of graph RAG is redundancy of retrieved context, not lack of it; retrieves key *relational paths* between query-relevant nodes with flow-based pruning and orders paths in the prompt.
papers.relevance: Path-level rather than node-level retrieval is what makes a multi-hop chain legible to the generator; also a concrete answer to graph RAG's context-bloat cost.

papers.title: Think-on-Graph: Deep and Responsible Reasoning of Large Language Model on Knowledge Graph
papers.core_idea: 'LLM⊗KG' paradigm: the LLM acts as an agent that iteratively beam-searches over the KG, choosing which entities and relations to expand next, and reasons over the retrieved paths.
papers.relevance: The query-time-traversal alternative to index-time summarization. No expensive pre-computation, but latency and token cost move to query time — the key architectural fork for a local store.

papers.title: Think-on-Graph 3.0: Multi-Agent Dual-Evolving Context Retrieval on Heterogeneous Graphs
papers.core_idea: Notes that existing GraphRAG depends on high-quality KGs — manual ones don't scale, automatic ones are bounded by extractor quality, especially with smaller locally deployed models — and proposes multi-agent context evolution and retrieval to compensate.
papers.relevance: Directly addresses the local-deployment case: small local extractors produce worse graphs, and the retrieval layer has to be built to tolerate that.

papers.title: LazyGraphRAG: Setting a new standard for quality and cost
papers.venue_or_id: Microsoft Research blog (microsoft.com/en-us/research/blog/lazygraphrag-setting-a-new-standard-for-quality-and-cost/); Project GraphRAG, github.com/microsoft/graphrag
papers.core_idea: Defers all LLM summarization to query time using best-first + breadth-first search with a relevance-test budget. Microsoft reports indexing cost identical to vector RAG and ~0.1% of full GraphRAG's, while matching or beating specialized local and global query mechanisms.
papers.relevance: The strongest published cost datapoint for the index-time-vs-query-time trade-off, and the design most suited to streaming/one-off agent memory. Not peer-reviewed — a vendor blog. UNVERIFIED: exact publication date (announced late 2024) and independent reproduction of the 0.1% figure.

papers.title: KET-RAG: A Cost-Efficient Multi-Granular Indexing Framework for Graph-RAG
papers.core_idea: Two-tier index: a knowledge-graph skeleton extracted by LLM only over a small set of key chunks, plus a cheap text-keyword bipartite graph over everything else, so cost scales with the skeleton rather than the corpus.
papers.relevance: The best-known concrete answer to 'LLM extraction over the whole corpus is unaffordable'. Directly transplantable to a laptop-local store where the LLM budget is wall-clock time.

papers.title: The Reasoning Bottleneck in Graph-RAG: Structured Prompting and Context Compression for Multi-Hop QA
papers.core_idea: Evaluating KET-RAG on HotpotQA, MuSiQue and 2WikiMultiHopQA: 77–91% of questions have the gold answer somewhere in the retrieved context, yet accuracy is only 35–78%, and 73–84% of errors are reasoning failures, not retrieval failures.
papers.relevance: Critical corrective. Building a better graph index buys you retrieval recall you may already have. For a memory store, this argues for investing in path-level context compression and structured prompting rather than a richer graph.

papers.title: In-depth Analysis of Graph-based RAG in a Unified Framework
papers.core_idea: Unifies representative graph-based RAG methods under one abstraction and compares them under identical experimental settings, which prior papers had not done.
papers.relevance: The reference apples-to-apples comparison; use it rather than each system's own reported numbers.

papers.title: RAG vs. GraphRAG: A Systematic Evaluation and Key Insights
papers.core_idea: Systematic head-to-head of text-based RAG against GraphRAG on general text organized into graph form, noting that existing GraphRAG systems are tailored to specific settings and do not generalize.
papers.relevance: Empirical grounding for 'when does the graph actually pay for itself'.

papers.title: When to use Graphs in RAG: A Comprehensive Analysis for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.core_idea: Directly confronts reports that GraphRAG frequently underperforms vanilla RAG on real-world tasks and analyzes in which scenarios graph structure provides measurable benefit.
papers.relevance: The honest scoping paper. Its conclusion pattern — graphs help on relational/global questions, hurt on single-fact lookup — should drive a hybrid router in any memory design.

papers.title: GraphRAG-Bench: Challenging Domain-Specific Reasoning for Evaluating Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.core_idea: Large-scale domain-specific benchmark built because standard QA datasets are too narrow in question type and metrics to show whether GraphRAG actually improves reasoning capacity.
papers.relevance: If you evaluate a local graph memory on HotpotQA alone you will not see the benefit or the cost; this benchmark is designed to expose both.

papers.title: A Pilot Empirical Study on When and How to Use Knowledge Graphs as Retrieval Augmented Generation
papers.core_idea: Systematizes KG-RAG methods and analyzes their performance across application scenarios and technical configurations to establish when KG-RAG is worth its complexity.
papers.relevance: Configuration-level guidance (graph granularity, retrieval mode) rather than yet another system.

papers.title: BM25 Wins at Scale: A Scaling Study of Retrieval-Augmented Generation Paradigms
papers.core_idea: Controlled study varying corpus size across 28 nested tiers spanning ~450x, with fixed questions, reader model and judging protocol, measuring accuracy, construction and query tokens, and latency across lexical, dense, graph-indexed and agentic paradigms.
papers.relevance: Rare controlled accuracy-vs-cost scaling curve. Sobering baseline: a well-tuned lexical index is a serious competitor, and any graph memory should be benchmarked against BM25 before graph complexity is accepted.

papers.title: A Triple-Robustness Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multi-Hop Requirements Traceability
papers.core_idea: Holds a five-pipeline architecture matrix fixed while varying embedder, corpus and LLM judge over ~8,880 main-matrix runs plus cross-corpus runs and thousands of faithfulness judgments. Finds reported GraphRAG-vs-vector verdicts flip with the measurement point, and that over-citation is architecturally universal (GraphRAG emits 11–15 IDs per answer).
papers.relevance: Explains why the literature disagrees about GraphRAG. Also flags a practical memory-system problem: graph retrieval floods the answer with citations, degrading citation precision.

papers.title: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey
papers.core_idea: Survey organizing GraphRAG into graph-based indexing, graph-guided retrieval, and graph-enhanced generation, with downstream tasks, benchmarks and applications.
papers.relevance: Standard entry point and taxonomy for the 2024–2025 literature.

papers.title: A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
papers.core_idea: Surveys GraphRAG for domain customization, framing three failures of flat text retrieval: complex query understanding, cross-document knowledge integration, and system efficiency.
papers.relevance: Useful complement focused on the customization/personalization angle closest to agent memory.

papers.title: HyperGraphRAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Hypergraph-Structured Knowledge Representation
papers.core_idea: Represents n-ary relational facts as hyperedges rather than forcing them into binary edges, with a full hypergraph construction, retrieval and generation pipeline.
papers.relevance: The core modeling argument for hypergraph memory: 'Alice met Bob in Tokyo in March about project X' is one fact, and binary-edge decomposition either loses the binding or requires reification.

papers.title: HyperRAG: Reasoning N-ary Facts over Hypergraphs for Retrieval Augmented Generation
papers.core_idea: Argues n-ary hypergraphs encode higher-order dependencies enabling shallower, more efficient reasoning paths than binary KGs, whose rigid retrieval and dense similarity search bring in irrelevant context.
papers.relevance: Quantifies the retrieval-depth benefit: a fact that takes 3 hops in a binary graph is 1 hyperedge lookup, which matters when each hop compounds error.

papers.title: PRoH: Dynamic Planning and Reasoning over Knowledge Hypergraphs for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.core_idea: Identifies three limits of knowledge-hypergraph RAG — static retrieval planning, non-adaptive execution, superficial use of hypergraph structure — and adds dynamic planning and reasoning.
papers.relevance: Shows hypergraph memory needs an adaptive retrieval planner to pay off; a static traversal wastes the extra structure.

papers.title: HyperMem: Hypergraph Memory for Long-Term Conversations
papers.core_idea: Hierarchical hypergraph memory architecture for conversational agents, explicitly modeling joint dependencies among multiple elements via hyperedges to avoid the fragmented retrieval caused by pairwise-only relations.
papers.relevance: The direct hypergraph-memory-for-agents datapoint; most relevant existing design if you want n-ary conversational memory.

papers.title: Cross-Granularity Hypergraph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multi-hop Question Answering
papers.core_idea: Argues GraphRAG over-relies on fine-grained word/phrase-level structure and under-uses passage semantics; combines hypergraph structure with cross-granularity retrieval for MHQA.
papers.relevance: Reinforces the recurring lesson that entity-only graphs collapse context and need chunk-level nodes alongside them.

papers.title: HyperSU: Corpus-Driven Semantic-Unit Hypergraph for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.core_idea: Notes existing HyperRAG methods build hyperedges from LLM-generated summaries — hallucination-prone and expensive to index — and that retrieval relying on one-hop expansion misses evidence while PageRank diffusion over-spreads. Builds hyperedges from corpus-driven semantic units instead.
papers.relevance: Names both cost failure modes of hypergraph memory in one abstract: LLM-summary hyperedges hallucinate, and PPR over hypergraphs drifts.

papers.title: TeRo: A Time-aware Knowledge Graph Embedding via Temporal Rotation
papers.core_idea: Models temporal evolution of an entity embedding as a rotation from initial time to current time in complex vector space; for interval facts each relation is a pair of dual relations for interval start and end.
papers.relevance: Canonical temporal KGE. Shows the alternative to explicit interval storage: encode time in the geometry. Useful for link prediction over agent memory, weak for exact 'as-of' queries.

papers.title: Diachronic Embedding for Temporal Knowledge Graph Completion
papers.core_idea: Introduces a diachronic entity embedding function that maps (entity, timestamp) to a hidden representation, so any static KGE model can be lifted to the temporal setting.
papers.relevance: The general recipe for making static embeddings temporal; the standard TKGE baseline (DE-SimplE).

papers.title: Tensor Decompositions for Temporal Knowledge Base Completion (TNTComplEx)
papers.core_idea: Order-4 tensor factorization for quadruples (s,r,o,t) with a temporal smoothness regularizer, and a decomposition separating temporal from non-temporal relation components.
papers.relevance: The strongest classical TKGE baseline; the temporal/non-temporal split matters for memory, where some facts (birthplace) never change and others (current employer) do.

papers.title: Temporal Knowledge Base Completion: New Algorithms and Evaluation Protocols (TIMEPLEX)
papers.core_idea: Joint link prediction and time-interval prediction in one compatible space, exploiting recurrence of relations and pairwise temporal ordering constraints between relations; also proposes better evaluation protocols.
papers.relevance: Time-*interval* prediction is exactly what a memory system needs when the source text says 'since last spring' rather than a date. The evaluation-protocol critique is also relevant.

papers.title: ChronoR: Rotation Based Temporal Knowledge Graph Embedding
papers.core_idea: Learns a k-dimensional rotation transformation parameterized jointly by relation and time, applied to the subject embedding.
papers.relevance: Rotation family alongside TeRo; the conceptual ancestor of RoMem's continuous phase rotation for agent memory.

papers.title: ATiSE: Temporal KG Embedding based on Additive Time Series Decomposition
papers.core_idea: Decomposes entity/relation representations into trend, seasonal and random components and maps them into multi-dimensional Gaussian distributions to model temporal uncertainty.
papers.relevance: Only TKGE line that models *uncertainty* about when a fact holds — important for memory extracted from vague conversational time expressions.

papers.title: Question Answering Over Temporal Knowledge Graphs (CRONQUESTIONS)
papers.core_idea: Largest temporal KGQA dataset at the time, stratified into buckets of structural complexity, with a baseline (CronKGQA) using TKG embeddings.
papers.relevance: The standard evaluation target for temporal multi-hop questions; useful for testing whether a bi-temporal memory actually answers 'who was X before Y' correctly.

papers.title: Complex Temporal Question Answering on Knowledge Graphs (EXAQT)
papers.core_idea: Two-stage temporal KGQA: compute a question-relevant compact subgraph tuned for recall, then rank with temporal-aware features for precision.
papers.relevance: The compact-subgraph-then-rank pattern is directly reusable as the retrieval stage of a temporal agent memory.

papers.title: ForecastTKGQuestions: A Benchmark for Temporal Question Answering and Forecasting over Temporal Knowledge Graphs
papers.core_idea: Points out CronQuestions lets models see future facts when answering questions about the past, and introduces a forecasting-style benchmark with strict temporal cutoffs.
papers.relevance: Exactly the leakage bug a bi-temporal memory must avoid: answering an 'as of March' question with facts ingested in June. Transaction-time filtering is the fix.

papers.title: IA-RAG: Interval-Algebra-Driven Temporal Reasoning for Dynamic Knowledge Retrieval
papers.core_idea: Represents facts as Interval Event Units and performs retrieval under formal temporal constraints (duration, overlap, containment) rather than coarse timestamps or metadata.
papers.relevance: Brings Allen interval algebra into RAG retrieval — the principled version of what bi-temporal memory stores approximate with range predicates.

papers.title: Temporal Knowledge-Graph Memory in a Partially Observable Environment
papers.core_idea: Room Environment v3: a configurable environment whose hidden state is an RDF KG and whose observations are RDF triples; the agent may extend observations into a temporal KG in long-term memory.
papers.relevance: A clean testbed where the memory representation is the independent variable — rare and useful for ablating graph vs flat memory without confounds.

papers.title: Bridging graph data models: RDF, RDF-star, and property graphs as directed acyclic graphs
papers.core_idea: Formalizes RDF, RDF-star and labeled property graphs in a common DAG-based framework, exposing where the models genuinely differ (triples with built-in semantics vs edges with inlined properties) versus where they are notational variants.
papers.relevance: The reference for choosing a memory data model. RDF gives you standard semantics, reasoning and PROV; LPG gives you cheap edge properties (which is where valid-time intervals naturally live).

papers.title: Reconciliation of RDF* and Property Graphs
papers.core_idea: First formalization of the property graph model and of RDF* (now RDF-star), with well-defined bidirectional mappings between them.
papers.relevance: Foundational (just before the 2015 window). RDF-star is what makes statement-level metadata — timestamps, confidence, provenance — expressible without n-ary reification blowup.

papers.title: Foundations of an Alternative Approach to Reification in RDF
papers.core_idea: Extends RDF and SPARQL to attach statement-level metadata, backwards compatible with standard reification but addressing its usability and data-management shortcomings; explicitly relates the approach to property graphs and hypergraphs.
papers.relevance: Reification is the unavoidable design decision for a temporal, provenance-carrying memory: every fact needs 'when valid', 'when recorded', 'from which source'. This paper is why RDF-star exists.

papers.title: Transforming RDF-star to Property Graphs: A Preliminary Analysis of Transformation Approaches
papers.core_idea: Analyzes transformation strategies from RDF-star to property graphs, noting RDF's rich inference ecosystem versus LPG's advantages in graph matching, path analysis and traversal.
papers.relevance: Practical guidance if you want to author memory in RDF-star (for standards/provenance) and execute traversals in an LPG engine.

papers.title: Directly Mapping RDF Databases to Property Graph Databases
papers.core_idea: Three formally defined direct mappings (schema-dependent and schema-independent) from RDF databases to property graph databases, covering both data and schema.
papers.relevance: Needed if a local memory store must interoperate with an RDF/PROV export while running on an embedded LPG engine.

papers.title: PROV-DM: The PROV Data Model / PROV-O: The PROV Ontology
papers.venue_or_id: W3C Recommendation, 30 April 2013 (PROV-DM eds. Moreau & Missier; PROV-O eds. Lebo, Sahoo & McGuinness); www.w3.org/TR/prov-dm/, www.w3.org/ns/prov-o.owl
papers.core_idea: Domain-agnostic provenance model of Entities (things), Activities (occur over time, act on entities) and Agents (bear responsibility), linked by wasGeneratedBy, used, wasAssociatedWith, wasDerivedFrom, wasAttributedTo, and time-stamped generation/usage/invalidation.
papers.relevance: The right vocabulary for 'where did this memory come from and which extraction run produced it'. Note PROV already carries generation and invalidation times — it covers transaction time natively, and you layer valid time on top.

papers.title: PAV Ontology: Provenance, Authoring and Versioning
papers.core_idea: Lightweight PROV-O extension distinguishing the roles of agents manipulating digital artifacts — authoring, contributing, curating — plus versioning and derivation-chain terms.
papers.relevance: For agent memory, distinguishes 'the user asserted this', 'the LLM inferred this', and 'this was imported' — a distinction that matters enormously for trust and for conflict resolution.

papers.title: Enhancing Data Integrity through Provenance Tracking in Semantic Web Frameworks
papers.core_idea: Industrial application of PROV-DM/PROV-O over RDF knowledge graphs, focusing on shared entity identification and choosing the right provenance granularity across data-processing domains.
papers.relevance: Practical treatment of the two costs of provenance in a KG: identity across sources, and how fine-grained to record before the provenance graph dwarfs the data graph.

papers.title: Representing provenance and track changes of cultural heritage metadata in RDF: a survey of existing approaches
papers.core_idea: Survey of models for representing provenance and tracking metadata change in RDF, and the limitations of core Semantic Web technologies for doing so.
papers.relevance: Closest thing to a survey of 'how do you version an RDF graph', which is the RDF-native form of the bi-temporal problem.

papers.title: A-MEM: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents
papers.core_idea: Explicitly Zettelkasten-based: each new memory becomes a structured note with contextual description, keywords and tags; the system analyzes historical notes to establish links where meaningful similarity exists; integrating a new note can trigger updates to the attributes of existing notes (memory evolution).
papers.relevance: The clearest transplant of Zettelkasten principles — atomic notes, explicit links, emergent structure rather than imposed taxonomy — into agent memory, and it beats graph-database-backed baselines across six foundation models.

papers.title: D-MEM: Dopamine-Gated Agentic Memory via Reward Prediction Error Routing
papers.core_idea: Notes that append-and-evolve systems like A-MEM incur O(N²) write latency and excessive token cost; routes writes by a surprise/utility critic so routine inputs bypass expensive restructuring.
papers.relevance: Names the scaling cost of Zettelkasten-style linking: every new note is compared against history, which is quadratic. Essential to know before adopting A-MEM on a laptop.

papers.title: How People Manage Knowledge in their "Second Brains": A Case Study with Industry Researchers Using Obsidian
papers.core_idea: Qualitative case study of how researchers actually build and explore personal knowledge bases in a linked-note tool.
papers.relevance: Empirical grounding for the human side of Zettelkasten memory: what linking behavior people sustain versus abandon, which constrains what an agent can assume about a user's note graph.

papers.title: PKG API: A Tool for Personal Knowledge Graph Management
papers.core_idea: End-to-end personal knowledge graph solution: a user-facing client that lets end users administer their own data via natural language statements, plus a service-oriented API, keeping fragmented personal data in one user-controlled place.
papers.relevance: Prior art for the user-controlled personal KG, including the representation and access-control questions a local agent memory inherits.

papers.title: Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory
papers.core_idea: Memory-centric architecture that dynamically extracts, consolidates and retrieves salient facts from ongoing conversations, with an enhanced graph-based variant capturing relational structure among conversational elements.
papers.relevance: The most widely deployed extract-and-consolidate memory design and the standard comparison point; its graph variant is the minimal-viable graph memory.

papers.title: Beyond the Context Window: A Cost-Performance Analysis of Fact-Based Memory vs. Long-Context LLMs for Persistent Agents
papers.core_idea: Compares a Mem0-based fact memory against long-context inference on LongMemEval, LoCoMo and PersonaMem v2, measuring accuracy and cumulative API cost. Long-context GPT-5-mini achieves higher factual recall on LongMemEval and LoCoMo; the memory system is competitive on PersonaMem.
papers.relevance: The uncomfortable baseline: for many memory questions, just paying for a long context still wins on accuracy. A structured memory must justify itself on cost, privacy or scale — not accuracy alone.

papers.title: Cost and Accuracy of Long-Term Memory in Distributed Multi-Agent Systems Based on Large Language Models
papers.core_idea: Independent reproducible testbed measuring accuracy, latency, CPU time, peak RAM, disk I/O and network usage for three VC-funded memory frameworks in a simulated cloud-edge environment — noting that published evaluations come from framework vendors and ignore system-level cost.
papers.relevance: The only source found that measures peak RAM and disk I/O, which is exactly what decides feasibility on a laptop.

papers.title: EraRAG: Efficient and Incremental Retrieval Augmented Generation for Growing Corpora
papers.core_idea: Multi-layered Graph-RAG using hyperplane-based locality-sensitive hashing to partition and organize the corpus so that new documents update only affected partitions instead of forcing full-graph reconstruction.
papers.relevance: Solves the single worst property of GraphRAG for agent memory: a static-corpus assumption. Memory grows every conversation, so incremental re-clustering and incremental summary invalidation are mandatory.

papers.title: E²GraphRAG: Streamlining Graph-based RAG for High Efficiency and Effectiveness
papers.core_idea: Builds an LLM summary tree plus a SpaCy-derived entity graph over chunks, with bidirectional entity↔chunk indexes, and adaptively selects local or global retrieval instead of requiring the user to pick a query mode.
papers.relevance: Two directly reusable ideas for a local store: use a cheap NLP pipeline (not the LLM) for the entity graph, and route queries automatically between local and global modes.

papers.title: Towards Practical GraphRAG: Efficient Knowledge Graph Construction and Hybrid Retrieval at Scale
papers.core_idea: Dependency-parsing-based KG construction reaching 94% of LLM-based extraction performance (61.87% vs 65.83%) at greatly reduced cost, plus a hybrid retrieval scheme.
papers.relevance: Concrete numbers for the extraction-quality-vs-cost curve; a strong argument that on a laptop you should parse first and call the LLM only where parsing is ambiguous.

papers.title: ContextRAG: Extraction-Free Hierarchical Graph Construction for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.core_idea: Derives graph topology with no LLM entity/relation extraction at all: a fuzzy concept graph over chunk embeddings via residual-quantization k-means and Formal Concept Analysis with Łukasiewicz residuated logic.
papers.relevance: The extreme of the cheap-index axis, and completely local: no LLM in the indexing loop means no extraction hallucination and no per-token indexing cost — at the price of losing typed relations.

papers.title: LiteSemRAG: Lightweight LLM-Free Semantic-Aware Graph Retrieval for Robust RAG
papers.core_idea: Fully LLM-free graph RAG that builds a heterogeneous semantic graph from contextual token-level embeddings, separating surface-level from semantic-level structure.
papers.relevance: Second independent datapoint that a useful retrieval graph can be built without any LLM calls — the key enabler for laptop-local indexing of large personal corpora.

papers.title: SlimRAG: Retrieval without Graphs via Entity-Aware Context Selection
papers.core_idea: Argues graph RAG's structural overhead buys imprecise retrieval — costly entity-linking and relation-extraction pipelines that still return subgraphs full of tangential content, because semantic similarity does not imply semantic relevance.
papers.relevance: The strongest 'don't build a graph' position paper. Worth adopting as the null hypothesis any graph memory must beat.

papers.title: RAGU: A Multi-Step GraphRAG Engine with a Compact Domain-Adapted LLM
papers.core_idea: Separates extraction from consolidation: two-stage typed extraction, DBSCAN-backed deduplication, LLM summarization, then Leiden community detection — arguing single-pass extraction produces noisy entities and brittle retrieval, and that a compact local extractor suffices.
papers.relevance: The clearest published architecture for the entity-resolution stage inside a GraphRAG pipeline, and it argues a small local model is adequate for extraction — exactly the laptop case.

papers.title: OMD-GraphRAG: Ontology-Guided Extraction, Multi-Dimensional Clustering and Dual-Channel Fusion
papers.core_idea: Adds a predefined schema to guide LLM extraction, multi-dimensional clustering instead of single-view Leiden, and dual-channel retrieval fusion, targeting extraction precision and community-report integrity.
papers.relevance: Schema-constrained extraction is the single highest-leverage fix for extraction accuracy: it converts open-ended generation into constrained classification.

papers.title: Structure Over Scale: Schema-Constrained Causal Graphs for RAG (HCG-RAG)
papers.core_idea: Replaces open-ended extraction with schema-constrained causal graphs over a fixed typed vocabulary distilled from the corpus, so graph size and construction cost scale with the reasoning a query requires rather than with corpus length.
papers.relevance: Reframes the cost problem correctly: unconstrained extraction makes index cost scale with corpus size, which is fatal for an ever-growing memory.
