papers.title: Enhancing Knowledge Graph Construction: Evaluating with Emphasis on Hallucination, Omission, and Graph Similarity Metrics
papers.core_idea: Evaluation framework for LLM-built KGs targeting hallucinated triples and omitted triples specifically, adding BERTScore-based graph similarity with a practical 95% graph-matching threshold.
papers.relevance: Gives you the two error types to actually measure on your extractor — hallucination and omission — rather than aggregate F1, which hides both.

papers.title: Text2KGBench: A Benchmark for Ontology-Driven Knowledge Graph Generation from Text
papers.core_idea: Benchmark evaluating whether an LM can generate KG triples from text that conform to a given ontology, with fact-extraction accuracy and ontology-conformance metrics.
papers.relevance: The standard way to measure whether schema-constrained extraction actually stays inside the schema — a prerequisite for trusting typed traversal.

papers.title: KGCQual: An Interpretable Framework for Evaluating Knowledge Graph Construction Quality from Text
papers.core_idea: Intrinsic KG-quality metric measuring how closely an automatically extracted graph approximates an 'ideal' graph of key noun phrases and predicates, since existing practice relies on downstream task metrics or small manual audits.
papers.relevance: Lets you monitor extraction drift in a running memory system without gold labels — necessary because a personal memory graph has no ground truth.

papers.title: Pre-trained Embeddings for Entity Resolution: An Experimental Analysis
papers.core_idea: Systematic comparison of 12 pre-trained language models across 17 established ER benchmarks, covering both blocking and matching, and measuring vectorization overhead as well as accuracy.
papers.relevance: The empirical baseline for the embedding-based blocking layer of a KG dedup pipeline, including the cost side (embedding time) that determines laptop feasibility.

papers.title: Match, Compare, or Select? An Investigation of Large Language Models for Entity Matching
papers.core_idea: Compares three LLM strategies for entity matching — pairwise matching, comparing candidates, and selecting among candidates — showing binary pairwise matching ignores global consistency among record relationships.
papers.relevance: Pairwise LLM merge decisions in a KG are not transitive; without a global consistency step you get contradictory merges. This is the concrete mechanism behind entity-resolution errors in graph memory.

papers.title: On Leveraging Large Language Models for Enhancing Entity Resolution: A Cost-efficient Approach
papers.core_idea: Uncertainty-aware batching and question selection to minimize LLM API calls in ER while preserving quality, since per-request billing makes naive LLM-based ER prohibitive at scale.
papers.relevance: ER is quadratic in candidate pairs; this is the budgeting strategy for calling an LLM only on genuinely ambiguous pairs — directly applicable when the 'budget' is local inference seconds.

papers.title: Auto-Configuring Entity Resolution Pipelines
papers.core_idea: Automatic configuration of the multi-step ER pipeline (blocking, similarity estimation, clustering), each stage of which normally requires dataset-specific manual tuning across a vast combinatorial space.
papers.relevance: An agent memory cannot ship a hand-tuned ER config per user; auto-configuration is the only realistic path.

papers.title: Adaptive Graph Refinement and Label Propagation with LLMs for Cost-Effective Entity Resolution
papers.core_idea: Critiques the dominant blocking→matching→clustering cascade for dirty ER: it yields a static, sparse graph with missing edges from blocking failures and noisy links from matching errors, and imposing rigid transitivity in clustering propagates those errors into bad clusters.
papers.relevance: The precise failure analysis for KG deduplication. In a memory graph, a false merge fuses two people's histories and a missed merge silently breaks every multi-hop path through that entity.

papers.title: OpenSanctions Pairs: Large-Scale Entity Matching with LLMs
papers.core_idea: 755,540 labeled pairs from 293 heterogeneous sources across 31 countries with multilingual/cross-script names, noisy and missing attributes, and set-valued fields; off-the-shelf LLMs substantially outperform a production rule-based matcher.
papers.relevance: The largest realistic ER benchmark found, and evidence that LLM matchers now beat hand-tuned rules — relevant to deciding how much of the ER stack to hand to a local model.

papers.title: ArchRAG: Attributed Community-based Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.core_idea: Attributed-community hierarchy over the KG with an index designed to reduce the large token consumption existing graph RAG incurs during online retrieval.
papers.relevance: Addresses the query-time (not just index-time) token cost of hierarchical community memory, which is what shows up as latency on a laptop.

papers.title: GAAMA: Graph Augmented Associative Memory for Agents
papers.core_idea: Notes entity-centric KGs over conversational data suffer 'mega-hub' effects that dilute graph-based relevance propagation; builds a concept-mediated graph with verbatim episode preservation plus LLM-derived concepts.
papers.relevance: Independent confirmation of the hub problem in PPR-based memory retrieval, with the concept-mediation fix. Conversational memory graphs are hub-dominated by construction (the user is in every fact).

papers.title: WorldDB: A Vector Graph-of-Worlds Memory Engine with Ontology-Aware Write-Time Reconciliation
papers.core_idea: Argues flat vector RAG fragments facts into chunks, loses cross-session identity, and has no first-class notion of supersession or contradiction; and that bitemporal KG systems (it names Graphiti, Memento, Hydra DB) add typed edges and valid-time metadata but leave the graph itself flat — no recursive composition, no content-addressed node invariants.
papers.relevance: Best statement of the second-order critique: bi-temporality alone does not give you compositional structure. Also a useful survey sentence of the current bitemporal memory landscape.

papers.title: Survey: On the Landscape of Graph Databases
papers.core_idea: Survey of property models, query languages and storage architectures, then recent advances in architecture, deployment, usage and development; highlights irregular/sparse graph layout inefficiency, the cost of traversal-based queries at scale, and OLTP scalability limits of centralized architectures.
papers.relevance: The systems-level reference for picking a storage engine. Note the index metadata dates are inconsistent (arXiv ID implies May 2025, index reports a 2026 revision) — treat the year as approximate.

papers.title: Beyond Vector Similarity: A Structural Analysis of Graph-Augmented Retrieval for Industrial Knowledge Graphs
papers.core_idea: Compares eight retrieval architectures from text retrieval through graph traversal to graph computation on a small typed KG (46 nodes, 64 typed edges) across 23 queries in 10 intent categories, and demonstrates five query classes that are structurally unreachable for vector retrieval. States an 'operator vocabulary thesis': the barrier to LLM graph reasoning is not model intelligence.
papers.relevance: The most explicit enumeration found of *which* query classes vector RAG cannot reach at all — the crisp answer to 'what does the graph buy you'. Caveat: tiny graph, single domain.

papers.title: EcphoryRAG: Re-Imagining Knowledge-Graph RAG via Human Associative Memory
papers.core_idea: Stores only core entities with metadata during indexing (reported up to 94% token reduction versus other structured RAG systems), then extracts cue entities from the query and performs scalable multi-hop associative search.
papers.relevance: Shows how far you can shrink the index and still support multi-hop, by pushing work to query time.

papers.title: Reliable Graph-RAG for Codebases: AST-Derived Graphs vs LLM-Extracted Knowledge Graphs
papers.core_idea: Benchmarks vector-only RAG, an LLM-generated KG, and a deterministic AST-derived KG (Tree-sitter, bidirectional traversal) on Java codebases for multi-hop architectural reasoning such as controller→service→repository chains.
papers.relevance: A controlled comparison isolating extraction accuracy: when a deterministic parser can produce the graph, it removes the dominant error source. The general lesson — derive structure deterministically wherever the domain permits — transfers to any local memory over structured artifacts.

methods.name: Flat dense-vector RAG (baseline / null hypothesis)
methods.mechanism: Chunk text, embed each chunk, ANN index (HNSW/IVF), retrieve top-k by cosine similarity to the query embedding, stuff into context. Optionally hybrid with BM25 and a cross-encoder reranker.
methods.strengths: Trivial to build and update (append-only, O(1) per write). No extraction step, so no extraction hallucination. Best-in-class on single-fact lookup. BM25 in particular scales extremely well (arXiv:2607.26497). Long-context baselines still beat structured memory on factual recall on LongMemEval and LoCoMo (arXiv:2603.04814).
methods.weaknesses: Scores each chunk independently against the query, so composition is impossible: for a bridge question, the hop-2 chunk shares no surface with the query and is never retrieved. No aggregation ('how many', 'what are the themes'). Cannot distinguish a superseded fact from the current one — cosine similarity separates contradiction from duplication at AUROC 0.59, near chance (arXiv:2606.26511). No provenance, no identity across sessions.
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local and trivially so. sentence-transformers or a GGUF embedding model via llama.cpp on Apple Silicon MPS; FAISS, hnswlib, sqlite-vec, LanceDB, or DuckDB VSS. A 100k-chunk personal corpus indexes in minutes and fits in a few hundred MB.

methods.name: GraphRAG-style hierarchical community summarization (Leiden)
methods.mechanism: LLM extracts an entity/relation graph from chunks; Leiden partitions it hierarchically; an LLM pre-generates a summary report per community per level. Global queries map over community summaries and reduce; local queries expand from matched entities (arXiv:2404.16130).
methods.strengths: The only method here that genuinely answers whole-corpus sensemaking questions ('what have I been working on this year', 'what are the recurring themes'). Community summaries are a compressed, human-auditable index. Leiden guarantees connected communities (Traag et al. 2019).
methods.weaknesses: Brutal index cost: an LLM pass over every chunk plus a summarization pass over every community at every level. Static-corpus assumption — new memories invalidate summaries and, in the worst case, force re-clustering. On sparse KGs, modularity optimization admits exponentially many near-optimal partitions, so the hierarchy is unstable run to run (arXiv:2603.05207). Over-cites: 11–15 IDs per answer (arXiv:2608.00705). Repeatedly reported to lose to vanilla RAG on ordinary lookup tasks (arXiv:2506.05690, arXiv:2502.11371).
methods.local_feasibility: Feasible but this is the expensive one. graspologic/leidenalg and igraph run natively and fast; the cost is the LLM. With a local 7–8B model on an M-series Mac expect roughly one extraction call per 600–1200-token chunk, so a 50MB corpus is hours of wall clock. Practical local pattern: run indexing as a background/overnight job, or restrict full community summarization to a curated subset (the KET-RAG skeleton idea).

methods.name: LightRAG dual-level graph index
methods.mechanism: Graph structure over the text index with two retrieval levels — low-level (specific entities/relations) and high-level (broader themes/keywords) — plus incremental index update for new documents (arXiv:2410.05779).
methods.strengths: Much cheaper than full GraphRAG, and incremental updates are a first-class feature rather than an afterthought — the decisive property for memory that grows every session. Covers both specific-recall and thematic queries.
methods.weaknesses: Still needs LLM extraction per chunk. Theme-level keys are LLM-generated and can drift. No temporal model at all — a fact and its correction sit side by side.
methods.local_feasibility: Good. Open-source reference implementation runs against local models and local storage backends; the graph fits in NetworkX or an embedded store for personal-scale data. This is the realistic starting point for a laptop graph memory.

methods.name: Open-KG + Personalized PageRank retrieval (HippoRAG family)
methods.mechanism: Schemaless LLM-extracted open KG; query entities are linked to graph nodes and used as the personalization vector for PPR; probability mass diffuses over the graph in one shot and top-scoring nodes/passages are returned (arXiv:2405.14831, arXiv:2502.14802).
methods.strengths: Single-step multi-hop: no iterative retrieve-read loop, so no per-hop LLM latency and no compounding of hop-wise retrieval errors. PPR is a principled soft reachability score, provably the same object as the successor representation (arXiv:2512.24722). Retrieval is pure linear algebra — no LLM at query time.
methods.weaknesses: Static transition probabilities set at index time ignore query-dependent edge relevance, so walks drift into high-degree hubs before reaching the target ('Static Graph Fallacy', arXiv:2602.01965). Conversational memory graphs are hub-dominated by construction (arXiv:2603.27910). Entity-only graphs lose sentence context; HippoRAG 2 has to add passage nodes back.
methods.local_feasibility: Excellent at query time. PPR over a few hundred thousand nodes is milliseconds with scipy sparse matrices or networkx; the whole retrieval path is CPU-only and offline. The cost stays in extraction — mitigated by TERAG-style cheap graph construction (arXiv:2509.18667), which reports ≥80% of the accuracy at far lower token cost.

methods.name: Bi-temporal property graph (Graphiti/Zep pattern)
methods.mechanism: Every edge/fact carries two closed-open intervals: valid time [when true in the world) and transaction time [when the store recorded it). Contradicting ingestion closes the prior edge's valid interval rather than deleting it. Queries are 'as of' filters over both axes (arXiv:2501.13956, arXiv:2607.26520, arXiv:2607.10265).
methods.strengths: The only design that answers all four question classes: what is true now, what was true then, what did I believe then, and what changed and when. Immutable history gives free audit and free rollback of bad extractions (close the transaction interval on a whole ingestion run). Prevents the temporal leakage that plagues TKGQA benchmarks (arXiv:2208.06501). Combines cleanly with HNSW vector indexes on the same nodes.
methods.weaknesses: Roughly doubles storage and complicates every query with range predicates. Naive post-filtering after ANN search dilutes the candidate pool — measured drop in temporal-reasoning recall from 50% to 37.5% (arXiv:2607.26520). LLMs are unreliable at the date arithmetic and identity handling these queries need, which is why TGMS pushes it into typed operators. And bi-temporality alone gives no compositional structure (arXiv:2604.18478).
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local. Neo4j Community runs on a Mac (JVM, a few GB heap) and is what the reference bitemporal store uses; embedded alternatives are Kuzu (embeddable C++ property graph with Cypher, MIT-licensed — note the project was archived in Oct 2025 after an Apple acquisition, with community forks and a successor, LadybugDB; UNVERIFIED beyond search snippets) or plain SQLite/DuckDB with (valid_from, valid_to, tx_from, tx_to) columns and recursive CTEs. For personal-scale memory, SQLite with proper interval indexes is genuinely sufficient and the least operationally risky.

methods.name: Temporal knowledge graph embeddings (TeRo / DE-SimplE / TNTComplEx / ChronoR / ATiSE)
methods.mechanism: Embed quadruples (s, r, o, t) in a space where time acts geometrically — rotation in complex space (TeRo, ChronoR), a diachronic entity function (DE), order-4 tensor factorization with temporal smoothing (TNTComplEx), or additive time-series decomposition into Gaussians (ATiSE).
methods.strengths: Predicts missing and future facts, not just retrieves stored ones. Handles interval facts and, in ATiSE, uncertainty about when a fact holds. TNTComplEx's temporal/non-temporal relation split matches the real structure of personal memory (birthplace never changes; employer does). RoMem (arXiv:2604.11544) shows the rotation idea working as a drop-in agent-memory module with no LLM call per ingestion.
methods.weaknesses: Approximate and uninterpretable — wrong for 'what exactly did I say on March 3'. Mostly transductive: new entities require retraining, which is fatal for memory where new entities arrive constantly (see arXiv:2302.05640, arXiv:2506.06367 on the extrapolation/inductive gap). Needs enough facts per entity to learn anything.
methods.local_feasibility: Trainable locally at personal scale — these are small models (a few hundred dims, tens of thousands of entities) and train in minutes on MPS in PyTorch. But the transductive retraining requirement makes them a periodic offline enrichment layer (link prediction, 'facts you probably know but never stated'), not the primary retrieval path.

methods.name: RDF / RDF-star triplestore with PROV-O provenance
methods.mechanism: Model memory as RDF triples; use RDF-star (or named graphs) to attach statement-level metadata — valid interval, confidence, extraction run — and PROV-O to record Entity/Activity/Agent with wasGeneratedBy, wasDerivedFrom, wasAttributedTo and generation/invalidation timestamps. Query with SPARQL; optionally run OWL/SHACL over it.
methods.strengths: Standardized, portable, and the only option with real reasoning and validation ecosystems. PROV natively carries generation and invalidation time, so transaction time comes for free; you layer valid time on top. PAV (arXiv:1304.7224) distinguishes user-asserted from LLM-inferred from imported — exactly the trust distinction agent memory needs for conflict resolution. Named graphs make it trivial to retract a whole bad extraction run.
methods.weaknesses: Reification is verbose: every qualified fact costs several extra triples, and provenance can outweigh the data (a granularity problem called out in arXiv:2501.09029). SPARQL path queries are slower than LPG traversal for analytics (arXiv:2210.05781, arXiv:2304.13097). Higher authoring friction; LLM extraction into a strict ontology is harder than into free-form triples.
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local: Apache Jena/Fuseki (JVM), Oxigraph (Rust, embeddable, RDF-star + SPARQL 1.1), or rdflib for small graphs. Oxigraph in particular is a single binary and a good fit for a laptop. Realistic hybrid: author and export in RDF-star/PROV for portability and audit, execute traversals in an LPG or in-memory graph (mappings are formalized in arXiv:1912.02127 and arXiv:2203.06393).

methods.name: Hypergraph / n-ary fact memory
methods.mechanism: Facts are hyperedges over 2+ entities rather than binary edges, so 'Alice met Bob in Tokyo in March about project X' is one object. Retrieval traverses hyperedges directly (arXiv:2503.21322, arXiv:2602.14470, arXiv:2510.12434, arXiv:2604.08256).
methods.strengths: Preserves the binding among all participants of an event — precisely what binary decomposition destroys and reification re-creates awkwardly. Shallower reasoning paths: a 3-hop binary chain becomes one hyperedge lookup, so fewer hops means less compounding error. Natural fit for episodic memory, where events are inherently n-ary.
methods.weaknesses: Less mature tooling; no standard query language or storage engine. Hyperedges are often built from LLM-generated summaries, which hallucinate and cost a lot to index (arXiv:2606.28351). PPR-style diffusion over hypergraphs over-spreads; one-hop expansion under-covers. Retrieval needs an adaptive planner to exploit the extra structure (arXiv:2510.12434).
methods.local_feasibility: Feasible with caveats. No embedded hypergraph DB worth depending on; in practice you encode hyperedges as reified event nodes in an LPG or RDF store, or keep an in-memory incidence structure (hypernetx, scipy sparse incidence matrices). Personal-scale hypergraphs fit in RAM easily. The real local cost is again LLM-driven hyperedge construction — use HyperSU's corpus-driven semantic units to avoid it.

methods.name: Zettelkasten / linked-note memory (A-MEM pattern)
methods.mechanism: Each memory becomes an atomic note with a contextual description, keywords and tags; on write, the system searches history for meaningful similarities and creates explicit links; integrating a new note can trigger updates to existing notes' attributes (memory evolution) (arXiv:2502.12110).
methods.strengths: Structure emerges from links rather than being imposed by a schema, so it degrades gracefully when extraction is wrong — a bad link is a weak edge, not a corrupted entity. Notes retain full context (no triple-level context collapse). Human-readable and human-editable, which matters enormously for a personal store; interoperates with an existing Obsidian/markdown vault. Beat graph-DB-backed baselines across six foundation models.
methods.weaknesses: Append-and-evolve is O(N²) in write latency and token cost as the note set grows (arXiv:2603.14597). No typed relations, so no precise structured query ('all meetings with X in Q2'). No temporal model. Link quality depends on the same embedding similarity that fails on contradictions.
methods.local_feasibility: Excellent and arguably the most natural local design: plain markdown files plus a SQLite link table plus a local embedding model. Everything is a file the user already owns and can inspect. Mitigate the O(N²) write cost with D-MEM-style surprise gating — only run the expensive linking pass on notes that are novel or contradict existing memory.

methods.name: Extraction-free / LLM-free graph construction
methods.mechanism: Build the retrieval graph with no LLM in the indexing loop: fuzzy concept graph over chunk embeddings via residual-quantization k-means plus Formal Concept Analysis (ContextRAG, arXiv:2605.19735); heterogeneous semantic graph from contextual token-level embeddings (LiteSemRAG, arXiv:2604.16350); dependency-parsing extraction reaching 94% of LLM-based performance (arXiv:2507.03226); SpaCy entity graph plus LLM summary tree (E²GraphRAG, arXiv:2505.24226).
methods.strengths: Eliminates the dominant cost and the dominant error source simultaneously — no per-token indexing cost, no extraction hallucination. Deterministic and reproducible, so the index can be rebuilt identically. Where a deterministic parser exists (code via AST, calendars, email headers, git history), it strictly dominates LLM extraction (arXiv:2601.08773).
methods.weaknesses: No typed relations and no semantics — you get co-occurrence and similarity structure, not 'X reports to Y'. Cannot capture relations stated implicitly across sentences. Community summaries, if you want them, still need an LLM.
methods.local_feasibility: The best local option by a wide margin. SpaCy, Stanza or a dependency parser plus scikit-learn clustering runs entirely on CPU and indexes gigabytes in minutes. Strongly recommended as the default indexing tier, with LLM extraction reserved for a small high-value subset.

methods.name: Two-tier / lazy indexing (KET-RAG, LazyGraphRAG)
methods.mechanism: KET-RAG: LLM extracts a KG skeleton over a small set of key chunks, and a cheap text-keyword bipartite graph covers everything else (arXiv:2502.09304). LazyGraphRAG: no index-time summarization at all — best-first plus breadth-first search at query time under a relevance-test budget (Microsoft Research blog).
methods.strengths: Decouples index cost from corpus size. Microsoft reports LazyGraphRAG indexing at vector-RAG cost and ~0.1% of full GraphRAG's while matching specialized local and global query mechanisms. The relevance-test budget is a tunable quality/cost dial — you can spend more only on hard queries. Ideal for streaming and one-off queries, which is what agent memory is.
methods.weaknesses: Query-time cost and latency rise, which is worse on a laptop where inference is the bottleneck. No pre-computed global summaries means true whole-corpus sensemaking still requires a big query-time budget. The 0.1% figure is vendor-reported and, as far as I found, not independently reproduced.
methods.local_feasibility: Very good, and probably the right architecture for a laptop: keep indexing cheap and deterministic, spend the local model's time only on queries the user actually asks. Budget-bounded search maps cleanly onto 'don't exceed N local LLM calls per query'.

methods.name: Query-time agentic graph traversal (Think-on-Graph family)
methods.mechanism: The LLM acts as an agent that beam-searches the graph, deciding which entities/relations to expand at each step, and reasons over the retrieved paths (arXiv:2307.07697, arXiv:2509.21710, arXiv:2510.08825).
methods.strengths: No index-time summarization cost. Query-adaptive: exploration is guided by the actual question. Produces explicit reasoning paths, which are auditable and directly citable. ToG-3 explicitly targets the case where the KG is low-quality because a small local extractor built it.
methods.weaknesses: Many sequential LLM calls per query — the worst latency profile of any option here, and the hardest to run on a laptop. Errors compound across expansion steps. Path selection is often only weakly connected to the reasoning requirement, causing premature pruning (arXiv:2510.08825).
methods.local_feasibility: Poor to marginal with a local model: each hop is a full generation, so a 4-hop question is seconds to tens of seconds on an M-series Mac. Viable only with a small fast local model, tight hop budgets, and deterministic tool operators doing the graph work (the TGMS approach: LLM plans, database computes).

methods.name: Entity resolution / deduplication layer
methods.mechanism: Blocking (embedding-based or rule-based) → pairwise matching (embeddings, cross-encoder, or LLM) → clustering into canonical entities, with alias tables and a merge/split audit log. Modern variants replace the rigid cascade with graph refinement plus label propagation (arXiv:2605.25814) or add global-consistency selection instead of independent pairwise decisions (arXiv:2405.16884).
methods.strengths: Indispensable — without it, 'Bob', 'Robert Chen' and 'my manager' are three unconnected nodes and every multi-hop path through that person is silently broken. RAGU shows the clean architecture: separate extraction from consolidation (two-stage typed extraction → DBSCAN dedup → summarize → cluster). LLM matchers now beat production rule-based matchers on realistic multilingual data (arXiv:2603.11051).
methods.weaknesses: This is where the worst errors live. Blocking failures cause missing edges; matching errors cause noisy links; imposing transitivity in clustering propagates both into bad clusters. A false merge fuses two people's histories into one and is nearly impossible to detect downstream; a missed merge is a silent recall failure. Pairwise LLM decisions are not transitive. Cost is quadratic in candidates before blocking. Pipelines need dataset-specific tuning that a shipped product cannot do by hand (arXiv:2503.13226).
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local. Local embeddings for blocking, RapidFuzz/dedupe/splink for candidate scoring, DBSCAN or connected components for clustering, and a small local LLM adjudicating only the ambiguous band. Critical local design rule: make merges *reversible* — store them as assertions with their own transaction time, so a bad merge can be retracted without rebuilding the graph. This is the single strongest argument for the bi-temporal model.

methods.name: Incremental / streaming graph maintenance
methods.mechanism: Update only the affected partitions when new memories arrive, rather than rebuilding: hyperplane LSH bucketing so a new document touches a bounded set of segments (EraRAG, arXiv:2506.20963); LightRAG's incremental index; persisting and extending the minimal reasoning subgraph across queries (arXiv:2602.04926).
methods.strengths: The property without which none of this works for agent memory — memory grows on every interaction, and full re-clustering per write is absurd. Bounds worst-case write latency and keeps summary invalidation local.
methods.weaknesses: Incremental clustering drifts from what a from-scratch clustering would produce, so periodic full rebuilds are still needed. Interacts badly with hierarchical summaries: one new fact can invalidate a summary at every level above it.
methods.local_feasibility: Essential locally, since you cannot afford a nightly full rebuild on battery. Practical pattern: append-only write path (cheap, always-on) plus a consolidation pass (extraction, ER, re-clustering, summary regeneration) triggered on idle/plugged-in, exactly the fast/slow split Engram and D-MEM describe.

methods.name: Hybrid router: vector + lexical + graph + bi-temporal filter
methods.mechanism: Classify the incoming query and route: single-fact lookup → BM25/dense top-k; relational or bridge question → graph traversal or PPR; global/thematic → community summaries; 'as of' or 'what changed' → bi-temporal range query. E²GraphRAG does this adaptively rather than making the user pick a mode.
methods.strengths: Matches the empirical finding that no single retrieval paradigm wins across query types (arXiv:2506.05690, arXiv:2503.04338, arXiv:2607.26497). Keeps the cheap path cheap: most memory queries are lookups and should never touch the graph. Degrades to vector RAG if the graph is bad.
methods.weaknesses: Router errors become a new error class, and the router itself costs a classification call. More components to maintain and evaluate. Harder to attribute failures.
methods.local_feasibility: Very good, and I would treat this as the recommended architecture. A small local classifier (or even keyword heuristics plus an embedding classifier) routes; SQLite/DuckDB holds the bi-temporal fact table with a vector index and a lightweight edge table; the graph layer is built extraction-free by default with optional LLM enrichment on an idle-time consolidation pass. Everything runs offline, and each tier can be evaluated and disabled independently.

takeaways: WHY GRAPHS BEAT FLAT VECTORS ON MULTI-HOP — the mechanism: dense retrieval scores every chunk independently against the query embedding, so relevance is not compositional. For a bridge question ('what did the person who wrote the March design doc later say about latency?'), the hop-2 chunk contains neither 'March' nor 'design doc' — it mentions only the person's name. Its similarity to the query is near zero, so no value of k retrieves it. A KG makes the bridge entity an explicit join key: entity-link the query, land on the person node, traverse. HippoRAG generalizes this to a soft score by running Personalized PageRank from the query's seed entities, so hop-2 evidence gets probability mass in one shot with no iterative retrieve-read loop and no per-hop LLM latency. arXiv:2606.06003 enumerates five query classes that are structurally unreachable for vector retrieval on a typed industrial KG.

FOUR QUESTION CLASSES FLAT RAG CANNOT ANSWER AT ALL: (1) bridge/compositional multi-hop, where the intermediate entity is absent from the query; (2) global aggregation and sensemaking ('what are the themes', 'how many times did X happen') — inherently query-focused summarization, not retrieval, which is the founding argument of GraphRAG (arXiv:2404.16130); (3) negative and structural queries ('who is NOT connected to X', 'what is the shortest path', 'which cluster is this in') — set and path operations, not similarity; (4) temporal state queries ('what was true in March', 'what changed since then', 'what did I believe before I learned this'), which need valid time and transaction time as first-class axes.

THE TEMPORAL ARGUMENT IS THE STRONGEST AND MOST UNDER-APPRECIATED ONE. arXiv:2606.26511 measures it directly: cosine similarity separates a contradicted fact from a duplicated one at AUROC 0.59, near chance, because a contradiction is often MORE embedding-similar to the original than a rephrasing is. So a flat store cannot self-correct — it retrieves the stale and current values together and the agent either abstains or serves the superseded one. Recency heuristics do not fix this (they bury old-but-permanent facts). Only explicit valid-time intervals with edge invalidation do. This, not multi-hop, is the clearest case for structured memory in a long-lived personal agent.

BI-TEMPORALITY IS TWO SEPARATE AXES AND CONFLATING THEM IS THE COMMON BUG. Valid time = when the fact was true in the world. Transaction time = when the store recorded it. Their independence is what lets you distinguish 'she changed jobs in June' (world change) from 'we extracted her employer wrong and fixed it in June' (correction). Only the second should be silently overwritten in a current-state view; the first is real history. Transaction time also prevents the leakage that ForecastTKGQuestions (arXiv:2208.06501) showed contaminates temporal KGQA benchmarks: answering an 'as of March' question with facts ingested in June. PROV-O already gives you transaction time for free via generation and invalidation timestamps — you layer valid time on top.

BUT BI-TEMPORAL FILTERING HAS A REAL RETRIEVAL COST, AND IT IS MEASURED. arXiv:2607.26520 found that its time-travel path reached 80% R@10 on knowledge-update questions while DROPPING temporal-reasoning recall from 50% to 37.5%, caused by post-filter dilution: filtering by time interval after ANN retrieval shrinks the candidate pool below what the question needs. The fix is to make the time predicate part of the index (partitioned or pre-filtered ANN), not a post-hoc filter. Do not assume bi-temporality is free at read time.

COST CENTER 1 — EXTRACTION. LLM extraction over every chunk makes index cost scale with corpus length rather than with the reasoning any query requires (arXiv:2607.22592). Extraction is also the dominant error source: measure hallucinated triples and omitted triples separately, not aggregate F1, which hides both (arXiv:2502.05239). Three mitigations, in descending order of leverage: (a) don't use an LLM where a deterministic parser exists — AST-derived code graphs beat LLM-extracted ones (arXiv:2601.08773), and dependency parsing reaches 94% of LLM extraction performance (61.87% vs 65.83%) at a fraction of the cost (arXiv:2507.03226); (b) constrain extraction with a schema, turning open generation into typed classification (arXiv:2603.25152, arXiv:2308.02357); (c) extract only over a small high-value skeleton and cover the rest with a cheap keyword index (KET-RAG, arXiv:2502.09304) or defer everything to query time (LazyGraphRAG, reported at 0.1% of full GraphRAG indexing cost).

COST CENTER 2 — ENTITY RESOLUTION, WHICH IS WHERE THE WORST FAILURES LIVE. The standard blocking→matching→clustering cascade produces a static sparse graph with missing edges from blocking failures and noisy links from matching errors, and rigid transitivity in clustering propagates both (arXiv:2605.25814). The two error modes are asymmetric and both are severe: a FALSE MERGE fuses two people's histories into a single node, silently corrupting every path through it and producing confidently wrong multi-hop answers; a MISSED MERGE leaves the graph disconnected and reverts you to flat-RAG recall on exactly the questions the graph was built for. Pairwise LLM match decisions are not transitive, so global consistency must be enforced separately (arXiv:2405.16884). Design implication: make merges reversible first-class assertions with their own transaction time, so a bad merge is retracted, not rebuilt around.

COST CENTER 3 — INDEX BUILD AND, CRUCIALLY, INDEX MAINTENANCE. Most GraphRAG work assumes a static corpus; agent memory is the opposite. Every new memory can invalidate community summaries at every level above it, and re-running Leiden changes the hierarchy — on sparse KGs, modularity optimization admits exponentially many near-optimal partitions, so the clustering is not even stable run to run (arXiv:2603.05207). Solutions: LSH-partitioned incremental updates (EraRAG, arXiv:2506.20963), LightRAG's incremental index, or a fast/slow split — append-only lossless writes always on, expensive consolidation (extraction, ER, re-clustering, summarization) deferred to idle time (Engram arXiv:2606.09900, D-MEM arXiv:2603.14597). Note also that Zettelkasten-style append-and-evolve linking is O(N²) in writes, which bites well before the graph gets large.

THE UNCOMFORTABLE COUNTER-EVIDENCE, WHICH A HONEST SURVEY MUST FOREGROUND: (a) GraphRAG frequently loses to vanilla RAG on real tasks (arXiv:2506.05690, arXiv:2502.11371, arXiv:2509.16780 on a math textbook); (b) a controlled 450x corpus-size scaling study found BM25 wins at scale on accuracy per token (arXiv:2607.26497); (c) long-context GPT-5-mini beat a Mem0 fact-memory on factual recall on LongMemEval and LoCoMo (arXiv:2603.04814); (d) SlimRAG argues graph pipelines buy structural overhead and imprecise retrieval because semantic similarity is not semantic relevance (arXiv:2506.17288); (e) reported GraphRAG-vs-vector verdicts flip depending on embedder, corpus, judge and where you measure citation quality (arXiv:2608.00705). Treat BM25 + a bi-temporal fact table as the null hypothesis any graph memory must beat.

RETRIEVAL IS OFTEN NOT THE BOTTLENECK — REASONING IS. Evaluating KET-RAG on HotpotQA, MuSiQue and 2WikiMultiHopQA, 77–91% of questions had the gold answer already in the retrieved context, yet accuracy was only 35–78%, and 73–84% of errors were reasoning failures (arXiv:2603.14045). Corollary: before investing in a richer graph, check whether your gold-in-context rate is already high. If it is, spend the effort on path-level context compression (PathRAG, arXiv:2502.14902) and structured prompting instead. Relatedly, graph retrieval over-cites — 11–15 IDs per answer — which degrades citation precision and dilutes the generator's attention (arXiv:2608.00705).

PERSONALIZED PAGERANK IS THE RIGHT RETRIEVAL PRIMITIVE BUT NEEDS HUB CONTROL. PPR is provably isomorphic to the successor representation (arXiv:2512.24722), it is pure sparse linear algebra (milliseconds locally, no LLM at query time), and it does multi-hop in a single step. Its known failure is the Static Graph Fallacy: index-time transition probabilities ignore query-dependent edge relevance, so walks get captured by high-degree hubs before reaching the target (arXiv:2602.01965). Conversational memory graphs are pathologically hub-dominated — the user appears in every fact — producing the 'mega-hub' dilution GAAMA documents (arXiv:2603.27910). Mitigate with degree normalization, concept-mediated intermediate nodes, or query-conditioned edge reweighting.

MODELING CHOICE — RDF vs PROPERTY GRAPH vs HYPERGRAPH. They are formally reconcilable (arXiv:1409.3288, arXiv:2304.13097) and mappable (arXiv:1912.02127, arXiv:2210.05781), so the choice is ecosystem, not expressiveness. RDF-star + PROV-O buys standards, portability, SHACL validation, named-graph retraction, and the PAV distinction between user-asserted, LLM-inferred and imported facts (arXiv:1304.7224) — which is exactly the trust signal you need for conflict resolution. Property graphs buy cheap inline edge properties, which is where valid-time intervals naturally live, plus far faster traversal. Hypergraphs are the honest model for episodic memory (an event binds actor, other party, place, time, topic in one fact) and shorten reasoning paths, but the tooling is immature and LLM-summary-derived hyperedges hallucinate (arXiv:2606.28351). Pragmatic answer: property-graph or relational storage for execution, RDF-star/PROV as the export and audit format.

ZETTELKASTEN IS NOT A METAPHOR HERE — IT IS A WORKING ARCHITECTURE. A-MEM (arXiv:2502.12110) implements Luhmann's principles literally: atomic notes with structured attributes, explicit links created on write where meaningful similarity exists, and memory evolution where a new note updates the attributes of existing ones. It beat graph-database-backed baselines across six foundation models. Its advantages for a personal store are underrated: notes retain full context (no triple-level context collapse), structure is emergent rather than schema-imposed so bad extraction degrades gracefully, and the whole thing is human-readable and human-editable markdown the user already owns. Its costs are the O(N²) write path and the absence of any typed relations or temporal model.

WHAT I WOULD ACTUALLY BUILD LOCALLY on a macOS laptop, synthesizing the above: a single SQLite or DuckDB file holding (a) an append-only episodic log, (b) a fact table with (valid_from, valid_to, tx_from, tx_to, source_ref, asserted_by) columns and interval indexes, (c) a vector index (sqlite-vec / LanceDB) over both chunks and facts, and (d) a lightweight edge table. Build the graph extraction-free by default (SpaCy/dependency parsing + embedding clustering), reserving a small local LLM for schema-constrained enrichment and ER adjudication during an idle-time consolidation pass. Retrieve through a router: BM25/dense for lookups, PPR over the edge table for bridge questions, community summaries only if you have paid to build them, bi-temporal range predicates pushed INTO the index for 'as of' queries. Keep merges reversible. Everything runs offline, each tier is independently disableable, and the fallback when the graph is wrong is plain vector RAG.

OPEN PROBLEMS worth flagging: (1) no standard, engine-independent semantics for bi-temporal edges in agent memory — Graphiti's four timestamps are a de facto convention, not a spec, and I could not verify they map exactly onto SQL:2011 valid/transaction time; (2) no benchmark cleanly isolates memory REPRESENTATION from extractor quality (arXiv:2408.05861's RDF-KG Room Environment is the closest); (3) memory-system leaderboards are harness-dependent and mostly vendor-published, with the same system scoring wildly differently across sources (arXiv:2606.09900, arXiv:2601.07978); (4) almost no work measures peak RAM, disk I/O or CPU time — the numbers that actually decide laptop feasibility — with arXiv:2601.07978 the notable exception; (5) incremental community re-clustering that provably tracks a from-scratch clustering remains unsolved, which is why hierarchical summarization and growing memory remain in tension.

area: Memory consolidation, forgetting, and continual learning theory (2015–2026), filtered for mechanisms that yield an implementable keep / promote / compress / evict score for a local agent memory store

papers.title: What Learning Systems do Intelligent Agents Need? Complementary Learning Systems Theory Updated
papers.venue_or_id: Trends in Cognitive Sciences; doi:10.1016/j.tics.2016.05.004; PMID 27315762
papers.core_idea: Updates McClelland/McNaughton/O'Reilly 1995 CLS. Two systems: hippocampus for fast, pattern-separated, instance-level encoding; neocortex for slow, interleaved, structured/generalized knowledge. Key update: consolidation rate should be modulated by consistency with existing schema (schema-congruent items consolidate fast; incongruent ones need slow interleaved replay), and replay should be goal-biased/prioritized rather than uniform.
papers.relevance: The canonical source. The three algorithmically load-bearing claims for a memory store are: (a) two tiers with different write rates and representations, (b) interleaved replay of OLD content whenever consolidating NEW content (anti-drift), (c) consolidation rate = f(schema congruence). Most agent systems copy (a) and ignore (b) and (c).

papers.title: Considerations arising from a complementary learning systems perspective on hippocampus and neocortex
papers.core_idea: Earlier CLS statement: hippocampal system stores episodes and replays them to neocortex, where slow interleaved learning avoids catastrophic interference.
papers.relevance: Establishes that interleaving (not just replay) is the mechanism that prevents forgetting. Directly implies your consolidation job must mix old memories into every batch, not just process new ones.

papers.title: DualNet: Continual Learning, Fast and Slow
papers.core_idea: Explicit CLS instantiation: a fast supervised learner over pattern-separated representations plus a slow self-supervised representation learner, trained asynchronously.
papers.relevance: Best-known concrete two-speed ML architecture derived from CLS; shows the slow system can be trained self-supervised on unlabeled stream data, which maps to unsupervised consolidation of raw agent logs.

papers.title: Continual Learning, Fast and Slow (DualNets)
papers.core_idea: Generalized DualNet framework; fast learner for specifics, slow learner for structure, with a synchronization mechanism between them.
papers.relevance: Journal-length treatment of the fast/slow split including the synchronization schedule, which is the part an agent memory store must decide (how often to run consolidation).

papers.title: A Complementary Learning Systems Approach to Temporal Difference Learning
papers.core_idea: CLS-TD: combines a slow parametric value learner with a fast non-parametric episodic value estimate, arbitrating between them by uncertainty.
papers.relevance: Gives a concrete arbitration rule between episodic and semantic memory: use the fast episodic estimate when the slow system is uncertain. Directly reusable as a retrieval-routing policy (raw episode vs. consolidated summary).

papers.title: Auto-Dreamer: Learning Offline Memory Consolidation for Language Agents
papers.core_idea: CLS-motivated learned offline consolidator for LLM agents; decouples online acquisition from offline consolidation so the consolidator has a global cross-session view to abstract recurring procedures and prune redundancy.
papers.relevance: Makes the exact argument that matters here: coupling acquisition and consolidation into one online pass is the design error. UNVERIFIED numbers (recent preprint), but the architectural claim is sound and matches CLS.

papers.title: Prioritized Experience Replay
papers.core_idea: Sample transitions with P(i) ∝ p_i^α / Σ p_j^α where p_i = |δ_i| + ε (proportional) or p_i = 1/rank(i) (rank-based), δ = TD error; correct the induced bias with importance weights w_i = (1/(N·P(i)))^β, β annealed to 1. Sum-tree gives O(log N) sample and update.
papers.relevance: The reference implementation of 'replay by expected learning progress'. Transferable engineering: rank-based priority (robust to heavy tails), sum-tree indexing, stale-priority refresh, IS bias correction. Note there is no TD error in an agent memory store; you must supply a surrogate error signal.

papers.title: Revisiting Prioritized Experience Replay: A Value Perspective
papers.core_idea: Links |TD| to the 'value of experience' — the value added to cumulative reward by accessing that experience — and shows |TD| upper-bounds it in certain settings.
papers.relevance: Provides the theoretical bridge from a raw error magnitude to a genuine utility, which is what you actually want to score a memory by.

papers.title: Regret Minimization Experience Replay in Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning
papers.core_idea: Derives an optimal prioritization from a regret-minimization objective rather than heuristics: weight by hindsight TD error, on-policiness, and Q-value accuracy.
papers.relevance: Explicitly argues TD error / recentness / corrective feedback are heuristics, and derives the replacement. The decomposition (error × relevance-to-current-policy × reliability) is exactly the factor structure an agent memory score needs.

papers.title: Uncertainty Prioritized Experience Replay
papers.core_idea: TD-error prioritization favors noisy transitions even when the value estimate is already correct in expectation — the 'noisy TV' problem. Prioritize epistemic (reducible) uncertainty instead of total uncertainty.
papers.relevance: The single most important caveat for surprise-based memory gating: surprise driven by aleatoric noise (garbled tool output, typos, one-off chatter) will dominate your store unless you separate reducible from irreducible uncertainty.

papers.title: Investigating the Interplay of Prioritized Replay and Generalization
papers.core_idea: Systematic study finding PER's benefits are inconsistent and interact strongly with function-approximation generalization; uniform sampling remains a strong baseline.
papers.relevance: Calibration: do not over-invest in elaborate prioritization. Benchmark everything against uniform/reservoir sampling before adding machinery.

papers.title: Improving Experience Replay with Successor Representation
papers.core_idea: Adds a 'need' term (expected future relevance, computed from the successor representation) to the usual 'gain' term (TD error), following neuroscience evidence that biological replay is prioritized by both.
papers.relevance: Shows gain×need is implementable in an ML system, with need approximated by an SR. For an agent store, the SR analog is an empirical transition matrix over topic/entity clusters built from your own retrieval logs.

papers.title: Prioritized memory access explains planning and hippocampal replay
papers.core_idea: Normative theory: replay the memory with maximal Expected Value of Backup, EVB(s,a) = Gain(s,a) × Need(s). Gain = improvement in expected return from updating the policy at s; Need = expected discounted future occupancy of s (the successor representation). Explains forward/reverse replay, reward-biased replay, and replay of remote states.
papers.relevance: The best available normative answer to 'should I promote this memory'. It factors cleanly into utility-if-used × probability-of-being-needed, and both halves are separately estimable from logs. It also diagnoses why recency (a crude Need proxy with no Gain) and query-similarity (a crude Gain proxy with no Need) each fail alone.

papers.title: Prioritizing replay when future goals are unknown
papers.core_idea: Challenges the pure value account: when future goals are uncertain, replay should build a general map rather than plan routes to a current goal.
papers.relevance: Directly on point for agent memory, where the future query is unknown at consolidation time. Argues for a map-building (structure/coverage) objective alongside a value objective.

papers.title: Gradient based sample selection for online continual learning
papers.core_idea: Formulates buffer selection as constraint reduction: choose the buffer that maximizes the diversity of sample gradient directions (minimize maximal pairwise cosine similarity of gradients). Includes a cheap greedy reservoir variant. No task boundaries or i.i.d. assumptions needed.
papers.relevance: Principled, task-boundary-free eviction. The transferable idea is diversity-of-influence rather than diversity-of-embedding: keep memories that affect different behaviors, not memories that merely look different.

papers.title: Online Continual Learning with Maximally Interfered Retrieval
papers.core_idea: Retrieve for rehearsal those stored samples whose loss increases most under the virtual parameter update induced by the incoming batch: score(x) = ℓ(x; θ − η∇ℓ_incoming) − ℓ(x; θ).
papers.relevance: The 'what will this new write break?' criterion — the missing operation in most agent memory stores, which dedupe by similarity but never test for contradiction. Surrogate for a retrieval store: replay the queries a memory historically served and check whether the new write changes those answers.

papers.title: GCR: Gradient Coreset Based Replay Buffer Selection For Continual Learning
papers.core_idea: Select a small weighted coreset whose summed gradient matches the gradient over all data seen so far ('gradient approximation'), then replay it.
papers.relevance: Formalizes 'a small buffer that behaves like the whole history' — the correct target for a bounded memory store. Also see arXiv:2203.14544 / 2112.05025 for the gradient-matching coreset variant that beats reservoir sampling across memory sizes.

papers.title: Continual Learning with Deep Generative Replay
papers.core_idea: Scholar = generator + solver. Instead of storing past data, train a generative model and replay synthesized pseudo-samples alongside new task data.
papers.relevance: The origin of generative replay. Constant memory footprint and privacy-friendly, but see the weaknesses note: hallucinated pseudo-memories are far more dangerous in a factual agent store than blurry digits are in MNIST.

papers.title: Brain-inspired replay for continual learning with artificial neural networks
papers.core_idea: Replays internal/latent representations rather than raw inputs, via generative feedback connections in the main model itself (no separate generator), plus context gating and internal-context replay. Scales generative replay to class-incremental CIFAR-100.
papers.relevance: Latent-level replay is dramatically cheaper than input-level. For an agent store this argues for replaying embeddings/summaries rather than regenerating full source text.

papers.title: Generative replay with feedback connections as a general strategy for continual learning
papers.core_idea: Identifies three distinct continual-learning scenarios (task-incremental, domain-incremental, class-incremental) by whether task identity is known/inferrable, and shows replay is required for the hardest one.
papers.relevance: The scenario taxonomy matters: agent memory is effectively class-incremental with no task labels — the regime where regularization-only methods (EWC/SI) demonstrably fail and replay is necessary.

papers.title: Continual Offline Reinforcement Learning via Diffusion-based Dual Generative Replay
papers.core_idea: Diffusion-based generative behavior model plus a task-conditioned diffusion generator that synthesizes pseudo-states, giving high-fidelity dual generative replay.
papers.relevance: Current state of the art for generative replay fidelity; relevant if you want to replay trajectories/procedures rather than facts.

papers.title: Overcoming catastrophic forgetting in neural networks (EWC)
papers.core_idea: Laplace approximation to the posterior over parameters. Penalty L = L_new + (λ/2) Σ_i F_i (θ_i − θ*_i)², with F_i the diagonal empirical Fisher, E[(∂ log p(y|x,θ)/∂θ_i)²], evaluated at the previous task's optimum.
papers.relevance: CRITICAL DISTINCTION: EWC scores PARAMETERS, not memories. It gives no per-item keep/forget score. It is only applicable to an agent memory store if you distill memories into a local adapter and want to protect that adapter. Widely misapplied as a metaphor in agent-memory papers.

papers.title: Continual Learning Through Synaptic Intelligence
papers.core_idea: Online path integral of each parameter's contribution to loss reduction: ω_i = Σ_t −g_i(t)·Δθ_i(t) accumulated during training; importance Ω_i = Σ_k ω_i^k / ((Δ_i^k)² + ξ). Same quadratic penalty form as EWC but computed for free online.
papers.relevance: Same parameter-not-memory caveat, BUT the underlying idea transfers cleanly and cheaply: accumulate, per memory item, the running sum of loss/utility reduction it has caused over its lifetime. That per-memory path integral is arguably the most useful single import from the regularization literature.

papers.title: Unifying Regularisation Methods for Continual Learning
papers.core_idea: Shows EWC (Fisher), SI (path integral), and MAS (output-sensitivity) are three ways of measuring the same parameter-importance quantity, and unifies them in one framework.
papers.relevance: Saves you from implementing three variants: they are near-equivalent. Pick one (SI is cheapest online).

papers.title: Elastic Weight Consolidation Done Right for Continual Learning
papers.core_idea: Systematic analysis finding EWC's reliance on the Fisher Information Matrix causes gradient vanishing near convergence, explaining its consistently suboptimal empirical performance.
papers.relevance: Direct evidence not to trust Fisher-based importance as a general-purpose salience measure. UNVERIFIED empirically (2026 preprint) but the gradient-vanishing argument is checkable.

papers.title: Continual Learning With Quasi-Newton Methods
papers.core_idea: Shows EWC's diagonal-Fisher Hessian approximation assumes uncorrelated parameters and gives poor curvature estimates; replaces it with a quasi-Newton (BFGS-style) approximation.
papers.relevance: Quantifies how bad the diagonal assumption is — relevant if you were considering Fisher-style importance for a correlated memory graph.

papers.title: A Trainable Spaced Repetition Model for Language Learning (Half-Life Regression)
papers.core_idea: HLR: recall probability p̂ = 2^(−Δ/ĥ) with estimated half-life ĥ_Θ = 2^(Θ·x), x a feature vector (past correct/incorrect exposure counts plus arbitrary item features), Θ fit by minimizing ℓ = (p − p̂)² + α(h − ĥ)² + λ‖Θ‖²₂. Trained on 13M Duolingo traces; >45% error reduction vs. baselines; +12% daily engagement in a live study.
papers.relevance: The cleanest LEARNABLE forgetting model, and the easiest to adapt: it is a log-linear model over arbitrary features, so you can add agent-specific ones (memory type, source reliability, user-stated vs. inferred, entity class). Fits in seconds on local logs. Caveat: exponential decay is empirically inferior to power-law at long intervals.

papers.title: A Stochastic Shortest Path Algorithm for Optimizing Spaced Repetition Scheduling (SSP-MMC)
papers.core_idea: Builds a Markov memory model from 220M review logs using half-life as the state, then solves for the review schedule that minimizes total memorization cost via stochastic shortest path. Deployed in MaiMemo; 12.6% improvement over prior SOTA.
papers.relevance: Reframes scheduling as an explicit cost-minimizing MDP rather than a heuristic — the right formulation if your consolidation budget (tokens, LLM calls) is the constrained resource. This is the DHP lineage that FSRS descends from.

papers.title: Optimizing Spaced Repetition Schedule by Capturing the Dynamics of Memory (SSP-MMC-Plus)
papers.venue_or_id: IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering
papers.core_idea: Journal extension of SSP-MMC; the DHP (difficulty–half-life–probability) model of memory dynamics that FSRS's DSR formulation is a variant of.
papers.relevance: The peer-reviewed backing for FSRS. Cite this rather than the FSRS GitHub when you need a refereed source for the three-variable memory state.

papers.title: Enhancing human learning via spaced repetition optimization (Memorize)
papers.core_idea: Models reviewing as a marked temporal point process and derives, via stochastic optimal control with jumps, that the optimal reviewing intensity is proportional to the recall probability — a simple closed-form optimal policy.
papers.relevance: Gives a provably optimal scheduling rule (review intensity ∝ recall probability) that is a one-liner to implement, in contrast to the 21-parameter FSRS fit. Strong default when you lack enough logs to fit FSRS.

papers.title: Unbounded Human Learning: Optimal Scheduling for Spaced Repetition
papers.core_idea: Queueing-network formalization of the review-vs-new-material trade-off with a provably optimal scheduler under an exponential-forgetting model.
papers.relevance: Formalizes the budget allocation between consolidating old memories and ingesting new ones — the scheduling problem a bounded agent store faces every night.

papers.title: Using a model to compute the optimal schedule of practice
papers.venue_or_id: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied; PMID 18590367
papers.core_idea: ACT-R base-level activation A_i = ln(Σ_j t_j^(−d)) + β, recall probability = 1/(1+e^(−(A_i−τ)/s)); decay d made a function of activation at time of practice, producing the spacing effect. Optimized schedule beat comparison conditions experimentally.
papers.relevance: The best ZERO-CONFIGURATION computable score: needs only the list of access timestamps, one parameter (d ≈ 0.5), no grades, no training. Power-law of practice and recency. Use this as your day-one baseline before fitting anything.

papers.title: Practice and forgetting effects on vocabulary memory: an activation-based model of the spacing effect
papers.core_idea: Empirically fits the activation-based spacing model: relative benefit of spacing grows with amount of practice and with longer retention intervals.
papers.relevance: Quantifies the spacing effect's interaction with practice count — tells you that promotion intervals should expand super-linearly, not by a fixed multiplier.

papers.title: Adaptive Forgetting Curves for Spaced Repetition Language Learning
papers.core_idea: Compares forgetting-curve model families (including HLR variants) with psychological and linguistic features for predicting per-user, per-item recall.
papers.relevance: Practical model-selection evidence for which forgetting-curve parameterization to fit, and shows content features (not just review history) carry real predictive signal.

papers.title: Why Empirical Forgetting Curves Deviate from Actual Forgetting Rates: A Distribution Model of Forgetting
papers.core_idea: Aggregate forgetting curves are confounded by the distribution of initial memory strengths across items; the population curve is not the individual-item decay rate.
papers.relevance: Important statistical warning: do not fit one global decay constant to your whole store and apply it per-item. Fit per-item or per-type, or you will systematically mis-schedule.

papers.title: Human-like Forgetting Curves in Deep Neural Networks
papers.core_idea: Computes a retention metric as the similarity between a network's current hidden state and stored prototype representations, shows it follows Ebbinghaus-like decay, and uses it to schedule review sessions that mitigate catastrophic forgetting.
papers.relevance: Demonstrates the full loop — measure retention in representation space, then schedule rehearsal from it — inside a neural system rather than a human learner. Closest existing work to 'FSRS for an agent'.

papers.title: Bayesian surprise attracts human attention
papers.core_idea: Defines surprise as S(D,M) = KL(P(M|D) ‖ P(M)), the divergence between posterior and prior beliefs, measured in 'wow' units. Crucially observer-relative: an event that is rare in Shannon terms but does not change your beliefs is NOT surprising. Predicts human gaze better than Shannon self-information.
papers.relevance: The formal definition to implement for a write-gate. The posterior-vs-prior framing is exactly right for a memory store: store what changes your model, not what is merely improbable. Distinguishes new information from restatement in a way embedding-similarity dedup cannot.

papers.title: Worth Remembering: Surprise-Gated Robot Episodic Memory
papers.core_idea: Uses Bayesian surprise computed in the semantically rich latent space of V-JEPA-2 as the gate for episodic memory formation, augmenting a 4D scene-graph spatial memory. Reports ≥12% improvement over prior robot memory methods on temporal/spatial/binary QA and beats supervised non-causal methods at event segmentation with an unsupervised causal method.
papers.relevance: The clearest working demonstration that Bayesian surprise is a viable, computable memory-write gate when future tasks are unknown a priori — precisely the agent-memory regime. Latent-space Gaussian KL is cheap to compute locally.

papers.title: Surprise as a Signal for Plasticity and Metacognition
papers.core_idea: A small predictor over a frozen encoder's latent space produces a prediction-error signal used both to gate episodic writes (write a new concept only when surprise is high) and as a metacognitive confidence substrate; a periodic offline replay phase consolidates recent traces into a slow linear readout. Recovers 17.7 points of retention on the oldest of 1000 ImageNet classes with a frozen DINOv2 backbone.
papers.relevance: A complete, small, local-friendly architecture: frozen encoder + tiny surprise predictor + surprise-gated write + periodic offline consolidation. Almost directly portable to a text agent store with a frozen embedding model.

papers.title: Titans: Learning to Memorize at Test Time
papers.core_idea: Neural long-term memory with a gradient-based surprise metric. Momentary surprise = ∇ℓ(M_{t−1}; x_t); past surprise with momentum S_t = η_t S_{t−1} − θ_t ∇ℓ(M_{t−1}; x_t); memory update M_t = (1−α_t) M_{t−1} + S_t with a data-dependent forget gate α_t ∈ [0,1] acting as adaptive weight decay.
papers.relevance: Fixes a real defect in naive surprise gating: the momentum term η_t keeps the write window open after a surprising event, so the AFTERMATH of a surprise is stored too — which is usually what actually matters. The triple (surprise, momentum window, decay gate) is directly portable to a discrete store even though Titans itself is parametric. Reproduction contested (see arXiv:2510.09551).

papers.title: Titans Revisited: A Lightweight Reimplementation and Critical Analysis of a Test-Time Memory Model
papers.core_idea: Independent reimplementation finding Titans does not always outperform established baselines (chunking is a key confound), while confirming the Neural Memory component itself is consistently useful.
papers.relevance: Calibration on Titans. Take the surprise-gating mechanism; discount the headline results.

papers.title: Active inference and epistemic value
papers.core_idea: Expected free energy decomposes into epistemic (information-gain / salience, formally Bayesian surprise) and pragmatic (expected utility) components; formally consistent with Infomax and generalizes salience-based active vision.
papers.relevance: Shows salience (what to attend/store) and utility (what is worth acting on) are two additive terms of one quantity. That decomposition is the principled justification for a two-term memory score: information gain + task utility, rather than either alone.

papers.title: Structured event memory: a neuro-symbolic model of event cognition
papers.core_idea: SEM: a Dirichlet-process mixture over latent event schemas. A new event is instantiated when the posterior favors a new latent cause over continuing the current one — Bayesian model selection, not a threshold on prediction error. Accounts for human segmentation, memory, and generalization jointly.
papers.relevance: The principled alternative to threshold-based segmentation. Gives a proper generative criterion for 'is this a new episode or a continuation of the current one', which is the same decision as 'new memory record vs. update existing record'.

papers.title: Bayesian Surprise Predicts Human Event Segmentation in Story Listening
papers.core_idea: Using a deep language model's belief updates over a story, shows human-annotated event boundaries coincide with transient increases in Bayesian surprise.
papers.relevance: Direct empirical validation, in TEXT with an LLM, that LM-derived Bayesian surprise locates the boundaries humans perceive. This is the closest thing to proof that surprise-based chunking of a dialogue transcript will produce human-sensible memory units.

papers.title: Human-inspired Episodic Memory for Infinite Context LLMs (EM-LLM)
papers.core_idea: Two-stage online segmentation: (1) tentative boundaries where token-level Bayesian surprise exceeds a running threshold computed from a sliding window (μ + γσ), (2) refinement by maximizing graph-theoretic modularity (equivalently minimizing conductance) over the token-similarity graph. Then a two-stage retrieval combining similarity-based search with temporally contiguous neighbors. No fine-tuning required.
papers.relevance: The most directly copyable segmentation recipe: both stages are training-free and run on a local model. The temporal-contiguity retrieval stage is also worth stealing — retrieving a memory should pull in its temporal neighbors, which pure vector search never does.

papers.title: ES-Mem: Event Segmentation-Based Memory for Long-Term Dialogue Agents
papers.core_idea: Applies event segmentation to dialogue memory granularity, arguing fixed chunking disrupts semantic integrity, and adds discourse-structural cues to retrieval rather than relying on surface semantic similarity alone.
papers.relevance: The dialogue-specific instantiation of segmentation-based memory granularity. UNVERIFIED results (recent preprint); the granularity argument is the durable part.

papers.title: Multiple event segmentation mechanisms in the human brain
papers.core_idea: Dissociates two boundary mechanisms: high prediction error (mismatch) versus high prediction uncertainty (reduced confidence). Both operate, in partly distinct systems.
papers.relevance: A pure prediction-error boundary detector is incomplete. Uncertainty spikes — the agent not knowing what comes next — also mark boundaries, and are separately computable as predictive entropy rather than NLL.

papers.title: Prediction error is out of context: The dominance of contextual stability in structuring episodic memories
papers.core_idea: Finds contextual stability, rather than prediction error per se, dominates in structuring episodic memory boundaries.
papers.relevance: Counterweight to surprise-only segmentation. Practical implication: track a running context/topic-stability signal alongside surprise and require both to agree before cutting a memory unit.

papers.title: Optimal forgetting: Semantic compression of episodic memories
papers.core_idea: Formalizes memory as lossy compression, but with the critical move of defining distortion in a LEARNED SEMANTIC LATENT SPACE rather than in raw stimulus space. Under this measure, optimal compression reproduces the characteristic human memory distortions — gist retention, detail loss, schema-consistent intrusions.
papers.relevance: The key theoretical result for compressing agent memories: 'optimal forgetting' is not deleting low-priority items, it is lossy re-encoding against a semantic distortion metric. Gives principled backing for LLM summarization as the compression operator — and predicts its failure mode (schema-consistent confabulation).

papers.title: Efficient data compression in perception and perceptual memory
papers.core_idea: Argues capacity-limited biological memory is shaped by the same efficient-compression pressures as engineered systems, and demonstrates this with rate-distortion-optimal models of perceptual memory.
papers.relevance: Establishes the rate-distortion framing as a general account of biological memory limits, not a loose analogy. Supports treating your token budget as a literal rate constraint.

papers.title: Rate-distortion theory of neural coding and its implications for working memory
papers.core_idea: Formalizes memory as a channel with an information rate (bits per stimulus) traded against distortion (cost of memory errors), and derives neural-coding predictions for working memory from the optimal rate-distortion curve.
papers.relevance: Makes the rate/distortion quantities concrete and measurable, and shows that capacity limits emerge from an optimal trade-off rather than a hard slot count — which argues for a soft, budget-driven eviction policy rather than a fixed max-items cap.

papers.title: Semantic Compression of Episodic Memories
papers.core_idea: Formalizes episode compression against a probabilistic generative model of the environment, showing the same generative model that underlies semantic memory can serve as the codebook for efficiently storing episodes.
papers.relevance: Precursor to the PLOS CB paper; the explicit statement that your semantic store IS the codebook for compressing episodes. Architecturally: compress each new episode conditioned on the current consolidated summary, and store only the residual.

papers.title: What to Keep, What to Forget: A Rate–Distortion View of Memory Compaction in LLMs and Agents
papers.core_idea: Argues KV-cache eviction/quantization, prompt pruning/distillation, bounded architectural state, and agent memory consolidation are four instances of ONE problem: a rate-distortion decision about what context-derived information to retain, at what fidelity, under a resource budget, to preserve downstream task utility. Contributes a single compaction objective, a layer-agnostic lower bound, and a seven-axis taxonomy. Key critique: existing systems decide by attention magnitude or recency, discarding information irreversibly before the query is known.
papers.relevance: The best available unifying frame for exactly this design problem, and it names the central failure mode explicitly. UNVERIFIED empirically (recent preprint) and the abstract does not expose closed-form equations — treat as framing plus taxonomy, not a turnkey algorithm.

papers.title: LLMLingua: Compressing Prompts for Accelerated Inference of Large Language Models
papers.core_idea: Coarse-to-fine prompt compression: a budget controller allocates compression across sentences, then an iterative token-level algorithm prunes tokens by self-information −log p(x_i | x_<i) computed with a SMALL language model, with distribution alignment to the target LLM.
papers.relevance: The practical, computable instantiation of MDL-style compression for text memory. Self-information under a small local model is fast and defensible as a bits-lost proxy. Danger: it preferentially deletes rare proper nouns and numbers — exactly what a factual memory must keep — so it needs an explicit carve-out list.

papers.title: Learning to Compress Prompts with Gist Tokens
papers.core_idea: Trains an LM, via a modified attention mask and no extra training cost, to compress a prompt into a small set of reusable cached 'gist' tokens that act as a learned sufficient statistic.
papers.relevance: A learned, fixed-ratio compression operator — the alternative to LLM summarization when you control the model. Gives a bounded, deterministic rate per memory rather than variable-length prose.

papers.title: Bridging Kolmogorov Complexity and Deep Learning: Asymptotically Optimal Description Length Objectives for Transformers
papers.core_idea: Defines asymptotically optimal description-length objectives grounded in Kolmogorov complexity, and establishes that a minimizer achieves optimal compression up to an additive constant as model resource bounds increase.
papers.relevance: The rigorous statement of what a 'Kolmogorov-motivated' objective can and cannot mean for a transformer. Use it to justify LM-compressibility as a principled proxy — and to be honest that K itself is uncomputable.

papers.title: Minimum Description Length Induction, Bayesianism, and Kolmogorov Complexity
papers.core_idea: Establishes the formal relationship between Bayesian inference and MDL via Kolmogorov complexity, defining ideal MDL from Bayes' rule and specifying the 'Fundamental Inequality' condition under which the principle is valid.
papers.relevance: The reference for why MDL and Bayesian surprise are two views of one quantity — which means your compression score and your salience score can and should share a single probabilistic model.

papers.title: The geometry of efficient codes: how rate-distortion trade-offs distort the latent representations of generative models
papers.core_idea: Shows how capacity limits, event frequency, and utility jointly determine which distortions of latent representation are rate-distortion-optimal.
papers.relevance: Makes explicit that the optimal compression depends on the FREQUENCY and UTILITY distribution over future uses, not just on the content — i.e., your distortion measure must be weighted by an expected-query distribution.

papers.title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
papers.core_idea: Memory stream with retrieval score = recency + importance + relevance (exponential recency decay over hours since last retrieval; LLM-rated 1–10 importance/poignancy assigned at write time; embedding cosine relevance), each min-max normalized. Plus reflection: when summed importance of recent memories crosses a threshold, the agent generates questions, answers them from memory, and stores the answers as higher-level memories. Ablations show observation, planning, and reflection each matter.
papers.relevance: The de facto baseline every agent memory store is compared against, and its reflection trigger (accumulate importance, fire consolidation at a threshold) is a genuinely good cheap heuristic. But: LLM-rated importance is uncalibrated, exponential recency is the wrong functional form, and relevance is a query-time signal wrongly used for write-time decisions.

papers.title: MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
papers.core_idea: Virtual context management by analogy to OS paging: a fixed main context (working set) plus external recall/archival storage, with the LLM issuing its own function calls to page data in and out, and interrupts managing control flow under context pressure.
papers.relevance: The tiering/promotion architecture. Self-paging means the eviction policy is decided in-context rather than hard-coded — flexible, but it burns tokens and degrades noticeably with small local models.

papers.title: Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory
papers.core_idea: Extract → consolidate → retrieve pipeline with explicit ADD / UPDATE / DELETE / NOOP operations against existing memories, plus a graph variant for relational structure. On LOCOMO: ~26% relative gain in LLM-as-a-Judge over a strong baseline, 91% lower p95 latency and >90% token savings vs. full-context.
papers.relevance: The ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP operation set is the single most important API-level lesson: most stores support only ADD, which is why they silently accumulate contradictions. Note the store carries no decay model — nothing ever expires on its own.

papers.title: A-MEM: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents
papers.core_idea: Zettelkasten-inspired agentic memory: each new memory becomes a structured note (contextual description, keywords, tags), the system finds and creates links to related historical notes, and integration triggers 'memory evolution' — updates to the attributes of the linked existing notes.
papers.relevance: Memory evolution is the write-time counterpart to MIR: a new write should modify what it touches, not just sit beside it. Caveat: cascading updates are expensive and can propagate errors.

papers.title: Learning What to Remember: A Cognitively Grounded Multi-Factor Value Model for Agentic Memory
papers.core_idea: V(m) = Σ_i w_i f_i(m) over seven interpretable factors (emotional intensity, goal relevance, value alignment, self/user relevance, task utility, reliability, usage history), weights fit by a gradient-free optimizer against a downstream objective. Evaluated on LongMemEval in a BLIND regime where future queries are unknown at consolidation time. Gold-evidence retention: 0.770 ± 0.011 learned vs. 0.657 uniform weights vs. 0.518 best single factor vs. 0.368 recency. Reliability, emotional intensity, and self/user relevance dominate; query-time similarity is downweighted for the forgetting decision.
papers.relevance: The most directly on-point recent result: it isolates the consolidation-time forgetting decision from query-time retrieval and shows recency and similarity are both mis-specified for it. The factor set and the blind evaluation protocol are both worth copying.
