UNVERIFIED beyond one benchmark; the linear-additive form cannot express interactions (high surprise × low reliability should be suppressed, not averaged).

papers.title: Caching for the Future: Scrub Jay Episodic Memory Principles for Agent Memory Systems (ScrubJay-MEM)
papers.core_idea: Encodes each memory as a What–Where–When tuple with an auto-classified perishability coefficient π_i and a utility term, giving per-memory TYPE-CONDITIONED temporal decay rather than a uniform decay rate.
papers.relevance: The cheapest high-value fix to a naive store: one classification call at write time, then free arithmetic forever. Directly targets stale-fact contamination ('user is in Berlin' must not decay like 'user's spouse's name'). UNVERIFIED (recent preprint).

papers.title: Oblivion: Self-Adaptive Agentic Memory Control through Decay-Driven Activation
papers.core_idea: Casts forgetting as decay in ACCESSIBILITY rather than explicit deletion, with decoupled read and write paths; the read path decides whether to consult memory at all based on agent uncertainty and buffer state.
papers.relevance: Two good ideas: (1) soft accessibility decay preserves recoverability, avoiding the irreversibility problem the rate-distortion paper flags; (2) gating whether to retrieve at all, rather than always retrieving, cuts interference and latency. UNVERIFIED (recent preprint).

papers.title: SIESTA: Efficient Online Continual Learning with Sleep
papers.core_idea: Wake/sleep framework for online continual learning: cheap online updates during wake, periodic offline consolidation during sleep, under a single-pass, no-distributional-assumptions streaming regime.
papers.relevance: A concrete, compute-budgeted schedule for splitting online ingestion from offline consolidation — the operational question for a nightly cron-driven local memory store.

methods.name: CLS two-tier store with schema-modulated, interleaved consolidation
methods.mechanism: Tier A (hippocampal): append-only, high-fidelity, timestamped raw episodes; fast write, no generalization; pattern-separated (dedup only on near-exact match). Tier B (neocortical): slowly updated, deduplicated semantic records — entity profiles, preferences, procedures. A scheduled offline job replays Tier A items INTERLEAVED with a sample of existing Tier B content, and writes generalizations to Tier B. The 2016 CLS update adds the rate rule: consolidation speed ∝ schema congruence. Computable congruence: c = 1 − normalized surprise of the item under the current Tier B state, e.g. c = exp(−NLL(item | Tier-B summary) / T) using a local LLM, or cosine to the nearest Tier-B centroid. High c → consolidate immediately; low c → hold in Tier A and consolidate slowly with heavy interleaving.
methods.strengths: Maps onto two SQLite tables plus a cron job. Interleaving is a concrete, cheap anti-drift mechanism that most agent stores omit entirely. Gives a principled reason to retain raw episodes after summarizing (you need them for future re-consolidation when the schema changes). Schema congruence doubles as a contradiction detector.
methods.weaknesses: Theory specifies no consolidation-rate constant — you must tune it. Interleaving costs tokens because it re-reads Tier B every pass. Congruence scoring needs a model call per item. Tier A grows without bound unless you also apply a decay/eviction policy to it.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes, fully. SQLite + a local embedding model + a local LLM (MLX/llama.cpp on Apple Silicon) + launchd/cron. No external service.

methods.name: FSRS / DSR retrievability as the primary keep-or-decay score
methods.mechanism: Per-item state (D, S, R). Forgetting curve: R(t,S) = (1 + FACTOR·t/S)^(−DECAY), with FACTOR = 0.9^(−1/DECAY) − 1 so that R(S,S) = 0.9. FSRS-4: R = (1 + t/(9S))^(−1), DECAY = −1, FACTOR = 1/9. Post-recall stability: S'_r(D,S,R,G) = S·(e^(w8)·(11−D)·S^(−w9)·(e^(w10(1−R)) − 1) + 1). Post-lapse: S'_f(D,S,R) = w11·D^(−w12)·((S+1)^(w13) − 1)·e^(w14(1−R)). Initial difficulty D_0(G) = w4 − (G−3)·w5; initial stability S_0(G) = w_(G−1). FSRS-6 has 21 parameters fit by maximum likelihood on review logs. Note the (1−R) terms: reviewing when retrievability is LOW yields a larger stability gain — that is the spacing effect, encoded directly.
methods.strengths: The single most directly computable keep/promote score in this entire literature. R(t,S) ∈ (0,1) is a number you can threshold today with nothing but timestamps and no model at all. Power-law (not exponential) decay is the empirically correct form. Parameters are MLE-fit on your own access logs. Battle-tested at Anki scale; open-source Python and Rust implementations exist. Naturally supports promotion: a successful 'review' (the memory was retrieved AND actually used) raises S, extending its life.
methods.weaknesses: Designed around graded recall feedback G ∈ {again, hard, good, easy}, which an agent store must synthesize — e.g. G from whether the retrieved memory was cited in the response, ignored, or corrected by the user. Assumes item independence, which is exactly wrong for a semantic store where similar memories interfere. 21 parameters need enough review history to fit; use ACT-R or the Memorize rule until you have it. Says nothing about content value — only about accessibility.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes, completely. Pure arithmetic over timestamps; the `fsrs` package is pip-installable and dependency-light; parameter fitting is a small local optimization over your own logs.

methods.name: ACT-R base-level activation (zero-configuration baseline)
methods.mechanism: A_i = ln(Σ_j t_j^(−d)) + β over all past access times t_j, with d ≈ 0.5; retrieval probability = 1/(1 + e^(−(A_i − τ)/s)). Pavlik & Anderson make d a function of activation at time of practice, which reproduces the spacing effect.
methods.strengths: Closed form, one free parameter, needs only a list of access timestamps — no grades, no features, no training, no model. Power law of practice AND recency in a single term. This should be your day-one baseline before anything more elaborate; it is often within a few points of far more complex schemes.
methods.weaknesses: No notion of item difficulty, content, or reliability. The sum over all past accesses is O(k) per item unless you cache a running value. A single global d across a heterogeneous store is a known statistical error (see the distribution-model-of-forgetting result) — fit d per memory TYPE at minimum.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes, trivially. A few lines of Python over a SQLite access-log table.

methods.name: Half-life regression with agent-specific features
methods.mechanism: p̂ = 2^(−Δ/ĥ) with ĥ_Θ = 2^(Θ·x); fit Θ by minimizing ℓ = (p − p̂)² + α(h − ĥ)² + λ‖Θ‖²₂ over observed (p, Δ, x) triples, where h = −Δ/log₂(p) is a clipped pseudo-observed half-life. x is any feature vector you like: exposure counts, memory type, source reliability, user-stated vs. inferred, entity class, was-it-corrected.
methods.strengths: The cleanest LEARNABLE forgetting model, and the easiest to extend — it is just a log-linear model, so adding an agent-specific feature is one column. Fits in seconds with numpy/sklearn. Duolingo reported >45% error reduction over baselines on 13M traces. Gives you interpretable per-feature coefficients telling you WHICH properties actually predict a memory's usefulness in your deployment.
methods.weaknesses: Exponential decay is empirically inferior to FSRS's power law at long intervals. The (h − ĥ)² regularizer relies on a heuristic pseudo-observation that is undefined at p ∈ {0,1} and must be clipped, which biases the fit. Linear in features, so no interactions.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes. Roughly fifty lines of numpy against a local review-log table; retrain nightly.

methods.name: Bayesian surprise as a query-independent write gate
methods.mechanism: S(D, M) = KL(P(M|D) ‖ P(M)) — how much the observation moves your beliefs, in 'wow' units. Three computable instantiations, cheapest first: (a) TOKEN-LEVEL — NLL of the new content under a local LLM conditioned on the current memory summary; high NLL means the store does not already predict this. (b) LATENT-LEVEL — maintain a running Gaussian (mean, covariance) over recent embeddings and compute the closed-form Gaussian KL before vs. after incorporating the new item; this is what the V-JEPA-2 robot-memory work does. (c) PARAMETER-LEVEL — ‖∇ℓ(M_{t−1}; x_t)‖, the Titans momentary surprise.
methods.strengths: This is the CORRECT signal for the write decision specifically, because it is defined without reference to any future query — exactly the regime a consolidation-time forgetting decision lives in. It automatically separates new information from restatement, which embedding-similarity dedup does not (a paraphrase with a changed number is similar but highly surprising). Observer-relative by construction: rare-but-irrelevant scores low. Empirically validated as the boundary signal humans use in text.
methods.weaknesses: Surprise is NOT importance. High-surprise noise — typos, garbled tool output, one-off jokes, malformed JSON — scores maximally. This is the 'noisy TV' problem, and the fix from Uncertainty PER is to score EPISTEMIC (reducible) rather than total uncertainty, e.g. by ensembling or by checking whether the surprise persists after one exposure. Must be paired with a reliability and a utility term. Also habituates: the second occurrence of the same surprising thing scores near zero, which is usually right but occasionally wrong for confirmation.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes. Option (a) is one forward pass of a small local model per write. Option (b) needs only an embedding model plus a running mean/covariance — essentially free.

methods.name: Surprise + momentum window + adaptive forget gate (Titans pattern)
methods.mechanism: S_t = η_t·S_{t−1} − θ_t·∇ℓ(M_{t−1}; x_t); M_t = (1 − α_t)·M_{t−1} + S_t. Momentary surprise is the gradient of the associative loss, η_t carries decaying past surprise, α_t ∈ [0,1] is a data-dependent forget gate equivalent to weight decay. For a discrete store, port the PATTERN rather than the parametrization: when surprise crosses threshold, open a write window that decays over the next k turns at rate η, so the AFTERMATH of a surprising event is captured too; and apply α as a per-type decay on stored accessibility.
methods.strengths: Fixes a genuine defect in naive surprise gating — the tokens or turns immediately following a surprising event are usually the ones that explain it, and a single-shot gate misses them entirely. The gates are data-dependent rather than hand-tuned. Cheap to approximate in a discrete store.
methods.weaknesses: Defined for a parametric memory matrix, not a record store, so the port is by analogy for the gradient term. Reproduction of the headline Titans results is contested. Training the gates end-to-end is a real project; hand-setting η and α loses most of the elegance.
methods.local_feasibility: The pattern (surprise → decaying write window → type-conditioned decay gate) is fully local and costs nothing beyond the surprise computation. The full parametric neural memory module is a training project, not a weekend.

methods.name: Event segmentation for memory-unit boundaries
methods.mechanism: Two-stage, training-free (EM-LLM recipe). (1) Place a tentative boundary wherever token/turn surprise exceeds a running threshold τ_t = μ_{t−W} + γ·σ_{t−W} over a sliding window W. (2) Refine boundary positions by maximizing graph-theoretic modularity (or minimizing conductance) of the similarity graph over the tokens/turns in the neighborhood, producing chunks that are internally coherent and externally distinct. The principled alternative is SEM: a Dirichlet-process mixture over event schemas where a new event is instantiated when the posterior favors a new latent cause — Bayesian model selection instead of a threshold. Recent human data says to ALSO track predictive entropy (uncertainty) and contextual stability, not prediction error alone.
methods.strengths: Fixes the arbitrary-chunk-size problem that plagues every RAG-style memory store. Boundaries land where the agent's predictions break, which is exactly where a memory unit should end. Both stages are training-free and run on a local model. Validated against human boundary annotations in text. EM-LLM's companion idea — retrieving a memory should also pull in its temporal neighbors — is worth stealing independently.
methods.weaknesses: Prediction-error-only detection over-segments, and human data (contextual-stability and multiple-mechanism results) shows PE alone will disagree with intuitions about where an episode ends. γ needs tuning per domain. SEM's DP-mixture inference is more work than a threshold. Modularity refinement is O(W²) per window in the similarity matrix.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes. Surprise from a local LLM's token NLL; modularity refinement is a small greedy or spectral computation on a per-window similarity matrix. Runs comfortably on a laptop.

methods.name: Expected Value of Backup: gain × need
methods.mechanism: EVB(m) = Gain(m) × Need(m). NEED(m) = expected future retrieval probability — estimable as an empirical successor representation: build a transition matrix over topic/entity clusters from your own retrieval logs, then Need(m) = Σ_k γ^k P(cluster(m) at t+k | current cluster). GAIN(m) = measured downstream improvement when m is in context — the counterfactual: quality(answer | with m) − quality(answer | without m), evaluated offline on the queries m historically served.
methods.strengths: The cleanest normative decomposition available for 'should I promote this memory': utility-if-used × probability-of-being-needed. Both halves are separately estimable from logs you already have. It also diagnoses precisely why the two dominant heuristics fail — recency is a crude Need proxy with no Gain term, query-similarity is a crude Gain proxy with no Need term — which is corroborated by the LongMemEval multi-factor result (recency 0.368 vs. learned 0.770).
methods.weaknesses: Need requires a model of future context, which is the hard part; the SR approximation is only as good as your topic clustering. Gain requires counterfactual evaluation, costing at least one extra LLM call per candidate. Both estimates are noisy for rarely-accessed memories — exactly the ones you are deciding about. When future goals are genuinely unknown, the neuroscience literature itself argues for a coverage/map objective alongside value.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes, with amortization. Need via an empirical cluster-transition matrix is nearly free. Gain via batch counterfactual evaluation with a local model, run nightly over a sampled subset rather than every item.

methods.name: Rate-distortion budgeted compaction (Lagrangian formulation)
methods.mechanism: Solve min_q I(M; M̂) subject to E[d(M, M̂)] ≤ D, i.e. minimize J = D + λR. The workable local version: RATE = token count of the stored representation; DISTORTION = measured probability that the compressed form changes the agent's answer, evaluated on a held-out set of queries drawn from your expected query distribution. Solve greedily or as a knapsack over candidate representations per memory (full text / structured extract / one-line summary / drop). Critically — following the optimal-forgetting result — define distortion in a LEARNED SEMANTIC space, not on surface text.
methods.strengths: The correct unifying frame for the whole keep/compress/evict problem, and it makes the key structural point explicit: attention-magnitude and recency heuristics discard information before the query is known, irreversibly. Gives you ONE knob (λ) trading tokens against fidelity, and one axis on which to compare summarization vs. eviction vs. quantization vs. dropping. Explains why capacity limits should be soft (budget-driven) rather than a hard max-items cap.
methods.weaknesses: I(M; M̂) is not directly computable over text — every practical version substitutes token count for rate, which is a real approximation. The distortion measure is the entire ballgame and is task-specific; get it wrong and you optimize confidently toward the wrong compression. Blahut–Arimoto does not apply to a discrete text store without heavy machinery. Treat this as a design principle plus a Lagrangian objective for a greedy solver, not as a closed-form algorithm.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes as the Lagrangian-plus-greedy-solver version: rate = tokens (free to compute), distortion = answer-change rate on a local held-out query set (costs local LLM calls, run offline). No external service.

methods.name: MDL / self-information pruning for memory summarization
methods.mechanism: Minimize L(H) + L(D|H). Computable instantiation (LLMLingua): score each token by self-information −log p(x_i | x_<i) under a SMALL local LM, then prune low-information tokens under a budget controller, coarse-to-fine (sentence granularity first, then token). Gisting gives the learned alternative: compress into k reusable cached tokens acting as a sufficient statistic.
methods.strengths: Self-information under a small local model is genuinely computable, fast, and a defensible proxy for bits-lost. Coarse-to-fine avoids destroying syntax. Gives a hard, predictable compression ratio, unlike free-form LLM summarization.
methods.weaknesses: TWO important honesty caveats. First: Kolmogorov complexity is uncomputable — every practical 'Kolmogorov-motivated' memory score is really LM-compressibility, and should be described that way. Second: self-information pruning is lossy in an UNCONTROLLED DIRECTION — it preferentially deletes rare proper nouns, numbers, and dates, which are precisely what a factual agent memory exists to hold. It requires an explicit protected-span carve-out (entities, numerals, identifiers) or it will quietly destroy your store.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes. A 0.5–1B model scoring self-information is fast on a laptop; the pruning itself is a sort and a threshold.

methods.name: Interference-aware write check (MIR surrogate)
methods.mechanism: Before committing a new write m', identify existing memories it would damage. Gradient form (MIR): score(m) = ℓ(m; θ − η∇ℓ_{m'}) − ℓ(m; θ). Retrieval-store surrogate, no gradients needed: retrieve the top-k memories most similar to m', replay the historical queries those memories served, and check whether adding m' changes those answers. If it does, that is a contradiction, not a duplicate — resolve it with UPDATE or DELETE rather than ADD.
methods.strengths: This is the missing operation in nearly every agent memory store. Existing systems dedupe by embedding similarity, which catches paraphrases but is blind to contradictions (an old and a new address are semantically similar and factually incompatible). MIR's 'what would this break?' framing is the right primitive, and the surrogate needs no differentiable model.
methods.weaknesses: The gradient forms assume a trainable learner with a loss, which a retrieval-only store lacks. The surrogate costs LLM calls proportional to k × (queries per memory), so it must be amortized or sampled. Requires you to have logged which queries each memory served — instrument this from day one or you cannot compute it later.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes for the surrogate: it is local LLM calls over local logs, batchable into the nightly consolidation pass. The gradient form needs a trainable local adapter.

methods.name: Coreset / diversity-of-influence buffer selection
methods.mechanism: GSS: choose the buffer that maximizes diversity of sample gradient directions (minimize maximal pairwise cosine similarity of gradients); includes a cheap greedy reservoir variant needing no task boundaries. GCR / gradient-matching: choose a small weighted subset whose summed gradient matches the gradient over all data seen. Retrieval-store analog: maximize diversity of INFLUENCE (which behaviors/queries a memory affects) rather than diversity of EMBEDDING.
methods.strengths: Principled, task-boundary-free eviction with a clear objective ('a small buffer that behaves like the whole history'). Gradient-matching coresets beat reservoir sampling across a range of memory sizes. The influence-diversity reframing is the right correction to embedding-diversity heuristics, which happily keep ten differently-worded memories that all serve one query.
methods.weaknesses: All variants assume a differentiable learner. The influence surrogate requires the same query-attribution logging as the MIR check. Selection is O(N) or worse per pass, so run it offline on a bounded candidate set.
methods.local_feasibility: The influence-diversity surrogate is fully local (logs + local LLM, offline). The true gradient forms need a trainable local model.

methods.name: Generative replay / synthesized rehearsal
methods.mechanism: Store a compact generator or schema instead of raw instances; sample pseudo-episodes at consolidation time and interleave them. Brain-inspired replay's key refinement: replay INTERNAL/LATENT representations via feedback in the main model rather than regenerating raw inputs, plus context gating. LLM analog: keep a compact profile/schema document and have the local model generate plausible instances from it for interleaving.
methods.strengths: Constant memory footprint regardless of history length. Privacy-friendly — raw text can be deleted after the schema is formed, which matters for a personal local store. Latent-level replay is dramatically cheaper than input-level.
methods.weaknesses: SERIOUS CAVEAT for agent memory. The failure mode in image classification is blurry samples; in a factual store it is confidently hallucinated memories that are indistinguishable from real ones. Compounding drift is well documented — a generator trained on its own output degrades. Do NOT use generative replay as the sole store for anything verifiable. It is appropriate for PROCEDURAL/skill memory ('how I usually handle X') and inappropriate for episodic facts.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes technically, and that is the danger. Recommendation: generative replay for procedures only; keep raw text for anything a user could contradict.

methods.name: EWC / Synaptic Intelligence parameter protection
methods.mechanism: EWC: L = L_new + (λ/2)·Σ_i F_i·(θ_i − θ*_i)², F_i the diagonal empirical Fisher. SI: online path integral ω_i = Σ_t −g_i(t)·Δθ_i(t), importance Ω_i = Σ_k ω_i^k / ((Δ_i^k)² + ξ), same penalty form. These are near-equivalent in the unified regularization framework, along with MAS.
methods.strengths: No data storage needed; SI's importance is accumulated for free during training. Well-understood and widely implemented.
methods.weaknesses: CRITICAL: these score PARAMETERS, not memories. They provide NO per-item keep/forget score, and any agent-memory paper claiming to 'apply EWC to memory' is using it as a metaphor unless it is protecting actual weights. Diagonal Fisher is a poor Hessian estimate; Fisher-based importance suffers gradient vanishing near convergence; penalties accumulate across tasks until the model freezes. In the class-incremental regime — which is what agent memory is — regularization-only methods are known to fail and replay is required.
methods.local_feasibility: Applicable ONLY if you distill memories into a local LoRA adapter (feasible with MLX/PEFT on Apple Silicon). Entirely inapplicable to a pure retrieval index. The one genuinely portable idea is SI's path integral reframed per-memory: accumulate each memory's running cumulative contribution to successful outcomes.

methods.name: Prioritized-replay ranking machinery (engineering, minus the TD error)
methods.mechanism: P(i) ∝ p_i^α / Σ p_j^α with RANK-based priority p_i = 1/rank(i) rather than proportional; sum-tree for O(log N) sampling and priority update; importance-sampling correction w_i = (1/(N·P(i)))^β with β annealed to 1; periodic refresh of stale priorities. Supply your own error signal in place of |TD| — e.g. counterfactual utility, or the log-likelihood surprise of an observed user correction.
methods.strengths: Mature, well-tested engineering that transfers wholesale even though the TD error does not. Rank-based priority is markedly more robust to the heavy-tailed score distributions you will get from LLM-derived signals. The sum-tree is thirty lines and gives you cheap weighted sampling over a large store.
methods.weaknesses: There is no TD error in an agent memory store — you must invent the error signal, and the whole scheme is only as good as that surrogate. Follow-up work found PER's gains inconsistent and entangled with generalization, so uniform/reservoir sampling remains a serious baseline you must actually beat. Stale priorities silently degrade the sampler if you never refresh.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes, trivially — a sum-tree over SQLite rowids in pure Python.

methods.name: Composite retrieval score (Generative Agents baseline)
methods.mechanism: score = α_rec·recency + α_imp·importance + α_rel·relevance, with recency = 0.995^(hours since last RETRIEVAL, not creation), importance = LLM-rated 1–10 poignancy assigned at write time, relevance = embedding cosine to the query; components min-max normalized, weights all 1 in the original. Plus the reflection trigger: when summed importance of recent memories crosses a threshold, generate questions, answer them from memory, and store the answers as higher-level memories.
methods.strengths: Implementable in an afternoon and it is the baseline everyone compares to, so you need it anyway. The reflection trigger — accumulate importance, fire consolidation at a threshold — is a genuinely good, cheap, self-pacing consolidation heuristic. Decaying from last RETRIEVAL rather than creation is the right choice and is often gotten wrong.
methods.weaknesses: LLM-rated importance is noisy, uncalibrated, and grounded in nothing downstream. Exponential recency is the wrong functional form (power law fits human and empirical data better). Hand-set equal weights are beaten by learned weights (0.657 uniform vs. 0.770 learned on LongMemEval). Most importantly, it uses RELEVANCE — a query-time signal — inside what is often applied as a write/retention decision, which is a category error.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes, fully local with any local LLM plus an embedding model.

methods.name: Learned multi-factor value function with blind evaluation
methods.mechanism: V(m) = Σ_i w_i·f_i(m) over interpretable factors — reliability, goal relevance, self/user relevance, task utility, emotional intensity, value alignment, usage history — with w fit by a gradient-free optimizer (CMA-ES, Nelder-Mead) against a downstream retention objective, evaluated BLIND: future queries withheld at consolidation time. Reported: 0.770 ± 0.011 gold-evidence retention vs. 0.657 uniform, 0.518 best single factor, 0.368 recency.
methods.strengths: Correctly separates the consolidation-time forgetting decision from query-time retrieval — the central methodological point of the recent literature. The empirical finding that reliability, emotional intensity, and self/user relevance dominate while query-similarity should be DOWNWEIGHTED for forgetting is directly actionable. Weight fitting is tiny: a few hundred held-out queries and a gradient-free optimizer.
methods.weaknesses: Factors are LLM-scored, so write-time cost scales with volume and inherits LLM miscalibration. The linear-additive form cannot express the interactions that matter most (high surprise × low reliability should be SUPPRESSED, not averaged to the middle). Results are from one benchmark in one preprint — UNVERIFIED at breadth. The blind-evaluation protocol is arguably more valuable than the specific factor list.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes. Factor scoring with a local model at write time; weight fitting is a minutes-long local optimization over a few hundred held-out queries.

methods.name: Type-conditioned perishability decay
methods.mechanism: Classify each memory at write time into a perishability class and attach a coefficient π_i that sets its decay rate (or its FSRS initial stability S_0). 'User's spouse's name' → effectively non-perishable; 'user is currently in Berlin' → hours-to-days; 'user prefers concise answers' → months. Encode as a What–Where–When tuple with π_i plus a utility term.
methods.strengths: The cheapest high-value fix to a naive store, by a wide margin. One classification call at write time, then free arithmetic forever. Directly targets the dominant real-world failure — stale facts contaminating retrieved context — which uniform decay cannot address at any decay rate, since the correct rate differs by orders of magnitude across types.
methods.weaknesses: The taxonomy is hand-designed and domain-specific. Misclassification is silent and effectively permanent unless you re-examine. Does not handle facts whose perishability changes (a temporary address that becomes permanent).
methods.local_feasibility: Yes, trivially. One small local LLM call per write, then arithmetic.

methods.name: Tiered promotion/demotion with a full ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP operation set
methods.mechanism: OS-paging architecture: bounded working context, external recall store, archival store, with explicit promotion and demotion between tiers under pressure. Crucially, the write path must support four operations against existing memories, not one: ADD (genuinely new), UPDATE (supersedes an existing record), DELETE (invalidates one), NOOP (already known). Optionally let the model itself issue paging calls (MemGPT self-paging), or add Zettelkasten-style linking where a new note triggers attribute updates on linked notes (A-MEM memory evolution).
methods.strengths: The four-operation set is the single highest-leverage API-level lesson in the agent-memory literature: most stores support only ADD, which is exactly why they accumulate contradictions and why retrieval quality degrades with age rather than improving. Reported gains are substantial (~91% lower p95 latency, >90% token savings vs. full-context on LOCOMO). Tiering gives you a natural place to apply different decay rates.
methods.weaknesses: Self-paging burns tokens on memory bookkeeping and degrades noticeably with small local models — with a 7B local model, prefer deterministic policy over LLM-issued paging. Cascading attribute updates (A-MEM style) are expensive and can propagate a single error across the graph. None of these architectures carry a decay model, so nothing expires on its own — you must bolt FSRS or ACT-R on top.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes. SQLite or a local vector DB (Chroma/Qdrant/sqlite-vec) plus a local LLM. Recommend deterministic paging rules over self-paging when the local model is small.

methods.name: Reservoir sampling (the honest baseline)
methods.mechanism: Retain each incoming item with probability k/N, evicting uniformly at random; O(1) per item, yields an unbiased uniform sample of the stream with no task boundaries.
methods.strengths: Zero configuration, zero model, zero cost. The baseline every prioritization scheme in this survey must beat — and in the continual-learning literature it frequently is not beaten by much. Build it first and keep it as a control arm; if your elaborate score cannot beat reservoir sampling on your own held-out queries, the score is not earning its complexity.
methods.weaknesses: No notion of value whatsoever: it will cheerfully evict a critical user preference to retain a routine log line. Unusable alone for a personal agent store.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes, trivially.

takeaways: TIER 1 — computable RIGHT NOW with no model and no training, from timestamps alone: FSRS/DSR retrievability R(t,S) = (1 + FACTOR·t/S)^(−DECAY); ACT-R base-level activation A = ln(Σ_j t_j^(−d)); half-life regression p̂ = 2^(−Δ/ĥ) with ĥ = 2^(Θ·x). All three output a number in (0,1) you can threshold today. FSRS is the most refined — power-law decay, 21 MLE-fitted parameters, and the spacing effect encoded directly via the (1−R) terms in its stability update. Start here; everything else is an increment on top.

TIER 2 — computable with ONE local model call per item at write time: Bayesian surprise (KL posterior‖prior, or simply NLL of the new content conditioned on the current memory summary), self-information for MDL-style pruning, type/perishability classification, and LLM-rated factor scores. These give you the WRITE gate and the COMPRESSION score. Cost scales with write volume, not store size.

TIER 3 — computable but only offline and amortized: EVB = Gain × Need; MIR-style interference/contradiction checks; counterfactual utility (answer quality with vs. without the memory). These are the most expensive and the most correct. Run them in a nightly consolidation pass over a sampled subset, not inline.

NOT a per-memory score, despite constant claims to the contrary: EWC and Synaptic Intelligence score PARAMETERS via Fisher information or a path integral, not memories. They yield no keep/forget decision for a record in a retrieval store. They only become relevant if you distill memories into a local adapter and want to protect its weights. Treat any paper that 'applies EWC to agent memory' without touching weights as using a metaphor.

The one genuinely portable idea from the regularization literature is SI's path integral, reframed per-memory: accumulate, for each memory, the running sum of loss/error reduction (or task successes) it has caused over its lifetime. That is a cheap, online, per-item importance signal with real theoretical pedigree — and almost nobody implements it.

Rate-distortion is the correct unifying FRAME for keep/compress/evict, but it is not a turnkey algorithm: I(M; M̂) is not computable over text. The workable version is the Lagrangian J = D + λR with rate = token count and distortion = measured answer-change rate on a held-out query set, solved greedily or as a knapsack over per-memory representation choices (full text / structured extract / one-line summary / drop). Its real contribution is naming the failure mode: attention-magnitude and recency heuristics discard information BEFORE the query is known, irreversibly.

Kolmogorov complexity is uncomputable. Every practical 'Kolmogorov-motivated' memory score is resource-bounded LM-compressibility — self-information under a small local model. Say it that way. It is still useful, but the honest framing matters because the approximation has a specific bias: self-information pruning preferentially deletes rare proper nouns, numerals, and dates, which are exactly what a factual memory store exists to hold. It needs a protected-span carve-out or it will quietly destroy your data.

THE central structural insight across the recent literature: the forgetting decision happens at CONSOLIDATION time, before the future query is known. Query-similarity is therefore the wrong signal for it, and so is recency. The blind-regime LongMemEval numbers make this concrete — gold-evidence retention 0.368 for recency, 0.518 for the best single factor, 0.657 for uniform-weighted multi-factor, 0.770 for learned weights. Design your evaluation to withhold future queries at consolidation time, or you will measure the wrong thing and conclude similarity works.

Bayesian surprise is the right WRITE signal precisely because it is query-independent: S = KL(posterior ‖ prior) is defined without reference to any future use. It also separates new information from restatement in a way embedding-similarity dedup cannot — a paraphrase with one changed number is highly similar and highly surprising. But surprise ≠ importance. Pair it with reliability and utility, and prioritize EPISTEMIC over total uncertainty, or the noisy-TV problem will fill your store with garbled tool output and typos.

Naive surprise gating misses the aftermath. The Titans construction — momentary surprise, plus a momentum term carrying decaying past surprise, plus an adaptive forget gate — captures the turns FOLLOWING a surprising event, which are usually the ones that explain it. Port the pattern (surprise → decaying write window → type-conditioned decay) even if you never build the parametric module.

Event segmentation should set memory-unit BOUNDARIES, replacing fixed-size chunking. The EM-LLM two-stage recipe is training-free and directly implementable: threshold surprise at μ + γσ over a sliding window, then refine boundaries by maximizing modularity of the local similarity graph. Bayesian surprise is empirically validated against human boundary annotations in text (story-listening work). But prediction error alone over-segments — recent human data shows predictive UNCERTAINTY and CONTEXTUAL STABILITY are separate, comparably important mechanisms, so require agreement between surprise and a stability signal before cutting.

Gain × Need (Mattar & Daw) is the best normative decomposition available for 'should I promote this memory', and it explains why the two standard heuristics each fail: recency is a crude Need proxy with no Gain term; query-similarity is a crude Gain proxy with no Need term. Need is estimable as an empirical successor representation over topic clusters from your own retrieval logs — that is the piece nearly every agent memory system is missing, and it is cheap.

CLS's algorithmic content — as opposed to its metaphorical content — is three things: (a) two stores with different write rates and representations, (b) INTERLEAVED replay of old content whenever consolidating new content, and (c) consolidation rate modulated by SCHEMA CONGRUENCE, fast for consistent items and slow-with-interleaving for inconsistent ones. Systems copy (a) constantly and (b) and (c) almost never — yet (b) is the actual anti-forgetting mechanism and (c) is the actual contradiction handler.

Generative replay is unsafe as the primary store for factual agent memory. The failure mode in image classification is blurry samples; in a fact store it is confidently hallucinated memories indistinguishable from real ones, compounding as the generator retrains on its own output. Restrict it to procedural/skill memory ('how I usually handle X') and keep raw text for anything a user could contradict. Latent-level replay (brain-inspired replay) is the cheap, safer variant when you do use it.

Most agent memory stores support only ADD, which is the root cause of contradiction accumulation and age-related retrieval decay. The minimum viable fix is the Mem0 four-operation set (ADD / UPDATE / DELETE / NOOP) plus an MIR-style check at write time: retrieve the memories most similar to the incoming write, replay the queries they historically served, and check whether the new write changes those answers. Similarity means duplicate; changed answers mean contradiction. These need opposite handling, and embedding dedup cannot tell them apart. Instrument query-to-memory attribution from day one — you cannot reconstruct it later.

Suggested composite, every term locally computable: keep_score = w1·log R_FSRS(t, S) + w2·surprise_at_write + w3·cumulative_utility (SI-style path integral) + w4·source_reliability − w5·redundancy, with S initialized by type-conditioned perishability and updated on each 'review' (retrieved AND used), and weights w fit by gradient-free optimization against BLIND held-out queries. Promote when the score crosses an upper threshold, compress at a middle band, evict at the bottom — and always benchmark against reservoir sampling, which is a stronger baseline than it looks.

Everything in this stack runs fully locally on a macOS laptop: SQLite (plus sqlite-vec or Chroma) for the store, a local embedding model and a small local LLM via MLX or llama.cpp for surprise/self-information/factor scoring, numpy/sklearn for HLR and weight fitting, the pip-installable `fsrs` package for scheduling, and launchd or cron for the nightly consolidation pass. No external service is required for any method surveyed here. The only components that genuinely need a trainable model are the true gradient forms of EWC/SI/GSS/MIR, and each has a viable gradient-free surrogate.

CALIBRATION WARNING on sourcing. Two distinct evidence tiers appear above. The foundations are refereed and durable: CLS (TiCS 2016), PER (ICLR 2016), EWC (PNAS 2017), SI (ICML 2017), Deep Generative Replay (NeurIPS 2017), brain-inspired replay (Nat Comms 2020), Mattar & Daw (Nat Neuro 2018), SEM (Psych Review 2020), optimal forgetting (PLOS CB 2020), Bates & Jacobs (Psych Review 2020), Jakob & Gershman (eLife 2023), HLR (ACL 2016), SSP-MMC (KDD 2022 / TKDE 2023), Memorize (PNAS 2019), Itti & Baldi (Vision Research 2009), EM-LLM (ICLR 2025). Against that, there is a large 2026 cluster of unrefereed agent-memory preprints (FadeMem, Oblivion, SF-AMS, ScrubJay-MEM, SCM, CraniMem, All-Mem, HiMem, LeanMem, GAM, Auto-Dreamer, and the multi-factor value model) that mostly recombine the same handful of ideas and report single-benchmark results. Take their MECHANISMS as a menu; treat every reported number as UNVERIFIED.

area: Storage/distributed-systems substrate for a durable, verifiable, local agent memory store: LSM trees, append-only event logs, content-addressable storage and Merkle DAGs, CRDTs, WAL/ACID in SQLite, idempotency and exactly-once, Bloom/Count-Min sketches, MinHash/SimHash LSH, content-defined chunking, and PROV-O/RO-Crate provenance — with focus on many parallel agents writing to one store without corruption, and on making every stored claim traceable and reproducible.

papers.title: The Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM-Tree)
papers.core_idea: Buffer writes in memory, flush as sorted immutable runs, merge them in the background so all disk I/O is sequential; trades read and space amplification for write throughput.
papers.relevance: The canonical write-optimized shape for an append-heavy memory store. Every embedded KV an agent store would sit on (RocksDB, LevelDB, Pebble) is this structure.

papers.title: Evolution of Development Priorities in Key-value Stores Serving Large-scale Applications: The RocksDB Experience
papers.venue_or_id: USENIX FAST 2021 (Dong, Kryczka, Jin, Stumm); also ACM TOS 2021
papers.core_idea: Eight years of production lessons: priorities shifted from write amplification to space amplification to CPU; data formats must stay backward/forward compatible; resource allocation must be managed across instances.
papers.relevance: Directly applicable operations guidance if you embed an LSM KV locally. The format-compatibility lesson matters for a memory store meant to outlive the agent version that wrote it.

papers.title: Rethinking LSM-tree based Key-Value Stores: A Survey
papers.core_idea: Survey of LSM compaction unpredictability, write/read/space amplification trade-offs, and tail-latency behavior in resource-constrained settings.
papers.relevance: Useful map of the design space if choosing/tuning an embedded LSM for a laptop-class store where compaction stalls are user-visible.

papers.title: Constructing and Analyzing the LSM Compaction Design Space (Updated Version)
papers.core_idea: Decomposes compaction policy into orthogonal primitives and shows how each choice moves write amplification, throughput, point/range lookup, space amplification, and delete latency.
papers.relevance: Lets you pick a compaction policy deliberately rather than inheriting RocksDB defaults — relevant because agent memory has heavy deletes/tombstones (forgetting, supersession).

papers.title: ARIES: A Transaction Recovery Method Supporting Fine-Granularity Locking and Partial Rollbacks Using Write-Ahead Logging
papers.venue_or_id: ACM TODS 17(1):94-162 (Mohan, Haderle, Lindsay, Pirahesh, Schwarz)
papers.core_idea: WAL with LSNs, repeating-history redo then undo via compensation log records, enabling fine-grained locking and partial rollback with correct crash recovery.
papers.relevance: The reference semantics for 'durable and crash-consistent.' Compensation log records are the direct ancestor of the saga-style inverse operations agent frameworks now need.

papers.title: SQLite: Past, Present, and Future
papers.venue_or_id: PVLDB 15(12):3535-3547 (Gaffney, Prammer, Brasfield, Hipp, Kennedy, Patel)
papers.core_idea: Analysis of SQLite's architecture and performance versus embedded analytical engines, including WAL mode behavior and its concurrency and workload limits.
papers.relevance: The strongest citable evidence for choosing SQLite as the local ACID spine, and for knowing where it stops being the right answer (analytics, very large scans).

papers.title: Life beyond Distributed Transactions: an Apostate's Opinion
papers.core_idea: Partition state into independently-transactional 'entities'; between entities use at-least-once messaging plus idempotence and activities that track message state, never distributed transactions.
papers.relevance: The architectural template for many parallel agents: one small ACID scope per entity, everything cross-entity handled by idempotent messages. This is exactly the agent-fanout problem.

papers.title: Idempotence Is Not a Medical Condition
papers.core_idea: Retries are inevitable in any at-least-once system; correctness comes from making the *effect* idempotent (natural idempotence, or dedup on a stable request key), not from trying to deliver exactly once.
papers.relevance: The clearest statement of why 'exactly-once delivery' is the wrong goal for an agent write path, and what to build instead (idempotency keys + a dedup table).

papers.title: Immutability Changes Everything
papers.core_idea: Cheap storage makes append-only, never-overwrite designs economically dominant; immutable data is trivially shareable, cacheable, replicable, and auditable.
papers.relevance: The justification for making the memory store append-only with derived views, rather than mutable rows — the precondition for both verifiability and safe concurrency.

papers.title: Consistency and Completeness: Rethinking Distributed Stream Processing in Apache Kafka
papers.venue_or_id: SIGMOD 2021 (Wang, Chen, Dikshit, Gustafson, Sax, Roesler, Blee-Goldman, Cadonna, Mehta, Madan, Rao)
papers.core_idea: Describes how a persistent log serves as both storage and communication layer, and how exactly-once processing is implemented via idempotent producers plus transactional atomic write+offset-commit protocols.
papers.relevance: A real, engineered answer to 'exactly-once semantics': atomically commit the output write together with the input consumption position. Portable to a local single-log design.

papers.title: A Digital Signature Based on a Conventional Encryption Function
papers.core_idea: Hash tree construction whose root commits to an unbounded set of leaves, with logarithmic-size membership proofs.
papers.relevance: The primitive underneath git, IPFS, Certificate Transparency, and every 'prove this claim was in the store at time T' scheme.

papers.title: Efficient Data Structures for Tamper-Evident Logging
papers.core_idea: A history tree giving logarithmic-size membership and incremental (append-only) proofs against an untrusted logger; reported 3 KB proofs where hash chains would need ~800 MB at 80M events.
papers.relevance: The correct data structure for an auditable memory log: you can prove a claim is present AND that the log was never rewritten, cheaply, at agent-log scale.

papers.title: Certificate Transparency (RFC 6962)
papers.core_idea: Append-only Merkle log with Signed Tree Heads, plus inclusion proofs and consistency proofs showing one tree is a prefix of another; split-view attacks are detectable by comparing roots.
papers.relevance: A deployed, specified protocol for exactly the guarantee an agent memory store needs: 'nothing was retroactively edited,' verifiable by an auditor holding only root hashes.

papers.title: IPFS - Content Addressed, Versioned, P2P File System
papers.core_idea: Generalized Merkle DAG over content-addressed blocks with content-addressed links, giving deduplication, versioning, and integrity by construction.
papers.relevance: The reference model for content addressing beyond git: every stored artifact gets a self-verifying identifier that can be cited from a claim.

papers.title: Design and Evaluation of IPFS: A Storage Layer for the Decentralized Web
papers.core_idea: Measurement-driven description of the deployed IPFS design (content routing, Bitswap, DHT) and its real performance characteristics.
papers.relevance: Sober counterweight to the 2014 vision paper: shows the network/DHT costs you avoid entirely by staying local while keeping the CID data model.

papers.title: Merkle-CRDTs: Merkle-DAGs meet CRDTs
papers.core_idea: Use a Merkle-DAG of operation blocks as the transport and persistence layer for CRDTs; the DAG's parent links act as a logical clock, so causality is carried by the hashes themselves.
papers.relevance: The single most on-point design for this task: parallel agents append hash-linked op blocks, causality is free, convergence is CRDT-guaranteed, and the whole history is content-addressed and verifiable.

papers.title: Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types
papers.core_idea: Strong Eventual Consistency from either a join-semilattice on state or commutative operations; replicas that have seen the same updates are equal, with no rollback or consensus.
papers.relevance: The foundational guarantee that lets N agents write concurrently to one logical store without a lock and without lost updates.

papers.title: Delta State Replicated Data Types
papers.core_idea: Ship small incremental delta-mutators instead of full states, while retaining state-based CRDTs' tolerance of unreliable, out-of-order, duplicate delivery.
papers.relevance: Makes CRDT sync affordable for a memory store that would otherwise resend a large state on every merge; duplicate-tolerance composes well with at-least-once agent writes.

papers.title: A Conflict-Free Replicated JSON Datatype
papers.core_idea: CRDT with formal semantics for arbitrarily nested maps and lists, so concurrent edits to a JSON document merge without losing updates.
papers.relevance: Agent memory records are JSON-shaped; this is the datatype (and the Automerge lineage) that merges concurrent structured edits rather than last-writer-wins clobbering them.

papers.title: Extending JSON CRDTs with Move Operations
papers.core_idea: Algorithm for move/reorder in JSON CRDTs that avoids duplicates and cycles under concurrent non-move operations.
papers.relevance: Reorganizing memory (re-parenting a fact under a different topic) is a move; naive merges corrupt the tree. Names a real failure mode for hierarchical agent memory.

papers.title: Approaches to Conflict-free Replicated Data Types
papers.core_idea: Tutorial survey of operation-based, state-based, pure operation-based, and delta-state CRDTs with their delivery assumptions and costs.
papers.relevance: The right single reference for choosing a CRDT flavor against your delivery guarantees (op-based needs exactly-once causal delivery; state/delta-based do not).

papers.title: Near Real-Time Peer-to-Peer Shared Editing on Extensible Data Types
papers.core_idea: YATA, the sequence CRDT behind Yjs, giving convergence and intention preservation for arbitrary data types with offline editing.
papers.relevance: The most widely deployed practical CRDT implementation; a realistic off-the-shelf merge engine for a local multi-writer store.

papers.title: Merkle Search Trees: Efficient State-Based CRDTs in Open Networks
papers.core_idea: Encode CRDT state as a deterministic, history-independent Merkle-ized search tree so replicas can diff by comparing subtree hashes and exchange only differences.
papers.relevance: Solves anti-entropy: two agent stores reconcile in O(diff), not O(state), and the same hashes serve as integrity proofs. Deployed in Bluesky's AT Protocol repositories.

papers.title: Local-first software: you own your data, in spite of the cloud
papers.venue_or_id: Onward! 2019, DOI 10.1145/3359591.3359737 (Kleppmann, Wiggins, van Hardenberg, McGranaghan)
papers.core_idea: Seven ideals for software where the local copy is primary and CRDT sync is secondary, preserving offline work, longevity, privacy, and user control.
papers.relevance: The design philosophy that matches the brief exactly: local durability first, sync as an optional layer, no service dependency.

papers.title: Byzantine Eventual Consistency and the Fundamental Limits of Peer-to-Peer Databases
papers.core_idea: Characterizes the class of applications that tolerate arbitrarily many Byzantine nodes, and gives a Byzantine causal broadcast algorithm achieving BEC with near-optimal performance.
papers.relevance: Sets the honest ceiling on what a hash-linked multi-writer store can guarantee when a writer misbehaves — important once agents are semi-trusted rather than trusted.

papers.title: A Composable CRDT Layer for Byzantine-Resilient Deterministic Reconstruction
papers.core_idea: Melda, a delta-state JSON CRDT where all updates are accepted but only a deterministically reconstructed subset contributes to state, giving convergence under arbitrary behavior.
papers.relevance: Accept-everything-then-reconstruct is a good fit for agents: you never discard a write (so provenance survives), but bad writes don't have to shape the answer. UNVERIFIED quality: recent preprint.

papers.title: Logical Physical Clocks (HLC) and Consistent Snapshots in Globally Distributed Databases
papers.venue_or_id: OPODIS 2014, pp.17-32 (Kulkarni, Demirbas, Madappa, Avva, Leone)
papers.core_idea: Hybrid logical clocks: monotonic timestamps that stay close to physical time while still capturing happens-before, without clock-sync assumptions.
papers.relevance: The right timestamp for agent writes: human-meaningful ordering for audit, causal correctness for merge, and bounded size (unlike vector clocks over many agents).

papers.title: Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors
papers.core_idea: Bit-array plus k hash functions gives set membership with no false negatives and a tunable false-positive rate in far less space than the set itself.
papers.relevance: The cheap gate in front of expensive work: 'have I already stored this claim / read this source / tried this fix?' Also the LSM read-path filter.

papers.title: Xor Filters: Faster and Smaller Than Bloom and Cuckoo Filters
papers.core_idea: Static filters within ~23% of the information-theoretic space bound with faster queries than Bloom or cuckoo filters, at the cost of immutability after construction.
papers.relevance: For an agent store's immutable segments (sealed SSTable-like batches), xor filters strictly dominate Bloom; use Bloom only where you must insert incrementally.

papers.title: Binary Fuse Filters: Fast and Smaller Than Xor Filters
papers.core_idea: Filters within ~13% of the storage lower bound with faster, less memory-hungry construction than xor filters.
papers.relevance: Current practical best-in-class static AMQ; the default choice for per-segment membership filters in 2026.

papers.title: Adversarial Correctness and Privacy for Probabilistic Data Structures
papers.core_idea: Formal security analysis of Bloom/cuckoo filters when inputs are adversarially chosen: false-positive rates can be inflated and internal state can leak information about inserted elements.
papers.relevance: Important caveat: an agent store ingesting untrusted web content must key its filters/hashes secretly, or an attacker can poison the dedup gate to suppress real memories.

papers.title: An improved data stream summary: the count-min sketch and its applications
papers.core_idea: d x w counter array with pairwise-independent hashes giving point-frequency estimates with additive error bounded by epsilon times the L1 norm, in sublinear space.
papers.relevance: Cheap 'how often has this entity/source/claim shown up' signal for salience, decay, and heavy-hitter detection over the agent's write stream — never overcounts, which matches conservative retention policy.

papers.title: On the Resemblance and Containment of Documents
papers.core_idea: Shingling plus min-wise hashing: the probability two sets share a minimum hash equals their Jaccard similarity, so short sketches estimate resemblance and containment.
papers.relevance: The basis for detecting that a new memory is a near-duplicate of an existing one — and for containment ('this new note is subsumed by that one').

papers.title: Similarity Estimation Techniques from Rounding Algorithms
papers.core_idea: Random-hyperplane LSH (SimHash): collision probability of compact sketches tracks cosine similarity, giving sublinear approximate near-neighbor search.
papers.relevance: 64-bit fingerprints that let you detect near-duplicate agent notes with bitwise Hamming distance — orders of magnitude cheaper than embedding search for exact-ish repeats.

papers.title: Detecting Near-Duplicates for Web Crawling
papers.core_idea: Demonstrates SimHash at web scale and gives the practical algorithm for finding all fingerprints within k bit-flips of a query using permuted sorted tables.
papers.relevance: The actual engineering recipe (not just the theory) for a near-duplicate index over millions of memory records on one machine.

papers.title: In Defense of MinHash Over SimHash
papers.core_idea: Theoretical and empirical argument that for binary/sparse data MinHash virtually always beats SimHash at equal sketch size.
papers.relevance: Settles the MinHash-vs-SimHash choice for token-set memory records: prefer MinHash on sparse binary features, keep SimHash for dense/fast Hamming filtering.

papers.title: LSHBloom: Memory-efficient, Extreme-scale Document Deduplication
papers.core_idea: Replaces MinHash-LSH's stored per-band buckets with Bloom filters, cutting deduplication memory footprint by large factors at comparable accuracy.
papers.relevance: The concrete way to run near-duplicate detection over a large local memory corpus inside a laptop's RAM budget — the composition of two primitives in this brief.

papers.title: Fingerprinting by Random Polynomials
papers.venue_or_id: Harvard Center for Research in Computing Technology, TR-15-81 (Rabin)
papers.core_idea: Fingerprints via arithmetic modulo a random irreducible polynomial over GF(2), yielding a cheap rolling hash with provable collision bounds.
papers.relevance: The rolling hash that makes content-defined chunk boundaries computable in one pass; still the reference point for CDC.

papers.title: A Low-Bandwidth Network File System
papers.core_idea: Split files at content-defined boundaries using Rabin fingerprints and transfer only chunks the peer lacks, achieving up to two orders of magnitude bandwidth reduction.
papers.relevance: The origin of content-defined chunking for deduplication, and the reason CDC survives insertions/deletions where fixed-size blocking does not.

papers.title: FastCDC: a Fast and Efficient Content-Defined Chunking Approach for Data Deduplication
papers.venue_or_id: USENIX ATC 2016 (Xia, Zhou, Jiang, Zhang, et al.)
papers.core_idea: Gear-hash-based chunking with simplified hash judgment, cut-point skipping below a minimum size, and normalized chunk-size distribution to recover the dedup ratio lost to skipping.
papers.relevance: The default modern CDC algorithm; makes chunking cheap enough that a local store can dedup every attachment, transcript, and tool output it ingests.

papers.title: A Thorough Investigation of Content-Defined Chunking Algorithms for Data Deduplication
papers.core_idea: Impartial theoretical and experimental comparison of leading CDC algorithms across four realistic datasets on four key metrics.
papers.relevance: Corrective evidence against picking a CDC algorithm from its own paper's benchmarks; the reference to consult before committing to FastCDC vs alternatives.

papers.title: Chunking Attacks on File Backup Services using Content-Defined Chunking
papers.core_idea: Attacks that extract per-user CDC parameters and then infer information about stored data from chunk boundaries.
papers.relevance: Security caveat for a local store that later syncs: CDC boundaries are a side channel. Keyed chunking parameters are not optional if the store touches untrusted peers.

papers.title: Content-defined Merkle Trees for Efficient Container Delivery
papers.core_idea: Combines content-defined chunking with Merkle tree structure so that a versioned artifact's unchanged subtrees are shared and only changed chunks are transferred.
papers.relevance: The exact composition an agent store wants: CDC for dedup plus Merkle for verification, in one structure rather than two bolted together.

papers.title: Provenance-Aware Storage Systems
papers.core_idea: Collect lineage automatically at the storage layer rather than as manual annotations in a side database; PASTA/PASS prototype on a modified kernel plus ext2fs.
papers.relevance: The founding argument for the design choice here: provenance captured by the store is complete and cheap; provenance asked of the writer is incomplete and drifts.

papers.title: PROV-O: The PROV Ontology
papers.core_idea: OWL2 ontology with Entity, Activity, Agent classes and properties wasGeneratedBy, used, wasAssociatedWith, wasDerivedFrom for machine-readable lineage in RDF.
papers.relevance: The interchange vocabulary for 'which agent, running which activity, derived this claim from which source' — the schema for the traceability half of the brief.

papers.title: Packaging research artefacts with RO-Crate
papers.core_idea: Lightweight community convention that packages data, code, and metadata with Schema.org JSON-LD annotations into a self-describing, machine-readable crate.
papers.relevance: The packaging format for exporting a reproducible snapshot of an agent's memory plus its evidence — deliberately lighter weight than full semantic-web tooling.

papers.title: Recording provenance of workflow runs with RO-Crate
papers.core_idea: Extends RO-Crate with three profiles capturing workflow plans and their executions at increasing granularity, with implementations across multiple workflow systems.
papers.relevance: The closest existing standard for 'record this agent run so someone else can re-execute it,' including the run/plan distinction agents need.

papers.title: PROV-AGENT: Unified Provenance for Tracking AI Agent Interactions in Agentic Workflows
papers.core_idea: Extends PROV-style provenance to LLM agent interactions across federated environments so that error propagation between agents (one agent's hallucination becoming another's input) is traceable.
papers.relevance: Directly targets the multi-agent traceability question, and names the specific failure it prevents: silent propagation of a bad claim through an agent chain.

papers.title: Attribution, Citation, and Quotation: A Survey of Evidence-based Text Generation with Large Language Models
papers.core_idea: Analyzes 134 papers into a unified taxonomy of evidence-based generation and surveys 300 evaluation setups for attribution and citation.
papers.relevance: Maps the layer above storage: even with perfect provenance in the store, the claim-to-source binding produced by the model must be separately evaluated.

papers.title: Cited but Not Verified: Parsing and Evaluating Source Attribution in LLM Deep Research Agents
papers.core_idea: Reproducible AST-based parser to extract inline citations from agent-generated reports and evaluate source accessibility, relevance, and factual consistency at scale.
papers.relevance: Empirical evidence that self-reported agent citations are unreliable — the argument for binding claims to content-addressed evidence at write time instead of trusting the model's citation.

papers.title: CoAgent: Concurrency Control for Multi-Agent Systems
papers.core_idea: MTPO fixes a serialization order at agent launch, serves order-filtered reads, applies writes speculatively in place, notifies affected readers to re-judge, and mechanically undoes/reorders misplaced writes via per-tool registered inverses; serializable at quiescence.
papers.relevance: The most direct systems treatment of the focus question. Key insight: agent transactions span minutes so 2PL blocks and OCC discards too much work; control must be advisory with LLM-driven repair.

papers.title: Verified Detection and Prevention of Concurrency Anomalies in Multi-Agent Large Language Model Systems
papers.core_idea: Formalizes four anomalies (stale-generation, phantom-tool, causal-cascade, tool-effect reordering) in TLA+ with a machine-checked L0-L4 consistency hierarchy and Verus-proved detectors; reproduces a silent lost update in a real framework and a reordering bug in LangGraph's ToolNode.
papers.relevance: Names, with counter-examples, exactly how parallel agents corrupt a shared memory store, and gives an isolation-level ladder to specify against. UNVERIFIED quality: recent single-author preprint, but the anomaly taxonomy is independently useful.

papers.title: Governed Shared Memory for Multi-Agent LLM Systems
papers.core_idea: Formalizes the fleet-memory problem via four failure modes (unauthorized leakage, stale propagation, contradiction persistence, provenance collapse) and four primitives (scoped retrieval, temporal supersession, provenance tracking, policy-governed propagation), evaluated on a production service.
papers.relevance: Reports a concrete pipeline-ordering bug worth designing around: a synchronous near-duplicate gate rejected contradictory writes before the async contradiction detector could see them — a direct warning about placing dedup ahead of conflict resolution.

papers.title: TOKI: A Bitemporal Operator Algebra for Contradiction Resolution in LLM-Agent Persistent Memory
papers.core_idea: Frames contradiction resolution as write-time concurrency control; types four production heuristics (LWW, evidence-weighted merge, await-confirmation, per-rule policy) as bitemporal operators over a dual-row schema, each with an isolation precondition and an audit row preserving the losing fact.
papers.relevance: Argues that keyed logging of the adjudicating judge is necessary for replay consistency — i.e. you must record *which* model/version resolved the conflict, or the store is not reproducible. UNVERIFIED quality: recent preprint.

papers.title: PROJECTMEM: A Local-First, Event-Sourced Memory and Judgment Layer for AI Coding Agents
papers.core_idea: Append-only plain-text log of typed events (issues, attempts, fixes, decisions, notes) deterministically projected into compact summaries served over MCP, with a pre-action gate that blocks repeating a known-failed fix; fully offline.
papers.relevance: A working existence proof of the target architecture on a laptop: append-only log plus deterministic projection plus provenance trail, three dependencies, no telemetry.

papers.title: The Log is the Agent: Event-Sourced Reactive Graphs for Auditable, Forkable Agentic Systems
papers.core_idea: Inverts the usual framework layering: the append-only event log is the source of truth and the working graph is a deterministic projection of it; behaviors react to graph changes and emit new events.
papers.relevance: Makes forkability and exact replay first-class — you can branch an agent's memory at any log offset, which is the reproducibility property the brief asks for.

papers.title: Deterministic Replay for AI Agent Systems
papers.core_idea: agrepl intercepts all external interactions at the transport layer via a MITM proxy and records them, so a prior agent run can be faithfully re-executed despite LLM sampling variance and external API state.
papers.relevance: The missing half of reproducibility: provenance tells you what the inputs were, transport-level record/replay lets you actually re-run against them.

papers.title: CodeCRDT: Observation-Driven Coordination for Multi-Agent LLM Code Generation
papers.core_idea: Agents coordinate by observing a CRDT-backed shared state with deterministic convergence rather than by message passing; 600 trials show up to 21.1% speedup on some tasks but up to 39.4% slowdown on others.
papers.relevance: Honest empirical result: CRDT coordination for agents is not a free win. Useful because it reports the negative cases rather than only the speedups.

papers.title: Multi-agent Collaboration with State Management (STORM)
papers.core_idea: Argues workspace isolation (one git worktree per agent) merely defers conflict to an expensive post-hoc merge, and instead mediates agent state during execution.
papers.relevance: Directly critiques the most common current practice (isolate-then-merge) that a naive local memory store would copy.

papers.title: Before the Pull Request: Mining Multi-Agent Coordination
papers.core_idea: grite, a serverless coordination substrate that stores its records inside git itself as an append-only signed event log, capturing how concurrent agents claim, divide, and collide over shared work.
papers.relevance: Demonstrates using git's own object store as the durable, signed, append-only coordination log — a very cheap local implementation path.

papers.title: Multi-Agent Memory from a Computer Architecture Perspective: Visions and Challenges Ahead
papers.core_idea: Position paper framing multi-agent memory as an architecture problem: shared vs distributed paradigms, a three-layer I/O/cache/memory hierarchy, and protocol gaps in cross-agent cache sharing and structured access control; names multi-agent memory consistency as the top open challenge.
papers.relevance: Independent confirmation from an architecture group that consistency, not retrieval quality, is the binding constraint for multi-agent memory.

papers.title: A Graph-Native Bitemporal Memory Store for Conversational AI Agents
papers.core_idea: Agent-local property graph with HNSW vector indexes and a full bitemporal model: immutable identity nodes linked to versioned content nodes carrying valid-time and transaction-time intervals.
papers.relevance: Concrete schema for non-destructive updates: nothing is overwritten, so 'what did the agent believe on date X' remains answerable — the core of auditability.

papers.title: SAFEFLOW: A Principled Protocol for Trustworthy and Transactional Autonomous Agent Systems
papers.core_idea: Protocol-level framework applying fine-grained information flow control to agent systems, tracking provenance, integrity, and confidentiality of every data object, with transactional execution.
papers.relevance: Ties provenance to security rather than only audit: IFC labels travel with a claim, so untrusted-source data cannot silently launder into a trusted memory record.

papers.title: ESAA: Event Sourcing for Autonomous Agents in LLM-Based Software Engineering
papers.core_idea: Separates the agent's probabilistic cognitive intention from deterministic state mutation using event-sourcing, addressing lack of native state and long-horizon context degradation.
papers.relevance: States the key architectural separation cleanly: the LLM proposes events, a deterministic reducer applies them. That boundary is what makes the store verifiable at all.

papers.title: An Empirical Characterization of Event Sourced Systems and Their Schema Evolution -- Lessons from Industry
papers.core_idea: Grounded-theory study of 19 production event-sourced systems, documenting the pattern's rationale, context, and — critically — how practitioners handle event schema evolution.
papers.relevance: The hard-won operational warning: an append-only log you can never rewrite means schema evolution is forever. This is the main long-term cost of the recommended design.

papers.title: Efficient and Robust Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Using Hierarchical Navigable Small World Graphs
papers.core_idea: Multi-layer proximity graph with exponentially decaying layer assignment and distance-scale-separated links, giving logarithmic-complexity approximate nearest-neighbor search.
papers.relevance: The standard in-memory semantic recall index; runs comfortably on a laptop for millions of memory vectors and is what sqlite-vec/hnswlib-backed local stores use.

papers.title: DiskANN: Fast Accurate Billion-point Nearest Neighbor Search on a Single Node
papers.core_idea: Graph index designed for SSD residency: indexes and searches a billion points on one workstation with 64GB RAM, over 5000 QPS at sub-3ms mean latency and 95%+ recall@1.
papers.relevance: Shows the vector-recall layer does not have to fit in RAM — the right answer if a single laptop's agent memory outgrows HNSW's memory footprint.

papers.title: MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
papers.core_idea: Virtual context management: OS-style paging between a fast in-context tier and slower external storage, with the model itself issuing the memory-movement calls.
papers.relevance: The reference point for the tiering layer above the storage substrate, and the baseline nearly every later agent-memory paper compares against.

papers.title: Zep: A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory
papers.core_idea: Memory-layer service built on a temporal knowledge graph that integrates ongoing conversation and business data dynamically rather than doing static document retrieval.
papers.relevance: The best-known production-oriented temporal-graph agent memory; the temporal-edge model is the practical ancestor of the bitemporal designs above.

papers.title: A-MEM: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents
papers.core_idea: Memory system where the agent dynamically organizes its own memory (linking, note evolution) rather than using fixed storage/retrieval operations.
papers.relevance: Represents the self-organizing end of the design space — and, per later critiques, the one with the worst write-latency and concurrency behavior, which is precisely the tension this survey is about.

methods.name: SQLite in WAL mode as the single transactional spine
methods.mechanism: Append committed pages to a -wal file, leave the main DB untouched, index the WAL through a shared-memory -shm file. Readers snapshot at the last commit 'end mark' and never block the writer; the writer never blocks readers. Checkpointing folds the WAL back into the DB. PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL fsyncs only at checkpoint (fast, but loses recent commits on power loss); FULL fsyncs each commit.
methods.strengths: Real ACID with decades of hardening; zero-ops; readers and one writer are genuinely concurrent; WAL mode is sticky across reopen so it survives process restarts; combines cleanly with sqlite-vec/FTS5 for hybrid recall in the same file and same transaction.
methods.weaknesses: Exactly one writer at a time — N agents must funnel through a lock and will hit SQLITE_BUSY without a busy_timeout and BEGIN IMMEDIATE discipline. Requires shared memory, so it does not work on network filesystems (no NFS/SMB/Dropbox-backed store). WAL is slow above ~100MB transactions. Long-running readers starve the checkpointer and the WAL grows unbounded. A WAL-reset corruption bug existed from 3.7.0 through 3.51.2 (fixed in 3.51.3) — pin a current version.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes, ideal. Ships with macOS, single file, no daemon. This should be the default durable core.

methods.name: Multi-writer SQLite via BEGIN CONCURRENT or hctree
methods.mechanism: BEGIN CONCURRENT (SQLite begin-concurrent branch, wal/wal2 mode) defers locking to COMMIT and validates optimistically at page granularity: if any page the transaction read was modified since it began, the commit aborts. hctree is a separate experimental backend using optimistic row-level locking with a different file format.
methods.strengths: Removes the single-writer funnel for genuinely disjoint agent write sets; COMMIT is still serialized so recovery semantics stay simple.
methods.weaknesses: BEGIN CONCURRENT's page-level conflict detection produces false conflicts: two agents updating unrelated rows that share a page will abort one of them. Both are experimental branches, not mainline SQLite — you inherit a fork. hctree changes the file format.
methods.local_feasibility: Possible but not recommended as a foundation. Prefer a single-writer funnel until profiling proves write contention is the bottleneck; revisit via Turso/libSQL if it lands in a shipped build.

methods.name: Embedded LSM key-value store (RocksDB / LevelDB / Pebble / redb)
methods.mechanism: Buffer writes in a memtable behind a WAL, flush to immutable sorted runs, compact in the background; Bloom/xor filters per SSTable short-circuit negative lookups.
methods.strengths: Very high sustained write throughput for an append-heavy memory stream; native ordered scans; tombstones give cheap logical deletes; mature.
methods.weaknesses: No SQL, no joins, no secondary indexes without hand-rolling them. Compaction causes unpredictable multi-second tail latency and write amplification of 10-30x under random workloads — visible as UI stalls on a laptop. Adds a native dependency and a large tuning surface. Format-compatibility discipline matters across versions.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes, but usually unnecessary. Justified only if write rate exceeds what SQLite's single writer sustains, which for agent memory is rare.

methods.name: Append-only event log with deterministic projection (event sourcing)
methods.mechanism: The only mutation primitive is 'append a typed, immutable event.' All queryable state (tables, graphs, indexes, summaries) is a pure function of the log prefix, rebuilt by a deterministic reducer. The log is the source of truth; projections are disposable caches.
methods.strengths: Concurrent writers only ever append, so there is nothing to overwrite and no lost-update class of bug. Gives time travel, fork-at-offset, and exact replay for free. Projections can be rebuilt when the schema changes or a bug is found. Provides the audit trail without extra bookkeeping.
methods.weaknesses: Event schema is effectively permanent — the dominant long-term maintenance cost reported by practitioners. Reads require a materialized projection, so you own cache-invalidation. Log grows without bound absent compaction/snapshotting. The reducer must be genuinely deterministic, which means no LLM calls inside it (LLM output belongs in the event, not the reduction).
methods.local_feasibility: Yes, excellent. Plain files or a SQLite events table plus a projection table in the same transaction. This is the recommended top-level architecture.

methods.name: Content-addressable object store + Merkle DAG (git object model / IPLD CIDs)
methods.mechanism: Hash every immutable artifact (source document, tool output, transcript chunk, claim record) and store it under its digest. Trees reference blobs by hash; commits reference trees and parents, forming a DAG. Identical content stores once.
methods.strengths: Integrity is intrinsic — a corrupted or altered object fails its own name. Dedup is free. A claim can cite its evidence by CID, and that citation can never silently drift to different content. Structural sharing across versions is automatic. git itself can be the storage engine (see grite).
methods.weaknesses: Mutable pointers still need a separate mechanism (refs/IPNS), and that mechanism is where the concurrency problem reappears. Garbage collection of unreachable objects is nontrivial. Loose objects are inefficient at high object counts without packing. git's SHA-1 legacy needs the SHA-256 object format for anything security-relevant.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes, trivially. A directory of hash-named zstd-compressed files, or an actual git repo. No network required — content addressing is orthogonal to IPFS's DHT.

methods.name: Merkle transparency log (RFC 6962 / history tree)
