methods.mechanism: Maintain an append-only Merkle tree over the event log. Publish a signed root after each batch. Serve inclusion proofs ('event E is in the log at size N') and consistency proofs ('the tree at size N is a prefix of the tree at size M') in O(log n) nodes.
methods.strengths: Turns 'durable' into 'provably unrewritten.' Detects retroactive edits and split views, not just corruption. Proofs are kilobytes where hash chains would be hundreds of megabytes. An external auditor needs only root hashes, not the data.
methods.weaknesses: Only tamper-*evident*, not tamper-proof — detection requires someone actually checking, and roots must be witnessed somewhere the writer cannot rewrite (a second machine, a co-signing witness, a timestamping service). Adds hashing cost on the write path.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes. Pure computation; a few hundred lines over the event log. The only external requirement is somewhere to anchor roots if you want protection against a compromised local machine.

methods.name: Merkle Search Tree for anti-entropy between agent stores
methods.mechanism: Deterministic, history-independent search tree whose node hashes depend only on the key-value set. Two replicas compare root hashes, descend only into subtrees that differ, and exchange the delta.
methods.strengths: Reconciliation cost is O(difference), not O(state). The same hashes serve as integrity proofs. History-independence means two replicas that converge on content converge on structure, so the diff terminates. Battle-tested at scale in Bluesky's AT Protocol.
methods.weaknesses: Only helps when there are multiple stores to reconcile; pure overhead for a single-process store. Needs a value-level merge rule (a CRDT) underneath — the MST solves 'what differs,' not 'who wins.'
methods.local_feasibility: Yes, and it is the right structure if agents ever run on separate machines or in separate sandboxes that must later merge.

methods.name: CRDTs for lock-free concurrent agent writes (op-based / delta-state / JSON)
methods.mechanism: Represent memory as a join-semilattice or as commutative operations, so any delivery order converges. Delta-state variants ship small increments while tolerating duplicate and out-of-order delivery. JSON CRDTs merge nested map/list edits.
methods.strengths: No locks, no coordination, no lost updates, no rollback; agents write while offline or sandboxed and merge later. Delta-state CRDTs are duplicate-tolerant, which composes perfectly with at-least-once agent retries. Automerge and Yjs are mature, embeddable implementations.
methods.weaknesses: Convergence is not correctness — CRDTs guarantee all replicas agree, not that they agree on something semantically right (concurrent 'X is true' / 'X is false' merges to a well-defined but useless set). Metadata/tombstone growth over long histories. Op-based CRDTs require exactly-once causal delivery from the layer below. CodeCRDT measured up to 39.4% slowdown on some agent tasks, so the coordination win is workload-dependent.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes. Automerge/Yjs run in-process. Best used for the *structured document* parts of memory (nested notes, task lists), with a semantic policy layer on top for contradictory facts.

methods.name: Single-writer serialization gateway (write-intent queue)
methods.mechanism: All agents submit write intents to one durable queue; a single writer process drains it, validates, and commits to SQLite in one transaction per intent (or batched). Agents get back a commit LSN/hash.
methods.strengths: Eliminates the entire concurrent-write corruption class by construction. Trivially matches SQLite's actual concurrency model. Gives a total order, which makes replay, audit, and provenance ordering unambiguous. Easiest thing to reason about and to test.
methods.weaknesses: The writer is a throughput ceiling and a single point of failure. Agents must tolerate write latency and asynchronous rejection. Does not by itself prevent *logical* conflicts (two agents writing contradictory facts) — it only serializes them.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes, and this is the pragmatic default for a laptop-scale store. One writer plus N readers is exactly what SQLite WAL is built for.

methods.name: Advisory concurrency control with agent-driven repair (MTPO / CoAgent)
methods.mechanism: Fix a serialization order at agent launch; serve each read the order-filtered value; apply writes speculatively in place; notify an affected reader that a conflicting write landed and let the LLM judge whether its plan is still valid and patch only the dependent operations. Misplaced writes are undone/reordered via a saga-style inverse each tool registers up front.
methods.strengths: Fits the actual shape of agent transactions — minutes long, opaque read sets, effects that take hold immediately and cannot be buffered. 2PL blocks for minutes; OCC throws away minutes of inference per abort. Reported within 5% of serial correctness at 1.4x speedup where 2PL and OCC surrendered nearly all concurrency gain.
methods.weaknesses: Requires every tool to register a correct inverse — a real engineering tax and a correctness dependency. Correctness rests partly on LLM judgment, so it is probabilistic, not proved. Recent (2026) and not yet independently replicated.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes in principle (it is middleware, not infrastructure), but it is research-grade. Adopt the *idea* — advisory notification plus registered compensations — before adopting the implementation.

methods.name: Idempotency keys + effect-dedup table
methods.mechanism: Every write carries a caller-generated stable key (or the content hash of the intent). The writer inserts into a unique-indexed dedup table inside the same transaction as the effect. A replay of the same key hits the constraint and returns the original result instead of re-applying.
methods.strengths: Turns unavoidable at-least-once retries into exactly-once *effects*, which is the only version of exactly-once that is achievable. Cheap: one unique index. Makes crashed-mid-write agents safe to restart blindly.
methods.weaknesses: Requires keys to be genuinely stable across retries — an agent that re-prompts and gets slightly different text generates a different key and defeats it. The dedup table needs a retention policy. Only covers the local store; external tool side effects need their own idempotency.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes, trivial in SQLite. Non-negotiable for a multi-agent write path.

methods.name: Bitemporal versioning with supersession and audit rows
methods.mechanism: Every fact carries two intervals: valid time (when the fact was true in the world) and transaction time (when the store believed it). Updates never overwrite — they close the old row's transaction interval and insert a new one. Contradiction resolution writes an audit row preserving the losing fact plus the identity of whatever adjudicated.
methods.strengths: 'What did the agent believe on date X, and why' stays answerable forever. Distinguishes 'the world changed' from 'we were wrong,' which agents constantly conflate. Contradiction resolution becomes an explicit, typed, auditable operation instead of a silent overwrite.
methods.weaknesses: Roughly doubles schema complexity and every query must be time-qualified or it will return superseded rows. Storage grows monotonically. Requires discipline: TOKI's result is that you must log *which judge* (model + version + prompt) resolved each contradiction, or replay is not consistent — most deployed systems omit this.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes. Pure schema design in SQLite; SQL:2011-style temporal columns plus an audit table.

methods.name: Approximate membership filters (Bloom / xor / binary fuse) as write-path gates
methods.mechanism: Maintain a compact filter over stored claim hashes, seen source URLs, and already-attempted actions. Query it before doing expensive work; no false negatives means a 'not present' answer is certain.
methods.strengths: Sub-microsecond, few bits per key. Binary fuse filters sit within ~13% of the storage lower bound; xor filters ~23%; Bloom ~44%. Also the LSM read-path accelerator if you use one. Enables the 'have I already tried this failed fix' pre-action gate cheaply.
methods.weaknesses: False positives mean occasionally skipping a genuinely new item — so a filter hit must be followed by an exact check before discarding data, never used as the final word. Xor and binary fuse filters are static (rebuild to insert), so pair them with a small mutable Bloom for the hot tier. Under adversarial input (untrusted web content) an attacker can inflate the false-positive rate and suppress real memories, and filter state can leak membership information — key the hashes secretly.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes. Pure in-memory computation, megabytes for millions of keys.

methods.name: Count-Min sketch for frequency and salience
methods.mechanism: d x w counter array with pairwise-independent hashes; point queries return the minimum counter, giving a never-underestimating frequency estimate with error bounded by epsilon times the stream's L1 norm.
methods.strengths: Sublinear space for 'how often has this entity/source/claim recurred,' which drives salience ranking, decay/forgetting policy, and heavy-hitter detection over the write stream. One-sided error is the safe direction for retention decisions.
methods.weaknesses: Overestimates on collisions, so it is poor for rare items — exactly the long tail agent memory often cares most about. No deletion in the basic form. Cannot enumerate the keys it counted.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes, trivial. A few hundred KB. Best used as a ranking signal, never as ground truth.

methods.name: MinHash-LSH / SimHash for near-duplicate memory detection
methods.mechanism: Shingle each record; MinHash sketches estimate Jaccard similarity via band-hashing into candidate buckets. SimHash projects onto random hyperplanes to produce a 64-bit fingerprint where near-duplicates differ in few bits, found via permuted sorted tables. LSHBloom replaces per-band bucket storage with Bloom filters.
methods.strengths: Stops the store from filling with near-identical restatements of the same fact from parallel agents. Orders of magnitude cheaper than pairwise embedding comparison. MinHash generally dominates SimHash on sparse binary data; SimHash's Hamming filtering is faster as a first-pass. LSHBloom makes corpus-scale dedup fit in laptop RAM.
methods.weaknesses: Detects surface similarity, not semantic equivalence — 'the drug is effective' and 'the drug is not effective' are near-duplicates by shingle overlap. Threshold tuning is empirical. Critically, a *synchronous* near-duplicate gate placed ahead of contradiction detection can reject a contradicting write before anything evaluates the contradiction (observed in a production system). Order the pipeline: contradiction check first, dedup second.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes. datasketch/simhash libraries; index over millions of records on one machine.

methods.name: Content-defined chunking (FastCDC / Gear / Rabin) for blob deduplication
methods.mechanism: Slide a rolling hash over the byte stream and cut a boundary when the hash matches a mask; boundaries follow content, so an insertion shifts only local boundaries. FastCDC adds simplified hash judgment, cut-point skipping below a minimum chunk size, and chunk-size normalization to recover the dedup ratio that skipping costs.
methods.strengths: Dedups revisions of the same document/transcript/tool output, where fixed-size blocking fails completely after a single byte insertion. FastCDC is fast enough to run on everything ingested. Composes directly with content addressing — each chunk is a CID, so dedup and verification are one mechanism (see content-defined Merkle trees).
methods.weaknesses: Chunking is often the throughput bottleneck of a dedup pipeline. Per-algorithm claims in the originating papers do not hold up uniformly under impartial comparison. Security: chunk boundaries are a side channel — CDC parameters can be extracted and used to infer stored content, so parameters must be secret/keyed if the store ever syncs with an untrusted peer.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes. Pure CPU; fastcdc bindings exist for Python/Rust/Go. Worth it for large artifacts, overkill for short text notes.

methods.name: PROV-O provenance graph + RO-Crate export
methods.mechanism: Model every claim as a prov:Entity generated by a prov:Activity (a specific agent run, with model id, prompt hash, tool version, timestamp) associated with a prov:Agent, derived via prov:wasDerivedFrom from source entities identified by content hash. Export a snapshot as an RO-Crate: data, code, and JSON-LD metadata in one self-describing package; Workflow Run RO-Crate profiles cover the plan/execution distinction.
methods.strengths: A W3C Recommendation with existing tooling and an interchange format others can consume. RO-Crate is deliberately lightweight (Schema.org JSON-LD) rather than full semantic-web machinery. Workflow Run RO-Crate is the closest existing standard to 'record this agent run so it can be re-executed.' Storage-layer capture (per PASS) is complete where agent self-annotation drifts.
methods.weaknesses: Provenance volume can exceed the data it describes. RDF/SPARQL tooling is heavy for a laptop app — most implementations store provenance relationally and only serialize to PROV-O on export. PROV-O has no built-in integrity: a provenance record is only as trustworthy as the log it sits in, so it must be anchored in the Merkle log to mean anything.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes. Store lineage as ordinary SQLite edge rows; generate PROV-O/RO-Crate only at export time.

methods.name: Transport-level record/replay for reproducibility
methods.mechanism: Interpose a recording proxy on every external interaction (model API calls with sampling parameters and seeds, tool calls, HTTP fetches) and persist request/response pairs keyed by content hash into the same log. Replay serves from the recording.
methods.strengths: This is what actually makes an agent run reproducible. Provenance alone tells you what the inputs were; without recorded responses you cannot re-execute against a changed web or a re-sampled model. Also gives deterministic tests and makes the 'which model version adjudicated this contradiction' requirement satisfiable.
methods.weaknesses: Recording volume is large. Recordings can contain secrets and personal data, so they need the same protection as the memory itself. Non-determinism inside the model still leaks through unless temperature/seed are pinned. Cross-host redirects, streaming, and time-dependent APIs all need special handling.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes — a local MITM proxy plus a content-addressed response cache. This is the highest-leverage piece most agent memory designs omit.

methods.name: Hybrid logical clocks for causal ordering of agent writes
methods.mechanism: Each event carries an HLC timestamp: a monotonic counter kept close to physical time, advanced on send/receive so that happens-before is captured without clock synchronization assumptions.
methods.strengths: Constant-size (unlike vector clocks over a growing agent set), human-interpretable for audit, and causally correct for merge. Enables consistent snapshot reads across concurrently-writing agents.
methods.weaknesses: Cannot detect concurrency as precisely as vector clocks — HLC gives a total order that may order genuinely concurrent events arbitrarily. Depends on the local clock not jumping backward wildly.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes, ~100 lines. Use HLC for ordering/audit and the Merkle-DAG parent links for true causality.

methods.name: Local vector index for semantic recall (HNSW in-memory, DiskANN on SSD, sqlite-vec in-file)
methods.mechanism: HNSW builds a hierarchical proximity graph with distance-scale-separated links for logarithmic-complexity ANN search. DiskANN keeps the graph on SSD, indexing a billion points on one 64GB workstation at 5000+ QPS and sub-3ms mean latency. sqlite-vec puts vectors in the same SQLite file as the relational data.
methods.strengths: Semantic recall over memories that share no keywords. sqlite-vec keeps vectors, metadata, and provenance in one file and one transaction — no dual-write consistency problem between a SQL store and a separate vector DB. DiskANN removes the RAM ceiling if the store grows large.
methods.weaknesses: HNSW is memory-hungry and expensive to delete from (soft-delete plus periodic rebuild). Embeddings are model-version-dependent: change the embedder and the whole index must be rebuilt, and old vectors are not comparable to new ones — record the embedding model in provenance. ANN recall is approximate, so a claim can be *stored* and still not be *found*, which is not an integrity failure but reads like one.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes. sqlite-vec or hnswlib for the common case; DiskANN only past tens of millions of vectors.

methods.name: Per-agent git worktree isolation with post-hoc merge
methods.mechanism: Give each agent its own branch/worktree, let it write freely, and merge at the end.
methods.strengths: Zero coordination during execution; complete isolation; git provides the content-addressed, signed, append-only substrate for free; failed agent runs are discarded by deleting a branch.
methods.weaknesses: Defers all conflict to an expensive post-hoc merge where recovery costs more than prevention would have, and where the merging party lacks the context each agent had. Agents cannot see each other's findings, so they duplicate work and re-derive the same facts. This is the most common current practice and it is the one explicitly criticized by recent work.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes, and it is what most setups do today — but treat it as a baseline to beat, not a target design.

takeaways: The two questions in the brief have different answers and should not be solved by one mechanism. Concurrency safety comes from making the write primitive an append of an immutable, idempotent, causally-stamped event. Traceability comes from content-addressing the evidence and hash-linking the log. Append-only is the hinge: it is simultaneously the reason parallel writes cannot corrupt anything (nothing is overwritten) and the reason every claim stays auditable (nothing is erased).

Recommended concrete stack for a macOS laptop, all local, no external service: SQLite in WAL mode (synchronous=NORMAL, busy_timeout set, BEGIN IMMEDIATE for writes) holding an append-only typed-event table plus deterministically-derived projection tables written in the same transaction; a content-addressed blob directory (BLAKE3, FastCDC-chunked for large artifacts) for evidence; an RFC-6962-style Merkle history tree over the event log with roots signed and periodically anchored off-machine; a single writer process draining a durable write-intent queue from N agents; idempotency keys with a unique index on the write path; bitemporal fact rows with audit rows for supersession; PROV-O-shaped lineage edges exported as RO-Crate; sqlite-vec plus FTS5 for recall in the same file; a recording proxy over all model and tool calls. Every component here is a single file or a library — nothing needs a daemon.

For parallel agents, the honest ordering of options by risk is: (1) single-writer funnel — eliminates the corruption class outright and matches SQLite's real concurrency model; (2) CRDTs for the structured-document parts of memory where concurrent edits should genuinely merge; (3) advisory control with registered compensations (the CoAgent/MTPO idea) once tool inverses exist; (4) optimistic multi-writer SQLite only after profiling proves the funnel is the bottleneck. Start at (1). Most agent memory workloads are nowhere near the write rate that justifies anything else.

Classical concurrency control genuinely does fit agents badly, and this is now documented rather than folklore. An agent transaction spans minutes of inference, its read set is broad and opaque rather than statically inferable, and its writes take effect the moment the tool runs — they can be neither buffered nor forked. Two-phase locking therefore blocks for minutes; optimistic concurrency control discards minutes of inference on every abort. This is the specific reason the naive answer ('just use transactions') underperforms.

The concurrency anomalies are now named and mechanically specified, which is more useful than any single system: stale-generation (an agent generates from a read that was invalidated before its write lands), phantom-tool, causal-cascade (one agent's bad output becomes another's premise), and tool-effect reordering. Silent lost updates have been reproduced in a real deployed framework and reordering demonstrated in LangGraph's ToolNode on unmodified output. Specify your store against this taxonomy rather than against a vague 'don't corrupt it.'

Exactly-once delivery is not achievable and is the wrong target; exactly-once *effect* is achievable and is the right one. The mechanism is Helland's: assume at-least-once, attach a stable idempotency key to every write intent, and insert into a unique-indexed dedup table inside the same transaction as the effect. Kafka's production answer is the same shape — atomically commit the output write together with the input position. The failure mode to watch is key instability: an agent that re-prompts and gets slightly different text produces a different key and silently defeats the whole scheme, so derive keys from the intent's semantic identity, not from generated prose.

Convergence is not correctness, and this is the most commonly misunderstood point about CRDTs in agent systems. A CRDT guarantees all replicas end up in the same state; it says nothing about that state being right. Two agents concurrently writing 'X is true' and 'X is false' merge to a well-defined, useless set. CRDTs solve structural conflict; semantic conflict needs a separate, explicit, logged adjudication layer on top. And the coordination win is not automatic — measured agent workloads show both 21% speedups and 39% slowdowns depending on the task.

Contradiction resolution is write-time concurrency control, not a retrieval-time nicety. Whatever heuristic you use (last-writer-wins, evidence-weighted merge, await-confirmation, per-rule policy), it has an isolation precondition it silently assumes. The non-obvious hard requirement: if an LLM sits on the write path as the adjudicator, you must log the judge's identity — model, version, prompt — keyed to the resolution, or the store is not replay-consistent. Essentially every deployed system omits this, and it is cheap to add.

Pipeline ordering is a real, observed bug class, not a hypothetical. A production multi-agent memory service placed a synchronous near-duplicate gate ahead of an asynchronous contradiction detector, so contradicting writes — which are textually near-duplicates of what they contradict — were rejected before anything could evaluate the contradiction. Order the write path: causality/idempotency check, then contradiction detection, then near-duplicate suppression, then indexing.

Make the LLM/deterministic boundary explicit and put the log on the deterministic side. The model proposes events; a pure reducer applies them. Nothing non-deterministic may live inside the projection function. This one rule is what makes replay, fork-at-offset, differential testing, and audit all work — and it is what most agent memory designs violate by calling a model during consolidation or merge.

Tamper-evidence is cheap and almost nobody does it. A history tree over the event log gives kilobyte-sized inclusion and consistency proofs where a plain hash chain would need hundreds of megabytes at comparable scale. But it is evident, not proof: detection requires an auditor, and roots must be anchored somewhere the writing machine cannot rewrite. For a purely local store, the realistic threat model is accidental corruption and buggy agents rather than an attacker with root, and Merkle roots cover both — just do not oversell it as tamper-proof.

Provenance captured by the store beats provenance asked of the writer. This is the twenty-year-old PASS argument and it holds exactly for agents: an agent asked to self-report its sources produces incomplete and drifting metadata, and recent evaluation of deep-research agents confirms model-generated citations cannot be relied on. Capture lineage at the write path — which activity, which model version, which source CIDs — and bind claims to content-addressed evidence at write time, so a citation can never silently drift to different content.

Content addressing is the piece that makes 'traceable' actually mean something. If a claim cites its evidence by hash rather than by URL or row id, the citation is immutable by construction: the cited bytes either still hash to that value or they are gone. This composes with content-defined chunking so that revisions of the same source share storage, and with Merkle structure so that verification and deduplication are one mechanism rather than two. None of this requires IPFS or a network — CIDs are useful entirely offline.

Reproducibility needs record/replay, not just provenance, and this is the most commonly missing component. Provenance tells you what the inputs were; it does not let you re-run, because the model resamples and the web changes. A transport-level recording proxy over all model and tool calls, with responses stored content-addressed in the same log, is what closes the gap. Budget for the storage and treat recordings as sensitive.

Sketches belong on the write path as gates, never as the final word. Bloom/binary-fuse filters answer 'definitely not present' cheaply — a hit must always be followed by an exact check. Count-Min never undercounts, which makes it safe for retention decisions but bad for the rare long tail agent memory often cares most about. MinHash-LSH detects surface duplication, not semantic equivalence, and will happily flag a claim and its negation as near-duplicates. Two adversarial caveats matter once the store ingests untrusted web content: probabilistic filters can be poisoned to inflate false positives (suppressing real memories) and can leak membership, and CDC chunk boundaries are a side channel — key the hashes and chunking parameters.

The costs to accept up front. Append-only means event schema is permanent — practitioners consistently report schema evolution as the dominant long-term cost of event sourcing, so version events from day one. Bitemporal schemas roughly double query complexity and every query must be time-qualified. Vector indexes are embedding-model-dependent: change the embedder and the index must be rebuilt while old vectors stay incomparable, so record the embedding model in provenance. LSM compaction produces multi-second tail latency that is user-visible on a laptop, which is a reason to prefer SQLite unless write rate forces otherwise.

Evidence-quality caveat on the recent literature. The classical layer (LSM, ARIES, CRDTs, Bloom, Count-Min, MinHash/SimHash, CDC, Merkle/CT, PROV-O, RO-Crate) is solid, replicated, and deployed. The multi-agent-memory layer is almost entirely 2025-2026 arXiv preprints, many single-author, several evidently LLM-assisted, with little independent replication and no shared benchmark for the write-path properties that matter here. Their anomaly taxonomies and failure-mode vocabularies are genuinely useful; their quantitative claims should be treated as UNVERIFIED. Independent multi-group confirmation exists for only one thing: that multi-agent memory *consistency*, not retrieval quality, is the binding constraint.

area: Memory and knowledge management for scientific / drug-discovery agents (2015-2026): FAIR data, RO-Crate research objects, ELN data models, computational-workflow provenance (CWL/Nextflow/Snakemake, WRROC), claim-evidence and argumentation graphs (nanopublications, micropublications, SEPIO/ECO/EVI), how AI-scientist agents (Coscientist, ChemCrow, The AI Scientist, Robin, Co-Scientist, Biomni, TxAgent, Kosmos) store and reuse intermediate results, and grounded-citation / attribution methods (AIS, RARR, self-citation verification). Central question: how to store a scientific CLAIM so that its evidence, uncertainty, and verification status are first-class and machine-checkable.

papers.title: The FAIR Guiding Principles for scientific data management and stewardship
papers.core_idea: Defines 15 measurable principles (F1-F4, A1-A2, I1-I3, R1.x) for Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable digital assets, explicitly aimed at machine-actionability, not just human readability. R1.2 mandates that data be 'associated with detailed provenance'.
papers.relevance: The normative base layer. For an agent memory store, F1 (globally unique persistent identifiers on every stored object), I1 (a shared formal knowledge-representation language), and R1.2 (provenance) translate directly into: every claim gets a resolvable ID, is stored in RDF/JSON-LD, and carries its derivation. Note FAIR says nothing about correctness or evidence quality - that gap is exactly what SEPIO/ECO/EVI/micropublications fill.

papers.title: The FAIR Cookbook - the essential resource for and by FAIR doers
papers.core_idea: Community recipe collection operationalising FAIR for life-science and pharma data, produced largely out of IMI/FAIRplus with heavy industry (drug-discovery) participation.
papers.relevance: The practical bridge between the 2016 principles and a working pharma data store; useful as a checklist source when designing what metadata an agent must emit alongside each result.

papers.title: A Fresh Look at FAIR for Research Software
papers.core_idea: Re-derives the FAIR principles for software, arguing software differs from data in being executable, versioned, dependency-bound, and continuously changing.
papers.relevance: An agent's stored claim depends on the exact software that produced it. FAIR4RS is the reason a claim record must pin software identity (version, container digest, environment lock) rather than just a tool name.

papers.title: Packaging research artefacts with RO-Crate
papers.venue_or_id: arXiv:2108.06503 (Soiland-Reyes, Sefton, Crosas, Goble et al.)
papers.core_idea: A lightweight, community-driven packaging format: a directory (or zip) plus ro-crate-metadata.json, a JSON-LD flattened graph using Schema.org, describing every contained entity, its identifiers, provenance, relations and annotations. Deliberately 'just enough' Linked Data.
papers.relevance: The most practical on-disk unit for agent memory. Each agent run, dataset, figure, or claim bundle becomes a crate with a machine-readable manifest. Low adoption cost (JSON-LD, no triplestore required), local-first, and already the substrate that WRROC, WorkflowHub and ARC build on.

papers.title: Recording provenance of workflow runs with RO-Crate (Workflow Run RO-Crate / WRROC)
papers.venue_or_id: arXiv:2312.07852; published version pmcid:PMC11386446 (Leo, Crusoe, Rodriguez-Navas, Kanitz, Colonnelli, Soiland-Reyes et al.)
papers.core_idea: Three nested profiles - Process Run Crate, Workflow Run Crate, Provenance Run Crate - capturing execution provenance at increasing granularity, aligned to W3C PROV, and implemented in six workflow management systems so runs from heterogeneous engines can be compared.
papers.relevance: This is the single most important existing standard for 'how did this number come to exist'. A claim record should carry a pointer to a WRROC crate: the workflow plan, the run, parameter values, input/output checksums, container images, and the agent(s) responsible. That makes re-derivation a machine action rather than a prose promise.

papers.title: Fusion of computational and experimental provenance in RO-Crate (ARC Workflow Run RO-Crate)
papers.venue_or_id: Journal of Integrative Bioinformatics; doi:10.1515/jib-2025-0050; pmid:42400369
papers.core_idea: Unifies the ISA framework (wet-lab protocols, samples, assays) with workflow-centric WRROC inside a single queryable provenance model, so a multimodal research object spans bench and compute.
papers.relevance: Drug discovery claims are hybrid: an IC50 comes from a plate reader plus an analysis pipeline. This is the only line of work found that interlinks experimental and computational provenance in one crate - the right template for a self-driving-lab agent memory.

papers.title: Sharing interoperable workflow provenance: A review of best practices and their practical application in CWLProv
papers.venue_or_id: GigaScience; doi:10.1093/gigascience/giz095; pmcid:PMC6824458 (Khan, Soiland-Reyes, Sinnott, Lonie, Goble, Crusoe)
papers.core_idea: Combines CWL workflow definitions, W3C PROV traces, and Research Object aggregation into a shareable bundle; surveys what prior provenance approaches got wrong (non-interoperable, engine-specific).
papers.relevance: The direct ancestor of WRROC and still the clearest statement of the interoperability requirements: prospective provenance (the plan) and retrospective provenance (the run) must both be captured and must be engine-neutral.

papers.title: Sustainable data analysis with Snakemake
papers.core_idea: Rule-based workflow definition with automatic per-rule software deployment (conda/containers), execution logging, and self-contained interactive HTML reports embedding results plus the code and parameters that produced them.
papers.relevance: Snakemake's report is a de facto claim-evidence bundle: each figure/table in the report is linked to its rule, code, and inputs. A useful existence proof that 'result carries its derivation' is achievable with modest tooling, entirely locally.

papers.title: nf-core: Community curated bioinformatics pipelines
papers.core_idea: Standardised, peer-reviewed, containerised Nextflow pipelines with mandated versioning, test data, and structured output/reporting conventions.
papers.relevance: Provides the pinned, reproducible execution substrate an agent should call rather than ad-hoc scripts; pipeline+version+container digest is a compact and honest provenance token to store in a claim record.

papers.title: End-to-End provenance representation for the understandability and reproducibility of scientific experiments using a semantic approach (REPRODUCE-ME)
papers.venue_or_id: Journal of Biomedical Semantics; doi:10.1186/s13326-021-00253-1; pmcid:PMC8734275 (Samuel & Koenig-Ries)
papers.core_idea: An ontology extending PROV-O and P-Plan to interlink data, computational steps, non-computational steps (instruments, materials, people), and results in one provenance graph.
papers.relevance: One of the few models that explicitly covers the non-computational half of an experiment - essential for drug-discovery agents whose claims rest partly on wet-lab steps that no workflow engine sees.

papers.title: FAIRSCAPE: A Framework for FAIR and Reproducible Biomedical Analytics
papers.venue_or_id: Neuroinformatics; doi:10.1007/s12021-021-09529-4; pmcid:PMC8760356 (Levinson, Al Manir, Clark et al.)
papers.core_idea: A microservices framework that mints persistent IDs with metadata for every dataset, software, and computation, and builds a complete Evidence Graph for every computational result, storing a URI to the graph root with the result.
papers.relevance: A working reference architecture for exactly the target requirement: 'every result resolves to the graph of what produced it'. Shows the pattern is implementable as a service layer over ordinary analytics.

papers.title: Evidence Graphs: Supporting Transparent and FAIR Computation, with Defeasible Reasoning on Data, Methods and Results
papers.venue_or_id: bioRxiv doi:10.1101/2021.03.29.437561 (EVI ontology; Al Manir, Clark et al.)
papers.core_idea: EVI, an OWL 2 ontology with inference rules extending PROV, treats any computational result or component of evidence as a DEFEASIBLE assertion supported by a DAG of computations, software, data, and agents; supports both supporting and challenging evidence across arbitrarily deep computation networks.
papers.relevance: The most directly applicable model for the core question. Defeasibility is the key insight: a claim's status is not a boolean stamped once, it is the current output of reasoning over a growing evidence DAG that can be overturned. Any agent claim store should be built this way rather than as an append-only 'facts' table.

papers.title: Micropublications: a Semantic Model for Claims, Evidence, Arguments and Annotations in Biomedical Communications
papers.venue_or_id: arXiv:1305.3506 (Clark, Ciccarese, Goble; later J Biomed Semantics 2014)
papers.core_idea: An OWL 2 + SWRL metadata model of scientific argumentation. Formalises claims, the statements and data/method specifications that support them, and typed relations for support, similarity and CHALLENGE. Statements in one work can cite individual statements in another; assertions in review articles can be transitively closed to their supporting evidence and methods.
papers.relevance: The canonical answer to 'how do you store a claim'. Three properties matter for agents: (1) evidence is a typed edge, not a citation string; (2) disagreement is representable, so refutations and negative results are storable; (3) transitive closure means you can mechanically ask 'what does this claim ultimately rest on', which is precisely the audit an agent needs before reusing a stored claim.

papers.title: Nanopublications: A Growing Resource of Provenance-Centric Scientific Linked Data
papers.core_idea: A nanopublication is an RDF container of three named graphs - assertion, provenance, and publication info - so that provenance and metadata attach at the granularity of a single atomic statement rather than a whole dataset or paper.
papers.relevance: The best-proven container format for a single machine-checkable claim. The three-graph split maps cleanly onto the requirement: assertion = the claim, provenance = evidence and derivation, pubinfo = who asserted it, when, under what license, with what confidence. Millions exist in the life sciences, so the pattern is battle-tested.

papers.title: Trusty URIs: Verifiable, Immutable, and Permanent Digital Artifacts for Linked Data
papers.core_idea: Embed a cryptographic hash of the content into the URI itself, computed at the RDF-graph level so the identifier survives format changes; entire reference trees become verifiable.
papers.relevance: Content-addressing is what makes a stored claim tamper-evident and makes 'this claim cites that claim' a checkable link rather than a dangling pointer. For a local agent store, a trusty-URI-style hash per claim record gives free deduplication, integrity checking, and stable cross-run identity.

papers.title: Broadening the Scope of Nanopublications (AIDA sentences)
papers.core_idea: Allows informal/underspecified claims to be nanopublished as controlled English sentences following the AIDA scheme - Atomic, Independent, Declarative, Absolute - remaining compatible with formal nanopublications.
papers.relevance: Very practical for LLM agents: forcing generated claims into atomic, self-contained, declarative, unhedged sentences makes them individually checkable, individually citable, and individually retractable. This is the cheapest possible claim normalisation step and should be applied before storage.

papers.title: Nanopublication-Based Semantic Publishing and Reviewing: A Field Study with Formalization Papers
papers.core_idea: Field study in which authors published results with machine-interpretable semantics from the outset, and reviews themselves were nanopublished and linked to the reviewed assertions.
papers.relevance: Demonstrates that VERIFICATION STATUS can itself be a first-class, separately-published, separately-attributed object linked to the claim - the model to copy for storing an agent's or a human's verification verdicts without mutating the original claim.

papers.title: ECO: the Evidence and Conclusion Ontology, an update for 2022
papers.core_idea: A community ontology of evidence TYPES and assertion methods (experimental assay classes, computational prediction, author statement, curator inference), used across GO and many biocuration pipelines.
papers.relevance: Supplies the controlled vocabulary for the 'what kind of evidence is this' field of a claim record. Critically it separates evidence type from assertion method (manual vs automatic), which is exactly the distinction needed when the asserter is an LLM agent rather than a curator.

papers.title: Bridging the Scientific Knowledge Gap and Reproducibility: A Survey of Provenance, Assertion and Evidence Ontologies
papers.venue_or_id: doi:10.1145/3701716.3715483; pmcid:PMC12376154 (Chhetri, Halchenko, Jarecka, Ghosh, Ray, Ng)
papers.core_idea: Reviews 23 ontologies split into 13 assertion/evidence ontologies (ECO, SIO, RDO, SEPIO, AMO, ARGO, EXPO, OBI, Nanopublication, SWAN, HOH, Evidence Ontology, EVI) and 10 provenance ontologies (RVO, PAV, OPMW, PROV, P-Plan, PMLM, NeuroBridge, HED, REPRODUCE-ME, PROPREO). Finds that provenance ontologies have converged on PROV but assertion/evidence ontologies have NOT converged: inconsistent terminology ('Argument' vs 'Assertion' vs 'Claim'), poor vocabulary reuse, and sustainability problems (several ontologies hard to locate or access).
papers.relevance: The most important negative result for this survey. There is no PROV-equivalent standard for claims and evidence. Anyone building a claim store today must pick a base (nanopub container + micropublication edge types + ECO evidence types + PROV derivation is the most defensible combination) and accept that no single off-the-shelf standard covers it. This paper is also the citation that confirms SEPIO's place in the landscape.

papers.title: ISA API: An open platform for interoperable life science experimental metadata
papers.core_idea: Programmatic implementation of the Investigation/Study/Assay metadata framework for describing experimental designs, samples, protocols, and assay outputs.
papers.relevance: The de facto data model behind many ELN integrations (eLabFTW/LISTER, DataPLANT ARCs). For a drug-discovery agent, ISA is the schema in which the experimental context of a claim (cell line, compound, dose, replicate structure) should be recorded, and it is what ARC WRROC fuses with computational provenance.

papers.title: Fact or Fiction: Verifying Scientific Claims (SciFact)
papers.core_idea: Introduces the scientific claim verification task and dataset: 1.4K expert-written claims paired with abstracts labelled SUPPORTS / REFUTES, plus annotated RATIONALE sentences justifying each label.
papers.relevance: Defines the minimal machine-checkable schema for verification status: a three-valued label plus the specific sentences that justify it. Any claim store should record the rationale spans, not just the verdict - a verdict without rationales cannot be re-audited when the model changes.

papers.title: MultiVerS: Improving scientific claim verification with weak supervision and full-document context
papers.core_idea: Jointly predicts the veracity label and selects rationale sentences using full-document context in a multitask setup, improving label-rationale consistency.
papers.relevance: Establishes that label and rationale must be produced jointly; storing them as independently-produced fields invites inconsistency between the verdict and its stated justification.

papers.title: Measuring Attribution in Natural Language Generation Models (AIS: Attributable to Identified Sources)
papers.core_idea: Defines the AIS predicate: a generated statement is attributable to a set of identified sources if a generic hearer would affirm 'according to these sources, <statement>'. Provides a two-stage human annotation pipeline (is the statement interpretable/decontextualised? then is it supported?).
papers.relevance: The cleanest formal definition of 'grounded'. Two design consequences for a claim store: (1) claims must be stored DECONTEXTUALISED (self-contained), because AIS is undefined for context-dependent fragments - this is the same requirement as the AIDA scheme; (2) attribution is a relation between a statement and a specific source set, so it must be stored as an edge with the source set pinned, not as a boolean on the claim.

papers.title: RARR: Researching and Revising What Language Models Say, Using Language Models
papers.core_idea: Retrofit Attribution using Research and Revision: post-hoc, model-agnostic pipeline that generates verification questions for an output, retrieves evidence, and minimally edits the text to be supported while preserving the original content as far as possible; reports attribution and preservation separately.
papers.relevance: The repair loop to run before a claim is committed to memory. The 'preservation' metric matters: an agent that rewrites its claim until it is trivially supported has destroyed the finding. Store both the pre-revision and post-revision claim plus the diff, so the revision itself is auditable.

papers.title: PURR: Efficiently Editing Language Model Hallucinations by Denoising Language Model Corruptions
papers.core_idea: Trains a compact editor by learning to undo deliberately corrupted (hallucinated) text, giving RARR-style attribution editing at far lower inference cost.
papers.relevance: Makes continuous, in-loop claim verification affordable on local hardware - relevant if the verification pass must run on every stored claim rather than only on final reports.

papers.title: Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations (ALCE)
papers.core_idea: First reproducible benchmark for automatic citation evaluation, scoring fluency, correctness, and citation quality decomposed into citation RECALL (is every statement supported by its citations) and citation PRECISION (is every citation actually relevant), computed with NLI models.
papers.relevance: Gives the two numbers that should be stored as machine-checkable quality fields on every agent-generated claim. Recall and precision are separable failure modes - an agent that cites everything scores high recall and terrible precision - so a single 'grounded' flag is insufficient.

papers.title: Attribute First, then Generate: Locally-attributable Grounded Text Generation
papers.core_idea: Decomposes generation into content selection, sentence planning, and sentence-by-sentence generation, so citations point to concise source SPANS rather than whole documents or paragraphs.
papers.relevance: Span-level attribution is what makes verification cheap enough to automate. A claim record should store the quoted span plus a character offset or fragment selector into a hashed source document, not a bare DOI.

papers.title: Model Internals-based Answer Attribution for Trustworthy Retrieval-Augmented Generation (MIRAGE)
papers.core_idea: Uses model internals (context-sensitivity of generated tokens) rather than the model's own self-report to attribute answer segments to context passages; motivated by self-citing LLMs referring to non-existent sources and failing to reflect actual context usage.
papers.relevance: Direct evidence that self-reported citations are not the same as actual evidence use. If a claim store records only what the agent said it used, it is recording a claim about provenance, not provenance. Where feasible, record an independent attribution signal (ablation- or internals-based).

papers.title: SelfCite: Self-Supervised Alignment for Context Attribution in Large Language Models
papers.core_idea: Defines a context-ablation reward: a citation is NECESSARY if removing the cited text changes the response, and SUFFICIENT if keeping only the cited text preserves it; uses this signal for best-of-N and preference optimisation without human annotation.
papers.relevance: Necessity and sufficiency are computable, storable, per-citation numbers. This is the most concrete recipe found for making 'is this claim actually grounded in this evidence' a machine-checkable field rather than a human judgement.

papers.title: PaperQA: Retrieval-Augmented Generative Agent for Scientific Research
papers.core_idea: A RAG agent over full-text scientific literature that performs iterative retrieval, evidence gathering with per-chunk relevance scoring, and answer synthesis with in-line provenance.
papers.relevance: The literature-grounding component that later AI-scientist systems (Robin, Kosmos) reuse. Its intermediate 'evidence' objects - scored, quoted, source-linked chunks - are exactly the kind of reusable intermediate result that should be persisted rather than discarded at the end of a query.

papers.title: Language agents achieve superhuman synthesis of scientific knowledge (PaperQA2)
papers.core_idea: A factuality-optimised literature agent evaluated against subject-matter experts on retrieval, summarisation, and contradiction detection over real literature tasks; also applied to generating cited encyclopedia-style articles.
papers.relevance: Two things matter for memory design: contradiction detection as an explicit first-class task (the store must be able to represent and surface contradictions between claims), and the demonstration that citation-grounded synthesis can be made reliable enough to be a memory-write path rather than only an output path.

papers.title: OpenScholar: Synthesizing Scientific Literature with Retrieval-augmented LMs
papers.core_idea: Retrieval-augmented LM over 45M open-access papers with an iterative self-feedback loop that critiques and repairs its own citation-backed answers; ships the ScholarQABench evaluation suite.
papers.relevance: Shows the self-feedback repair loop (generate, critique for unsupported statements, retrieve more, revise) working at literature scale - the RARR pattern instantiated inside a scientific agent.

papers.title: Autonomous chemical research with large language models (Coscientist)
papers.venue_or_id: Nature; doi:10.1038/s41586-023-06792-0; pmcid:PMC10733136 (Boiko, MacKnight, Kline, Gomes)
papers.core_idea: GPT-4-driven system that designs, plans and executes chemical experiments via a Planner plus modules for web search, documentation search, Python execution, and direct control of liquid-handling and cloud lab hardware.
papers.relevance: Storage model is essentially a working transcript plus generated code plus instrument output files. Intermediate results are reused only through the context window and the filesystem; there is no persistent, queryable claim or evidence store, so nothing is reusable across sessions. Representative of the 2023 state of the art and of the gap.

papers.title: Augmenting large language models with chemistry tools (ChemCrow)
papers.venue_or_id: Nature Machine Intelligence; doi:10.1038/s42256-024-00832-8; pmcid:PMC11116106 (Bran, Cox, Schilter, Baldassari, White, Schwaller)
papers.core_idea: ReAct-style LLM chemistry agent with 18 expert-designed tools spanning synthesis planning, reaction execution, safety checks and molecule property lookup.
papers.relevance: Memory is the ReAct scratchpad: thought/action/observation traces. Tool outputs are authoritative grounding (a real retrosynthesis engine, a real database), which is a cheap and effective hallucination control - but the grounding is not recorded in any durable, re-checkable structure once the episode ends.

papers.title: The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery
papers.venue_or_id: arXiv:2408.06292 (Lu, Lu, Lange, Foerster, Clune, Ha)
papers.core_idea: End-to-end pipeline: idea generation with a novelty check against Semantic Scholar, code execution, experiment iteration, LaTeX write-up, and an automated reviewer.
papers.relevance: Its persistent memory is an idea archive used for novelty deduplication plus per-experiment logs and notes. This is the clearest example of memory serving EXPLORATION (don't repeat yourself) rather than EPISTEMICS (know what you actually established, and how well).

papers.title: The AI Scientist-v2: Workshop-Level Automated Scientific Discovery via Agentic Tree Search
papers.core_idea: Replaces human-authored templates with an agentic tree search over experiment plans, managed by an experiment manager agent, plus a vision-language reviewer for figures.
papers.relevance: The search tree is itself a memory structure: nodes are experiment attempts with results. Storing the whole tree (including failed branches) is closer to a real lab notebook than a linear log, and is a good model for how a drug-discovery agent should retain negative results.

papers.title: Autonomous LLM-driven research from data to human-verifiable research papers (data-to-paper)
papers.core_idea: Guides interacting LLM agents through a stepwise research process while PROGRAMMATICALLY BACK-TRACING INFORMATION FLOW, so the produced manuscript is inherently verifiable: results, methods and data can be chained programmatically. Reports 80-90% recapitulation of peer-reviewed findings for simple goals, with human co-piloting needed as goal complexity rises.
papers.relevance: The most explicit prior attempt to make an AI-generated claim machine-traceable by construction. Its key trick - every number in the text is a handle into the analysis output that produced it, enforced by the framework rather than by the model's good behaviour - is directly transplantable to an agent claim store.

papers.title: Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist
papers.venue_or_id: Nature; pmid:42428019; pmcid:PMC13345588; preprint arXiv:2502.18864 (Gottweis, Weng, Tu, Natarajan et al., Google)
papers.core_idea: Gemini-based multi-agent system with Generation, Reflection, Ranking, Evolution, Proximity and Meta-review agents, coordinated by a supervisor over an asynchronous task queue; hypotheses compete in an Elo-rated tournament with debate-style pairwise comparison, and a proximity graph clusters related hypotheses.
papers.relevance: The most developed hypothesis memory in a deployed system: hypotheses persist as objects with reviews, Elo scores, and similarity-graph neighbours, and the meta-review agent feeds accumulated critique back into generation. Notably, the stored quantity is a PREFERENCE RANKING, not an evidence-grounded confidence - Elo measures which hypothesis wins debates, not which is supported by data. Good architecture, wrong uncertainty semantics for a claim store.

papers.title: AI-assisted Drug Re-purposing for Human Liver Fibrosis
papers.core_idea: Uses the AI co-scientist to propose repurposing candidates for liver fibrosis, then experimentally characterises them in a microfluidic human liver organoid (microHO) platform.
papers.relevance: A rare closed-loop case where agent-generated hypotheses were wet-lab validated. Illustrates the missing link in practice: the experimental outcome does not flow back into a structured store where the original hypothesis's verification status is updated.

papers.title: A multi-agent system for automating scientific discovery (Robin)
papers.venue_or_id: Nature; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10652-y; pmcid:PMC13346116; preprint arXiv:2505.13400 (Ghareeb, Rodriques, White et al., FutureHouse)
papers.core_idea: Integrates literature-search agents (Crow/Falcon, built on PaperQA-style retrieval) with a data-analysis agent (Finch) to run the full loop: hypothesis, experiment proposal, interpretation of experimental data, and refinement. Applied to dry AMD, it proposed ripasudil (a ROCK inhibitor) and identified ABCA1 upregulation as a mechanism.
papers.relevance: The strongest demonstration that literature evidence and newly generated experimental data can be fused in one agentic loop. Its memory is a set of generated reports and analysis notebooks passed between agents; the epistemic content (which claim, supported by which experiment, at what confidence) is embedded in prose rather than in a structured, queryable form.

papers.title: Kosmos: An AI Scientist for Autonomous Discovery
papers.venue_or_id: arXiv:2511.02824 (Mitchener, Narayanan, White, Rodrigues et al.)
papers.core_idea: Runs up to 12 hours over ~200 agent rollouts using a STRUCTURED WORLD MODEL as the shared memory between a data-analysis agent and a literature-search agent, enabling coherence across ~42,000 lines of code and ~1,500 papers per run. Cites every statement in its reports to either code or primary literature; independent scientists judged 79.4% of statements accurate.
papers.relevance: The closest existing system to the target design, and the strongest evidence that a structured shared memory - not a longer context window - is what buys long-horizon coherence. Also the most useful calibration point: even with universal citation-to-code-or-paper, ~1 in 5 statements was inaccurate. Citation presence is necessary but far from sufficient; the store needs an independent verification field, not just an attribution field.

papers.title: TxAgent: An AI Agent for Therapeutic Reasoning Across a Universe of Tools
papers.core_idea: Fine-tuned agent performing multi-step reasoning over 211 biomedical tools (ToolUniverse) for drug interactions, contraindications and patient-specific therapy, retrieving live biomedical knowledge at each step.
papers.relevance: Grounding-by-tool-call: each therapeutic assertion is backed by a specific FDA-label or database lookup rather than parametric memory. The tool-call trace IS the evidence chain and is the obvious thing to persist as a claim's provenance graph - but TxAgent treats it as transient reasoning rather than a durable record.

papers.title: Autonomous biomedical research with an artificial intelligence agent (Biomni)
papers.venue_or_id: Science; doi:10.1126/science.adz4351; pmid:42424436; preprint doi:10.1101/2025.05.30.656746, pmcid:PMC12157518 (Huang, Zhang, Wang, Roohani, Leskovec, Zitnik et al.)
papers.core_idea: General-purpose biomedical agent mapping the biomedical action space into a curated environment (Biomni-E1) of tools, databases and software, combining LLM reasoning with retrieval-augmented planning and code-based execution.
papers.relevance: Its persistent memory is an ENVIRONMENT (tools, datasets, code) rather than a knowledge store: procedural memory, well curated; epistemic memory, absent. Reuse of intermediate results happens through files on disk and re-execution, not through a claim index.

papers.title: STELLA: Self-Evolving LLM Agent for Biomedical Research
papers.core_idea: Multi-agent system that grows two persistent stores: an evolving Template Library of reasoning strategies and a dynamic 'Tool Ocean' expanded by a Tool Creation Agent, with performance improving as the libraries grow.
papers.relevance: Best current example of accumulating reusable procedural knowledge in biomedicine. Worth contrasting explicitly: template/tool memory improves HOW the agent works, and does nothing for WHAT the agent knows or how well it is justified.

papers.title: OriGene: A Self-Evolving Virtual Disease Biologist Automating Therapeutic Target Discovery
papers.core_idea: Self-evolving multi-agent system integrating 600+ specialised tools via MCP, acting as a virtual disease biologist for therapeutic target identification at scale.
papers.relevance: Shows the scale that drug-discovery agent tool ecosystems have reached, which sharpens the memory problem: with hundreds of tools producing heterogeneous outputs, an unstructured log is unusable and a typed claim/evidence store becomes mandatory rather than optional.

papers.title: PROV-AGENT: Unified Provenance for Tracking AI Agent Interactions in Agentic Workflows
papers.core_idea: Extends W3C PROV to agentic workflows so that agent actions, LLM calls, tool invocations and inter-agent message passing are captured in one provenance graph across federated/heterogeneous environments, explicitly to assess hallucination risk and trace error propagation when one agent's output becomes another's input.
papers.relevance: The direct answer to 'how do you apply classical scientific provenance to LLM agents'. Error propagation between agents is the dominant failure mode in multi-agent scientific systems, and a PROV graph over agent interactions makes it traceable after the fact.

papers.title: From Agent Traces to Trust: A Survey of Evidence Tracing and Execution Provenance in LLM Agents
papers.core_idea: Surveys how agent behaviour can be verified, debugged and audited beyond final-answer accuracy: which evidence supported each claim, whether tool calls were justified, how memory influenced later decisions, where failures originated.
papers.relevance: The most current framing of the audit requirements an agent memory store must satisfy. Useful as a requirements checklist.

papers.title: Autonomous Research Agents: A Survey of AI Scientists and the Verification Gap
papers.core_idea: Screens 125 works, includes 35, full-text codes 26 (24 runnable systems). Central finding: end-to-end AI-scientist systems produce paper-like manuscripts whose CLAIMS are much harder to verify than their CODE is to run.
papers.relevance: Names the gap this survey is about. Runnability has been solved reasonably well (containers, workflow engines, WRROC); claim verifiability has not. Design implication: verification infrastructure must attach to claims, not to code artefacts.

papers.title: ScientistOne: Towards Human-Level Autonomous Research via Chain-of-Evidence
papers.core_idea: Introduces Chain-of-Evidence (CoE), a verifiability framework requiring every claim to be traceable to its evidence source, and an end-to-end research system that maintains evidence chains BY CONSTRUCTION through literature review, experimentation and writing. Motivated by verifiability failures invisible to surface evaluation: fabricated citations, unreproducible scores, method descriptions diverging from implementation.
papers.relevance: The clearest 2026 statement of the 'by construction, not by post-hoc check' design principle for agent claim memory. Also names the specific failure mode - method text diverging from the code actually run - that post-hoc citation checking cannot catch.

papers.title: Toward Auditable AI Scientists: A Hypothesis Evolution Protocol for LLM Agents
papers.core_idea: Argues that in current agents, hypotheses, tests and belief updates are buried in unstructured logs with no mechanism for the agent or a human to audit the process; proposes an explicit protocol for recording hypothesis states and belief revisions over time.
papers.relevance: Directly addresses the 'verification status must be first-class' requirement, and specifically the temporal dimension: a claim's status is a trajectory of belief updates, each with a trigger and an evidence delta, not a single stored value.

papers.title: Evidence-Ledger Adjudication for Claim-Evidence Traceability
papers.core_idea: A workflow pairing each claim with an evidence packet, assigning a support relation, and routing unsupported/contradicted/mixed-evidence claims back to the author; benchmarked on 2,335 rows drawn from AVeriTeC, CLIMATE-FEVER and SciFact with gold labels hidden at prediction time.
papers.relevance: A concrete, evaluated schema for the verification-status field: {supported, contradicted, mixed, unsupported} plus the evidence packet, plus a routing decision. 'Mixed' is the important category most agent systems omit.

papers.title: From Fluent to Verifiable: Claim-Level Auditability for Deep Research Agents
papers.core_idea: Position paper arguing that as research generation becomes cheap, auditability becomes the bottleneck, and the dominant risk shifts from isolated factual errors to scientifically-styled outputs whose claim-evidence links are weak, missing or misleading.
papers.relevance: Frames the economics: the cost of verification, not generation, now governs. This is the strongest argument for investing in a machine-checkable claim store rather than better prose generation.

papers.title: Cited but Not Verified: Parsing and Evaluating Source Attribution in LLM Deep Research Agents
papers.core_idea: An AST-based parser extracts inline citations from LLM-generated Markdown reports at scale and evaluates source accessibility, relevance and factual consistency, rather than trusting self-citation or assuming RAG retrieval implies support.
papers.relevance: Practical tooling pattern for an automated verification pass over an agent's stored claims. Also documents that source ACCESSIBILITY (does the URL still resolve) is a distinct failure mode from relevance - an argument for storing content hashes and cached snapshots, not just URLs.

papers.title: LLM hallucinations in the wild: Large-scale evidence from non-existent citations
papers.core_idea: Audits 111 million references across 2.5 million papers on arXiv, bioRxiv, SSRN and PubMed Central; finds a sharp rise in non-existent references after widespread LLM adoption, conservatively estimating 146,932 hallucinated citations in 2025 alone, diffusely spread across many papers.
papers.relevance: Quantifies the scale of the citation-fabrication problem in the actual scientific record. Justifies making bibliographic existence-checking (Crossref/OpenAlex/PubMed resolution) a mandatory, non-optional gate on any claim written into an agent's memory.

papers.title: High Rates of Fabricated and Inaccurate References in ChatGPT-Generated Medical Content
papers.core_idea: Empirical audit finding high rates of fabricated and inaccurate references in LLM-generated medical content.
papers.relevance: Early biomedical-specific evidence that fabricated citations are the default failure mode in exactly the domain where drug-discovery agents operate; the baseline that grounding infrastructure must beat.

papers.title: The strength of clinical evidence is recoverable from language model representations but not from their stated grades
papers.core_idea: Compiles 45,134 clinical claims from six sources, harmonises 20,611 into a four-level evidence grade under three independent frameworks, and tests 22 open-weight models: evidence strength is linearly recoverable from internal activations but the models' STATED grades are unreliable.
papers.relevance: The single most important finding for the uncertainty field of a claim record. Do not store a model's self-reported confidence or self-assigned evidence grade as if it were an evidence grade. Store the objective study-design facts (design type, n, effect size, CI) and derive the grade with a rule, or use a probe - never the verbalised number.

papers.title: Knowing When Not to Answer: Abstention-Aware Scientific Reasoning
papers.core_idea: Decomposes scientific claims into minimal conditions, audits each condition against available evidence with NLI, and selectively supports, refutes, or ABSTAINS; argues unsupported conclusions are more harmful than abstention in scientific settings.
papers.relevance: Establishes abstention as a first-class stored status distinct from 'unsupported'. A claim store needs at minimum {supported, refuted, mixed, insufficient-evidence/abstain, unchecked} - conflating 'not yet checked' with 'not supported' is a common and dangerous modelling error.

papers.title: A step towards quantifying, modelling and exploring uncertainty in biomedical knowledge graphs
papers.core_idea: Automatically quantifies and models the uncertainty of facts in biomedical knowledge graphs from their textual supporting evidence using deep learning, attaching uncertainty to each fact.
papers.relevance: Concrete precedent for uncertainty-annotated edges in a biomedical KG - the substrate a drug-discovery agent would query. Confirms that uncertainty can be derived from the evidence text rather than asserted by the writer.

papers.title: Evaluating Agentic Bioinformatics through Function, Evidence, and Validation
papers.core_idea: Proposes the Function-Evidence-Validation (FEV) framework, treating the INSPECTABLE WORKFLOW TRAJECTORY - not the architecture or the final output - as the primary unit of analysis for agent accountability in biology.
papers.relevance: Argues for exactly the storage decision this survey recommends: persist the trajectory as a structured, inspectable object. Useful as an evaluation rubric for whatever claim store gets built.

papers.title: Inspectable AI for Science: A Research Object Approach to Generative AI Governance
papers.core_idea: Proposes AI-as-a-Research-Object (AI-RO): treat AI interactions as structured, inspectable research components, recording model configuration, prompts and outputs, drawing explicitly on Research Object theory and FAIR principles.
papers.relevance: The explicit bridge between the RO-Crate/FAIR tradition and LLM agents: the agent session itself becomes a crated, citable research artefact. This is the cleanest packaging answer for 'where does the agent's memory live on disk'.

papers.title: Traxia: A Framework for Verifiable, Agent-Native Scientific Publishing
papers.core_idea: Agent-native publishing framework in which every paper carries a reasoning trace, every claim carries a confidence interval, every agent has a cryptographically signed identity, and agents peer-review one another in a shared provenance model.
papers.relevance: An end-state design for claim records with signed authorship and per-claim uncertainty. Worth reading as a design source, though ambitious and not (as of this survey) an established standard - treat as a proposal rather than infrastructure.

papers.title: WorkflowHub: a registry for computational workflows
papers.venue_or_id: Scientific Data; doi:10.1038/s41597-025-04786-3; pmcid:PMC12095652 (Gustafsson, Wilkinson, Soiland-Reyes, Goble et al.)
papers.core_idea: A cross-engine registry (CWL, Nextflow, Snakemake, Galaxy, WDL) that stores workflows as Workflow RO-Crates with Bioschemas markup, mints DOIs, and links to community repositories.
papers.relevance: The findability layer for the 'method' half of a claim. A claim record should cite a registered, versioned, DOI-bearing workflow rather than an inline script.

papers.title: Applying the FAIR Principles to computational workflows
papers.venue_or_id: arXiv:2410.03490; published pmcid:PMC11850811 (Workflows Community Initiative FAIR Workflows Working Group)
papers.core_idea: Reinterprets each FAIR principle for workflows, distinguishing the workflow as a digital object from the workflow's execution and from the data it produces.
papers.relevance: Important conceptual distinction for a claim schema: plan, run, and result are three different entities with three different identifiers, and conflating them is the most common provenance modelling error.

papers.title: An Ecosystem of Services for FAIR Computational Workflows
papers.core_idea: Describes the interoperating service stack - WorkflowHub, RO-Crate, Bioschemas, workflow testing services - that makes FAIR workflows operational rather than aspirational.
papers.relevance: Shows what a mature FAIR infrastructure looks like when it works; the agent-claim equivalent does not yet exist and this is the closest model for what it should look like.

papers.title: Croissant: A Metadata Format for ML-Ready Datasets
papers.core_idea: A JSON-LD metadata format layering RecordSets and field-level semantics over Schema.org so datasets are discoverable, portable and loadable across ML frameworks; adopted by major dataset repositories and required by NeurIPS dataset tracks.
papers.relevance: The ML-side analogue of RO-Crate, and the same JSON-LD/Schema.org substrate, so the two compose. Relevant when an agent's evidence includes model training/eval datasets whose exact composition must be pinned.

papers.title: Evaluating FAIR-Compliance Through an Objective, Automated, Community-Governed Framework (FAIR Evaluator)
papers.core_idea: Software infrastructure for registering and executing machine-actionable tests of FAIR-metric compliance, letting communities select relevant metric subsets.
papers.relevance: Precedent for making a metadata quality property automatically testable rather than self-declared. The same architecture - registered, executable, versioned checks - is what a claim store needs for verification status.

papers.title: Rethinking Memory in LLM based Agents: Representations, Operations, and Emerging Topics
papers.core_idea: Categorises agent memory into parametric (in weights) and contextual (external, structured or unstructured), and defines six atomic operations: Consolidation, Updating, Indexing, Forgetting, Retrieval, Condensation.
papers.relevance: Gives the operational vocabulary. For a scientific claim store the two hardest operations are Updating (belief revision when new evidence arrives) and Forgetting (which in science means retraction/supersession with history preserved, never deletion).

papers.title: Memory for Autonomous LLM Agents: Mechanisms, Evaluation, and Emerging Frontiers
papers.core_idea: Survey covering 2022-early 2026 that formalises agent memory as a write-manage-read loop and reviews designs, implementations and evaluation.
papers.relevance: Current general-purpose reference point; useful mainly to show that the general agent-memory literature optimises for recall and coherence, and essentially never for evidential warrant - the scientific requirement is a distinct research problem.

papers.title: Bridging note: SEPIO (Scientific Evidence and Provenance Information Ontology)
papers.core_idea: Monarch Initiative OWL ontology providing a domain-agnostic core model of assertions, the evidence lines that support them, and the provenance of both, plus a UML-like closed-world information model for building application schemas. Distinguishes an Assertion from the Evidence Line(s) supporting it, each with its own provenance and evidence-type.
papers.relevance: The most directly on-target ontology for the central question, and the model that separates assertion from evidence-line most cleanly. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: I verified SEPIO exists as an active Monarch Initiative artefact and that it is one of the 13 assertion/evidence ontologies catalogued in the 2025 Chhetri et al. survey, but I did NOT locate a peer-reviewed SEPIO paper with a verifiable venue and year. Treat the ontology as verified and any specific SEPIO publication citation as UNVERIFIED.

methods.name: Nanopublication container (assertion / provenance / publication-info named graphs) + content-addressed identifier
methods.mechanism: Store each claim as three linked RDF named graphs: the assertion itself (ideally one atomic triple or one AIDA-style sentence), a provenance graph (what evidence, what derivation, what method), and a publication-info graph (who asserted it, when, license, confidence). Give the whole bundle a content-hash-derived identifier (Trusty URI pattern) so it is immutable and tamper-evident. Supersession and retraction are new nanopubs pointing at the old one, never edits.
methods.strengths: Atomic granularity means provenance attaches per-claim, not per-document. Immutability plus hashing gives free deduplication, integrity checking, and stable cross-session identity. Millions of life-science nanopubs exist, so vocabularies and tooling are mature. Retraction-by-new-record preserves the full belief history, which is what auditability requires.
methods.weaknesses: RDF/SPARQL is a real skills and ergonomics cost for an agent codebase. Atomicity is awkward for genuinely compound scientific claims ('X reduces Y in Z model but not in W'), forcing either lossy decomposition or heavy reification. Immutability means the store grows monotonically and needs a materialised current-belief view on top.
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local. Oxigraph (Rust, embeddable, macOS-native) or Apache Jena/RDFLib for the triplestore; the nanopub Python library handles signing and trusty-URI hashing; no network needed unless you publish to the public nanopub network. Hundreds of thousands of claims fit comfortably on a laptop.

methods.name: Micropublication-style typed argumentation graph (supports / challenges / qualifies, statement-cites-statement)
methods.mechanism: Model claims as nodes and evidence as TYPED EDGES to other claims, data entities, and method specifications. Include negative edge types (challenges, contradicts) and qualifying edges. Allow a statement in one artefact to cite an individual statement in another, and compute transitive closure from a claim down to its supporting data and methods.
methods.strengths: Directly answers 'what does this claim ultimately rest on' as a graph query. Representing disagreement is native, so refuted claims and contradictory literature are storable rather than silently dropped - critical in drug discovery where a target's evidence base is usually mixed. Transitive closure lets an agent decide whether a cached claim is still safe to reuse after an upstream retraction.
methods.weaknesses: Edge-type taxonomy is a design burden and the field has not converged (the 2025 ontology survey found 'Argument' vs 'Assertion' vs 'Claim' used inconsistently across 13 ontologies). Requires disciplined extraction: an LLM asked to emit typed edges will over-produce 'supports'. Graph grows fast and needs pruning/summarisation policies.
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local. Either the same RDF store (OWL 2 as in the original micropublications implementation) or a plain property graph in SQLite/DuckDB/NetworkX if you do not need OWL reasoning. For most agent use cases a typed property graph is sufficient and far cheaper than OWL.

methods.name: ECO / SEPIO evidence typing on every evidence edge
methods.mechanism: Every evidence link carries a controlled-vocabulary term for the KIND of evidence (direct assay, high-throughput screen, computational prediction, sequence similarity, author statement, curator inference) and, separately, the ASSERTION METHOD (manual vs automatic, and which agent/model).
methods.strengths: Makes 'this is supported' interpretable: an agent can weight a direct binding assay above a text-mined author statement without any bespoke logic. The type/method split is exactly the distinction needed when the asserter is an LLM. ECO is a maintained, widely used community resource with GO adoption.
methods.weaknesses: Requires the writer to classify evidence correctly; an LLM will do this inconsistently without few-shot anchoring and validation against the ontology. ECO is biocuration-flavoured and does not cover every drug-discovery evidence type (e.g. specific ADMET or docking evidence classes need local extension).
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local. Download ECO as OWL/OBO and load into a local ontology lookup (pronto, owlready2, or a simple term table); term validation is a dictionary lookup, no service dependency.

methods.name: EVI-style defeasible evidence graph over computations
methods.mechanism: Treat every result and every component of evidence as a DEFEASIBLE assertion supported by a DAG of the computations, software, data, and agents that produced it. Run inference rules over the DAG to derive current support status; new evidence can overturn a previously derived conclusion without any record being deleted.
methods.strengths: The only surveyed model where 'this claim's status can change' is a first-class semantic rather than an application-level hack. Scales across arbitrarily deep computation networks, so a claim that depends on a claim that depends on a pipeline output is handled uniformly. FAIRSCAPE proves the service architecture works on real biomedical analytics.
