methods.weaknesses: Defeasible reasoning in OWL is non-standard and the tooling is thin; you will likely reimplement the rule evaluation. Deep DAGs make status recomputation expensive if done naively - needs incremental/dirty-marking evaluation. Small research community, sustainability risk.
methods.local_feasibility: Feasible locally with effort. The EVI ontology and FAIRSCAPE are open; the DAG plus rule evaluation can be reimplemented in Python over SQLite/NetworkX in a few hundred lines if full OWL semantics are not required. Recommended as a design pattern to copy rather than a dependency to adopt.

methods.name: W3C PROV + Workflow Run RO-Crate as the derivation record attached to each claim
methods.mechanism: Every quantitative claim points to a WRROC crate capturing the workflow plan (prospective) and the run (retrospective): parameter values, input/output file checksums, container image digests, tool versions, start/end times, and responsible agents. Choose the profile by granularity need - Process Run Crate for single tool calls, Workflow Run Crate for pipelines, Provenance Run Crate for step-level detail.
methods.strengths: An interoperable, cross-engine standard already implemented in six workflow systems, so provenance from Nextflow, Snakemake, CWL and Galaxy runs is comparable. Makes re-derivation a machine action. RO-Crate's JSON-LD manifest is human-readable and diffable, which matters for review. Aligns to PROV so it composes with PROV-AGENT-style agent-interaction provenance.
methods.weaknesses: Only covers what runs inside a workflow engine; ad-hoc notebook analysis and LLM reasoning steps fall outside unless separately instrumented. Crates can get large if outputs are embedded rather than referenced. Says nothing about whether the result is CORRECT - it records derivation, not warrant.
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local and mature. ro-crate-py for authoring; Nextflow, Snakemake, Galaxy and StreamFlow can emit WRROC directly; crates are plain directories on disk. This is the lowest-risk, highest-value piece to adopt first.

methods.name: ISA / ARC for wet-lab experimental context, fused with computational provenance
methods.mechanism: Record the experimental design in Investigation/Study/Assay tables with ontology-annotated terms (cell line, compound, concentration, replicate structure, instrument), and link those assay outputs into the same crate as the computational provenance (the ARC Workflow Run RO-Crate approach).
methods.strengths: The only surveyed approach that closes the bench-to-compute provenance gap in one queryable object. ISA is established with a maintained API and broad ELN integration (eLabFTW via LISTER, DataPLANT ARCs, Chemotion). Essential for drug-discovery claims, which are almost never purely computational.
methods.weaknesses: ISA tables are verbose and tedious to populate; automatic extraction from free-text protocols is still an active research problem. Ontology annotation quality is the binding constraint on interoperability, and agents are mediocre annotators without validation.
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local. ISA API (Python) plus a local ELN (eLabFTW and Chemotion both self-host) plus local ontology term files. Realistic for a laptop-scale setup; the human effort, not the compute, is the cost.

methods.name: Attribution gate: AIS-style decontextualised claims + sentence-level span citation + ablation-based necessity/sufficiency scores
methods.mechanism: Before writing any claim to memory: (1) rewrite it decontextualised and atomic (AIDA / AIS interpretability precondition); (2) attach span-level quotations with offsets into content-hashed source documents, not document-level citations; (3) compute per-citation NECESSITY (does removing the cited span change the answer) and SUFFICIENCY (does the cited span alone reproduce it) via context ablation, and store both numbers; (4) compute ALCE-style citation recall and precision.
methods.strengths: Turns 'is this grounded' into stored numbers rather than a boolean or a vibe. Necessity/sufficiency are self-supervised - no human annotation needed. Span-level offsets make later re-verification cheap. Decontextualisation is also what makes the claim reusable in a different context months later.
methods.weaknesses: Ablation scoring costs extra forward passes per citation, which is significant at scale. Necessity/sufficiency measure whether the MODEL used the source, not whether the source is TRUE or the inference valid; a confidently wrong inference from a correctly-cited span scores perfectly. Decontextualisation rewrites can subtly change meaning.
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local with an open-weight model. Ablation scoring needs a local model you can call repeatedly (Llama/Qwen class runs on Apple silicon with MLX or llama.cpp); NLI-based ALCE scoring runs on a small local cross-encoder. Budget the extra inference cost.

methods.name: RARR-style retrofit research-and-revise loop with preserved pre/post claim diff
methods.mechanism: For each drafted claim, generate verification questions, retrieve evidence, and minimally edit the claim so it becomes attributable while maximising preservation of the original content. Store the original claim, the revised claim, the diff, the questions asked, and the evidence retrieved.
methods.strengths: Model-agnostic and post-hoc, so it works over any generator. Reporting attribution and preservation separately catches the degenerate case where the agent 'fixes' a claim by hollowing it out. PURR shows a distilled compact editor makes this cheap enough to run on every claim.
methods.weaknesses: Retrieval-bound: it can only attribute to what it finds, so a true but poorly-indexed claim gets wrongly revised or dropped. Encourages regression toward well-documented, unsurprising statements - exactly the wrong pressure for a discovery agent. Does not detect fabricated but retrievable-sounding reasoning.
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local if your evidence corpus is local (a downloaded PubMed/PMC OA subset, ChEMBL, internal reports). Local vector index (FAISS, sqlite-vec, LanceDB) plus a local editor model. Fully offline operation is realistic for a fixed corpus.

methods.name: Bibliographic existence gate (Crossref / OpenAlex / PubMed resolution + accessibility check)
methods.mechanism: Every citation in a stored claim must resolve to a real record in at least one authoritative index before the claim is committed. Store the resolved canonical ID (DOI/PMID/PMCID), the retrieval timestamp, and a content hash or cached copy of the specific passage cited.
methods.strengths: Catches the dominant, highest-embarrassment failure mode outright and cheaply. The 2026 large-scale audit (146,932 estimated hallucinated citations in 2025 alone across arXiv/bioRxiv/SSRN/PMC) makes this non-negotiable. Caching the passage defends against link rot, which the deep-research-agent attribution work shows is a distinct failure mode from irrelevance.
methods.weaknesses: Existence is a very low bar - a real paper cited for a claim it does not make passes this gate. Must be paired with span-level support checking. Index coverage gaps (preprints, patents, internal reports, non-English) cause false rejections.
methods.local_feasibility: Needs network for the initial resolution, then fully local. A local OpenAlex or PubMed baseline snapshot makes it fully offline; both are downloadable. Cached passages live on disk with the claim.

methods.name: Verification status as a separate, dated, agent-attributed attestation object
methods.mechanism: Never store a boolean 'verified' on the claim. Store attestations: {claim_id, checker_identity_and_version, check_type, corpus_snapshot_id, timestamp, verdict in {supported, refuted, mixed, insufficient-evidence/abstain, unchecked}, rationale_spans, score}. Multiple attestations accumulate; an attestation expires when its corpus snapshot or checker version is superseded.
methods.strengths: Makes verification re-auditable and re-runnable. Handles the fact that the same claim can be supported against one corpus snapshot and refuted against a later one. Multiple independent checkers can disagree, which is information, not a bug. Mirrors the nanopublished-review pattern shown to work in the nanopublication field study.
methods.weaknesses: Storage and query complexity: the 'current status' of a claim becomes a computed view over attestations with precedence rules you must define. Risk of attestation spam from cheap automated checkers drowning out expensive human review - needs checker weighting.
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local and simple. A second table in SQLite/DuckDB keyed on claim_id, with a materialised current-status view. This is the cheapest high-value structural decision in the whole design.

methods.name: Three-field uncertainty (statistical / evidence-grade / agent-confidence) with abstention
methods.mechanism: Store uncertainty as three orthogonal fields, never one number: (1) STATISTICAL - effect size, CI, p, n, test, multiple-comparison correction, extracted from the analysis output; (2) EVIDENCE GRADE - derived by RULE from study-design facts and the ECO evidence type, not asserted by the model; (3) AGENT CONFIDENCE - the model's own estimate, stored explicitly LABELLED as unreliable and never used as the evidence grade. Add an explicit abstain/insufficient-evidence status distinct from unsupported.
methods.strengths: Prevents the most common and most dangerous collapse, where a model's verbalised 0.9 gets treated as evidential strength. The 2026 clinical-evidence-strength study is direct empirical support: evidence strength is recoverable from model activations but stated grades are unreliable. Rule-derived grades are reproducible and auditable; verbalised ones are not.
methods.weaknesses: Requires reliably extracting statistical facts from analysis output, which is easy for your own pipelines and hard for literature-derived claims. Grading rules are domain-specific and need curation. Three fields is more schema for the agent to fill correctly.
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local. Field (1) comes from your own analysis code, so instrument the pipeline to emit it structurally rather than parsing it back out of prose. Field (2) is a rule table. Field (3) is free. A local probe over open-weight activations is optional and feasible on Apple silicon.

methods.name: Structured shared world model between agents (Kosmos pattern) rather than transcript passing
methods.mechanism: Maintain a single structured store - entities, findings, open questions, evidence links - that all sub-agents read from and write to, instead of passing prose summaries or growing a single context window. Every statement in any downstream report must cite either a code artefact or a primary source in the store.
methods.strengths: Empirically the mechanism that buys long-horizon coherence: Kosmos sustained ~200 rollouts, ~42,000 lines of code and ~1,500 papers per run without losing the objective, which context-window approaches cannot do. Also makes intermediate results reusable across agents by construction, and gives a natural insertion point for the claim schema.
methods.weaknesses: Kosmos still reported only 79.4% statement accuracy despite universal citation-to-code-or-literature, so a shared world model plus mandatory citation does NOT get you to reliability - it gets you to auditability. Concurrency and write-conflict handling between parallel agents is real engineering. Schema rigidity can constrain what the agent is able to express.
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local. SQLite (WAL mode) or DuckDB handles the concurrency for laptop-scale parallelism; the world model is just a schema plus read/write tools exposed to the agents. This is the most immediately actionable architectural pattern from the 2025-2026 agent literature.

methods.name: Programmatic information back-tracing (data-to-paper pattern): every number is a handle
methods.mechanism: Enforce at the framework level that every quantitative statement in any generated output is not a literal but a reference to a specific analysis output cell, which in turn references the code and the input data. The chain is constructed by the framework, so the model cannot produce an untraceable number even if it wants to.
methods.strengths: By-construction traceability beats post-hoc checking: it structurally prevents the ScientistOne-identified failure of method text diverging from the implementation, and prevents transcription errors between analysis and prose. Verified in practice at 80-90% recapitulation of peer-reviewed findings for simple research goals.
methods.weaknesses: Only covers quantities derived from the agent's own analysis, not claims drawn from literature or from reasoning. Constrains the writing step, which reduces expressiveness. Degrades as goal complexity rises - the original authors report human co-piloting becomes critical.
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local; it is a framework discipline, not a service. Implementable as a templating layer over analysis outputs plus a validator that rejects any output containing a bare numeral not bound to a handle.

methods.name: Skill / tool / procedural memory (Biomni environment, STELLA template library and tool ocean, OriGene MCP tool graph)
methods.mechanism: Persist reusable procedures: validated tool wrappers, reasoning templates, successful analysis recipes, with retrieval by task similarity and refinement from execution feedback.
methods.strengths: Demonstrably improves capability and efficiency, and prevents rediscovering the same analysis. Well supported by 2025-2026 systems in biomedicine specifically. Cheap to implement and immediately useful.
methods.weaknesses: Solves a completely different problem from the one asked about. Procedural memory records HOW the agent works; it carries no evidence, no uncertainty, and no verification status about WHAT the agent has established. Including it in a 'memory' design without a separate claim store is the most common category error in current systems, and it can actively hurt: a confidently reused recipe propagates its embedded assumptions silently.
methods.local_feasibility: Fully local and easy. Skills as files plus a vector index; MCP servers for tool exposure. Adopt it, but keep it in a separate namespace from the claim store and never let a skill's success rate be read as evidence for a scientific claim.

methods.name: Recommended local stack for a macOS laptop agent claim store
methods.mechanism: Layer it: (a) RO-Crate directories on disk as the durable artefact packaging, one crate per run, WRROC profile where a workflow engine is involved; (b) SQLite or DuckDB holding claims, evidence edges, attestations, and the three uncertainty fields, with claim IDs as content hashes; (c) a local vector index (sqlite-vec, LanceDB or FAISS) over decontextualised claim text and cached evidence spans for retrieval; (d) optionally Oxigraph or RDFLib exporting the same content as nanopub-shaped JSON-LD/RDF for interchange; (e) a local open-weight model for NLI support-checking and ablation scoring; (f) a cached corpus snapshot (PMC OA subset, ChEMBL, internal reports) so verification is reproducible against a pinned evidence base.
methods.strengths: Every layer is offline-capable and file-based, so the whole store is backup-able, diffable, and git-trackable. Relational core keeps queries fast and the schema honest; RDF export preserves interoperability without forcing SPARQL on the application code. Corpus pinning makes attestations meaningful over time.
methods.weaknesses: Dual representation (relational + RDF) risks drift unless one is authoritative and the other is generated. Corpus snapshots are large (PMC OA full text is on the order of tens of GB). Local NLI/ablation models are weaker than frontier models, so verification quality is bounded by what fits on the machine.
methods.local_feasibility: Yes - this is specifically designed to run fully locally on a macOS laptop with no external service. SQLite/DuckDB, sqlite-vec/LanceDB, Oxigraph, ro-crate-py, and MLX or llama.cpp for local inference are all native or trivially installable on Apple silicon. Network is needed only for initial corpus download and for bibliographic existence checks unless an OpenAlex/PubMed snapshot is held locally.

takeaways: There is no PROV-equivalent standard for claims and evidence, and this is the field's central unsolved problem. The 2025 survey of 23 ontologies (Chhetri et al., doi:10.1145/3701716.3715483) found provenance ontologies have converged on W3C PROV, while the 13 assertion/evidence ontologies have NOT: they use 'Argument', 'Assertion' and 'Claim' inconsistently, reuse each other's vocabularies poorly, and several are hard even to locate. Anyone building a claim store today must compose one rather than adopt one.

The best available composition is: nanopublication CONTAINER (assertion / provenance / pubinfo named graphs, content-addressed identifier) + micropublication EDGE TYPES (supports, challenges, qualifies; statement cites statement; transitive closure to data and method) + ECO/SEPIO EVIDENCE TYPES on each edge + W3C PROV / Workflow Run RO-Crate for the DERIVATION + EVI-style DEFEASIBILITY so status can be overturned. Each of these four pieces is independently mature; the composition is what nobody has standardised.

Verification status must be a separate, dated, agent-attributed attestation object, never a boolean field on the claim. Store {checker identity and version, check type, corpus snapshot, timestamp, verdict, rationale spans, score} and compute current status as a view. A claim can be supported against one corpus snapshot and refuted against a later one; a boolean cannot represent that, and cannot be re-audited when the checker changes.

The verdict vocabulary needs at least five values: supported, refuted, mixed, insufficient-evidence/abstain, and unchecked. Conflating 'not yet checked' with 'not supported' is a common and dangerous modelling error, and the 2026 abstention work argues explicitly that in scientific settings an unsupported conclusion is more harmful than an abstention. Evidence-ledger adjudication work shows 'mixed' is a real and frequent category that most agent systems omit entirely.

Uncertainty must be three orthogonal fields, never one number: statistical (effect size, CI, n, test), evidence grade (derived by RULE from study design and evidence type), and agent confidence (stored explicitly labelled as unreliable). The 2026 study over 45,134 clinical claims found evidence strength is linearly recoverable from open-weight model ACTIVATIONS but the models' STATED grades are unreliable - so never let a model's verbalised confidence occupy the evidence-grade field.

Citation presence is not verification. Kosmos cites every statement in its reports to either code or primary literature and still had only 79.4% of statements judged accurate by independent scientists. Grounding infrastructure buys AUDITABILITY, not correctness. A claim store must therefore carry an independent verification field alongside the attribution field, and must not treat 'has a citation' as evidence of anything except checkability.

Self-reported citations are not evidence of actual evidence use. MIRAGE and SelfCite both show self-citing LLMs cite non-existent sources and fail to reflect real context usage. Where you can afford it, store an INDEPENDENT attribution signal - context-ablation necessity and sufficiency scores are self-supervised, need no human annotation, and are the most concrete recipe found for making groundedness a stored number rather than a claim about a claim.

Bibliographic existence checking against Crossref/OpenAlex/PubMed must be a hard, non-optional gate. The 2026 audit of 111 million references across 2.5 million papers found a sharp post-LLM rise in non-existent references, conservatively estimating 146,932 hallucinated citations in 2025 alone. Existence is a low bar - a real paper cited for a claim it does not make passes it - so pair it with span-level support checking.

Store spans and content hashes, not URLs and DOIs alone. Deep-research-agent attribution work identifies source ACCESSIBILITY (does it still resolve) as a failure mode distinct from relevance and from factual consistency. Cache the cited passage with a character offset or fragment selector; the 2026 fragment-level FAIRness work extends ISA to sub-file data references for exactly this reason.

Attribution checks are only meaningful against a pinned corpus snapshot. Store the snapshot identifier in the attestation. Without it, re-running a verification later against a different corpus silently changes the meaning of the recorded verdict.

Claims must be stored DECONTEXTUALISED and atomic. This is the shared requirement of the AIDA scheme (Atomic, Independent, Declarative, Absolute) from the nanopublication line and of the AIS definition's interpretability precondition. It is the cheapest possible normalisation step, it makes each claim individually checkable, citable and retractable, and it is what makes a claim still usable when retrieved six months later in a different context.

Negative results, refutations and contradictions must be first-class. Micropublications provide challenge edges; PaperQA2 treats contradiction detection as an explicit task; EVI makes overturning a claim a semantic operation. Almost every current agent memory stores only successes, which for drug discovery - where the evidence base for any target is genuinely mixed - produces a systematically optimistic store.

Retraction means supersession with history preserved, never deletion. The nanopublication pattern (immutable records plus a separate retraction record) is the right model. Combined with transitive closure over the evidence graph, this lets an agent mechanically ask whether a cached claim is still safe to reuse after something upstream was retracted - which is the whole point of storing the graph.

Separate plan, run and result as three distinct entities with three distinct identifiers. The FAIR-for-workflows working group makes this explicit and it is the most common provenance modelling error. A claim references a result; the result references a run; the run references a plan. Collapsing any two makes re-derivation ambiguous.

Traceability by construction beats post-hoc checking. data-to-paper enforces at the framework level that every number in the output is a handle into the analysis that produced it, and ScientistOne's Chain-of-Evidence maintains evidence chains by construction. Post-hoc citation checking cannot catch the failure both target: method text that diverges from the code actually run.

A structured shared world model, not a bigger context window, is what buys long-horizon coherence. Kosmos sustained ~200 rollouts, ~42,000 lines of code and ~1,500 papers per run on this basis. This is also the natural insertion point for the claim schema: make the world model BE the claim store rather than bolting a claim store on beside it.

Do not mistake procedural memory for epistemic memory. Biomni's curated environment, STELLA's template library and tool ocean, and OriGene's 600+ MCP tools are genuine advances in accumulating reusable HOW-TO knowledge, and they carry zero information about what has been established or how well. Keep the skill store and the claim store in separate namespaces, and never let a recipe's success rate be read as evidence for a scientific conclusion.

Current AI-scientist systems store transcripts, code, files and rankings - not claims. Coscientist keeps a working transcript plus generated code; ChemCrow keeps a ReAct scratchpad; The AI Scientist keeps an idea archive for novelty deduplication plus per-run logs; Co-Scientist keeps hypotheses with Elo tournament scores (a PREFERENCE ranking, not an evidence-grounded confidence); TxAgent's tool-call trace is the evidence chain but is treated as transient. Kosmos and data-to-paper are the two closest to the target, and neither exposes a queryable, defeasible claim-evidence store that survives the run.

The economics have inverted: generation is cheap, verification is the bottleneck. This is the core argument of the 2026 claim-level auditability position paper and the finding of the AI-scientist verification-gap survey - runnability of code has largely been solved by containers, workflow engines and WRROC, while verifiability of claims has not. Investment should go into the claim store, not into better prose.

The whole recommended stack runs fully locally on a macOS laptop with no external service: RO-Crate directories on disk for artefacts, SQLite or DuckDB for claims/edges/attestations with content-hash IDs, sqlite-vec or LanceDB for retrieval, Oxigraph or RDFLib for nanopub-shaped RDF export, a local open-weight model via MLX or llama.cpp for NLI and ablation scoring, and a pinned local corpus snapshot (PMC OA subset, ChEMBL, internal reports). Network is needed only for initial corpus download and bibliographic resolution, and even those can be made offline with an OpenAlex or PubMed snapshot.

Adoption order if building this: (1) emit WRROC crates for every pipeline run - lowest risk, highest immediate value, standard already exists; (2) add the attestation table with the five-valued verdict - cheapest high-value structural decision; (3) enforce decontextualised atomic claims with span-level citations and a hard existence gate; (4) add typed evidence edges and ECO evidence types; (5) add defeasible status recomputation over the evidence DAG last, since it is the piece with the least mature tooling.

Two caveats on this survey's coverage. SEPIO is verified as an active Monarch Initiative artefact and appears among the 13 assertion/evidence ontologies catalogued in the 2025 survey, but I did not locate a peer-reviewed SEPIO paper with a verifiable venue and year - treat any specific SEPIO citation as UNVERIFIED. Separately, several relevant ELN and metadata papers surfaced in search (LabIMotion, LISTER/eLabFTW, DataPLANT ARC integration, Chemotion BFO knowledge graph, FAIRshake, FAIR-Checker) whose publication years I could not confirm from the search results; they are described in the methods section but deliberately omitted from the paper list rather than cited with a guessed year.
